In this essay
  1. I. Two Similar Questions, Two Opposite Answers
  2. II. A New Technique with Real Competitive Results
  3. III. A Boundary Drawn Only When It Is Crossed
  4. IV. A Safety Rationale and an Incomplete Record
  5. V. Another Reason Given at the Time
  6. VI. For Another Innovation, the Rules Had Already Left a Door Open
  7. VII. A Principle Emerging from the Cases
  8. VIII. A Line That Was Never Written Down

I. Two Similar Questions, Two Opposite Answers

Two developments had almost the same shape.

In one, someone invented a new long-jump technique: the forward somersault. It was banned.

In the other, someone introduced a new material into pole vaulting: the fibreglass pole. It was not banned, and all the records it produced were retained.

Both were new things appearing within the sport, capable of improving performance. Both provoked controversy and were challenged as unfair. Yet the construct gave opposite answers: prohibition for one, admission for the other.

The previous two essays concerned the silence of the rules. High-jump rules did not prescribe how to clear the bar, so the flop entered that silence and survived. Shot-put rules did not prescribe the glide or the rotation, so the two techniques coexisted within that silence for more than half a century, since the 1970s. This essay asks when that silence ends. A construct cannot remain silent about everything forever. At some point it must speak. By comparing these opposite outcomes, we will try to locate the boundary between speaking and remaining silent.

The comparison is not arbitrary. The cases resemble one another in several important respects yet have opposite outcomes: both belong to athletics, promise improved performances, and provoke debate about fairness and safety. But this is not a controlled experiment eliminating every other difference. It helps identify a question that a safety debate can obscure: whether an innovation is still understood as part of the same event. Following that question brings the essay to one word: definition.

One point should be clear at the outset. Saying “for safety” does not fully explain the opposite outcomes. Contemporary reporting raised both possible neck injury and whether somersaulting remained within the spirit of long jumping. The accessible material does not supply complete statistics with which to assess the risk. That does not establish that decision-makers never considered safety or that it was merely a pretext. This essay concentrates on the other reason already present in the discussion: whether an innovation crossed the event's understanding of itself.

This essay and the previous two thus form a complete sequence. They concerned the silence of the rules; this one concerns its endpoint. A construct cannot remain silent about everything. It has a limit beyond which it must speak. But reading the rules cannot tell us where that limit lies, because the rules are precisely what remain silent beyond it. We can only infer the boundary's position by observing when the silence breaks. The somersault made the construct speak; fibreglass did not. Together, they mark the line.

II. A New Technique with Real Competitive Results

In 1974, Delamere used the somersault long jump in major American collegiate competition.

Sports Illustrated's report of 29 July 1974 said that he used the technique at the NCAA championships in Austin without reaching the final. Three weeks earlier, at the Pacific-8 meet, he had jumped 25 feet 6¾ inches with it, tying Olympic champion Williams. The same report gave Delamere's best wind-assisted jump using a conventional technique as 25 feet 9½ inches.

This was therefore no circus stunt. With a forward somersault, he matched an Olympic champion's performance. The technique genuinely worked.

That must be established first, because it determines the nature of the entire case. If the somersault had merely been an acrobatic trick that produced short jumps, banning it would hardly matter. The construct would simply have disposed of a harmless oddity, without any real question of boundaries. But this was different. It matched an Olympic champion's performance and was thought to be far from its limit. Precisely because it could really produce distance, banning it was a consequential decision the construct had to weigh. The more effective a thing is, the greater the significance of prohibiting it. The somersault was highly effective.

Nor was Delamere alone. The same 1974 report identified Nielsen of the University of Iowa as an early demonstrator. The rotation had improved his personal best to 22 feet 6 inches. It reported that he showed the technique to Lagerqvist, after which West Germany's Stierle adopted it and reached 7.5 metres. By mid-1974, according to the article, demand for information suggested that several hundred people, mostly of school age, were experimenting with it.

A circulating error must immediately be corrected. Quande does not belong on the list of somersault long-jump practitioners. The available record places him in the high-jump story before Fosbury: a Montana high jumper who experimented earlier with backward clearance. Essay 8 discussed him. Inserting him into the somersault long jump of 1974 is a later error repeated from one account to another.

The contemporary argument for the technique's potential was mechanical, not merely visual. Sports Illustrated's 1974 article summarised Ecker's reasoning: the somersault exploited forward rotation rather than resisting it; the tucked body reduced drag; and it might allow a faster take-off at a more favourable angle. Delamere himself told the magazine he believed that once his injury healed and his technique improved, he could reach twenty-eight feet.

A larger claim requires caution. One popular account suggests that the somersault long jump would very likely have broken thirty feet. Later commentary repeatedly invokes that possibility, but it was never demonstrated in competition and should not be exaggerated. Modern summaries and popular physics accounts repeat thirty feet as a possibility, yet it remains speculation resting on theory and simulation, not a result achieved under ratifiable conditions. The accurate statement is that the technique could genuinely produce very long jumps and matched an Olympic champion's performance. Thirty feet was a projection, not an event that happened.

Separating these matters is important because they are often conflated. A technique is banned, and its potential achievement is a projection. Put those facts together and the story easily becomes one of a construct banning a technique that could have exceeded thirty feet, as though that distance were a definite achievement killed by prohibition. In fact, thirty feet never happened. It existed only in simulation and conjecture. The construct banned a technique that could already match an Olympic champion and appeared to have further potential. It did not ban an accomplished thirty-foot jump, because no such accomplishment existed. Exaggerating what was prohibited is no more accurate history than understating it.

III. A Boundary Drawn Only When It Is Crossed

The technique was banned. The process demonstrates the proposition in this essay's title.

Begin with the rule text, which is clear. Later IAAF and World Athletics rules, continuing to the present, explicitly make a long-jump attempt a failure if the athlete employs any form of somersault during the run-up or take-off. This wording appears in the current World Athletics Technical Rules and shows clear continuity with earlier IAAF language.

The 1974 NCAA rules already contained a provision prohibiting somersaults in an attempt. On the IAAF side, it is not even the case that the relevant meeting cannot be located. Contemporary reporting in Athletics Weekly on 5 October 1974 explicitly places the ban at the Rome Congress and records the Technical Committee's reasons concerning safety and the nature of the event. Contemporary reporting helps locate the decision, but is not the original resolution.

The archival gap should therefore be defined more narrowly. Contemporary reporting establishes the Congress and the ban. What has not yet been found is the original resolution, the record of adoption of the precise wording, and the complete discussion. A decision's trace in the news does not mean its formation is available to us without omission. This series is concerned precisely with how far evidence can take us, and where it stops.

Now consider when the prohibition appeared.

The somersault long jump appeared in major competition in 1974. The rule banning it was also written in 1974. The dates almost coincide.

This is the heart of the essay, but its scope matters. Reporting from 1974 shows an emerging technique, tried in competition and training, becoming the subject of an explicit international ban. It does not establish that no relevant restriction existed in every earlier rulebook of every governing body. Nor does a technique's novelty prove that rules never prohibit an action before it is tried. What we can see is this rotation forcing an insufficiently articulated boundary into debate and decision.

This is a mirror image of the high-jump situation in Essay 8.

The flop entered a space in which high-jump rules did not prescribe one clearance style. The removal of earlier restrictions and the spread of soft landing mats provided conditions for its adoption. The somersault also found room for experiment in some competitions and training. It met a different response: an explicit international rule making the movement a failed attempt. The spaces available to the two innovations differed; these were not two controlled tests under one identical silent rule.

Material conditions helped the flop; an explicit prohibition caught up with the somersault. One possible difference concerns the pace of development. The flop spread with soft mats, accumulating performances and habits. The somersault drew concentrated attention through experiments, one result matching an Olympic champion and large projections of thirty feet. That difference in attention may have mattered to decisions. It does not establish that the flop went unnoticed, or that conspicuousness alone caused the somersault's ban.

The construct spoke. As it did, the previously nonexistent boundary was drawn.

One interpretation concerns conspicuousness. An innovation entering a space without a clear answer may be received differently depending on its pace of development, established results and public attention. A later ban confronts habits already formed; an early decision may meet different resistance. The contrast between the flop and the somersault makes that possibility worth examining. It does not eliminate safety, the movements' features or the choices of particular officials as contributing explanations. Their fates cannot be assigned wholly to which grew more quietly.

IV. A Safety Rationale and an Incomplete Record

The ban invoked safety. The publicly accessible material examined here does not provide enough evidence to reconstruct the size of the risk.

Official objections at the time were explicitly framed in terms of safety, but there was a second, more conceptual objection. Sports Illustrated reported that members of the IAAF Technical Committee both feared the technique might endanger athletes' necks and considered it so different that it might not be traditional long jumping. Those are two distinct reasons and should not be merged.

Look at them separately. The first is safety: fear of neck injury. The second is not about safety. The movement is too different; it no longer looks like long jumping. That objection has nothing to do with whether athletes will be hurt. It asks whether this still counts as the long jump. Later accounts commonly compress both reasons into banned for safety, losing the second. Yet the second comes closer to the dividing line this essay seeks.

Now examine the evidence for the safety rationale.

No contemporary injury dataset, medical appendix or quantified risk study has been found attached to the decision. The debate in Sports Illustrated in 1974 was almost entirely hypothetical. What if an athlete mistimed the tuck? What if the ankle could not withstand it? What about neck injuries? Ecker and Washington State University assistant coach Sloan explicitly denied that the technique was particularly dangerous, but offered no injury statistics of their own either.

In the debate presented by this contemporary report, neither side supplied injury statistics that could be checked. Those calling the technique dangerous described possible hazards; those defending it offered a different judgment. We can describe those public arguments. The absence of numbers in a magazine report does not establish that every item of information available to the committee was absent too.

That deserves comparison with earlier essays. Record ratification normally requires timing, measurement, wind and equipment evidence that can be checked against specific standards. A technical ban also involves another judgment: a body may have to assess a potential danger before many accidents have accumulated. The question is how its reasons are made public and open to examination, not whether failure to locate statistics proves that it had no grounds at all.

This difference does not exempt judgment from evidence. Measurement usually concerns a defined quantity; a safety decision also weighs possible harm, uncertainty and the cost of waiting. It may not produce a number of the same precision, but it still needs reasons, attention to contrary evidence and room for revision. An institution can use different standards for different tasks without treating its own unease as a conclusion that requires no explanation.

This does not establish that the ban was wrong. The somersault may have posed real risks, and precautionary prohibition may have had grounds. The material available does not justify declaring the decision pure intuition. What remains worth examining is the other reason contemporaries stated: that the movement did not fit traditional long jumping. That reason about the event's character need not disappear behind the word safety, and recognizing it does not require calling safety a pretext.

V. Another Reason Given at the Time

It was so different that it might not be traditional long jumping.

This is another reason worth examining on its own. It lets the essay ask how an event's boundary becomes explicit.

A long jumper runs up, takes off, turns a somersault and lands in the sand. In a competition permitting that movement, the distance can be measured by the existing method. Some committee members nevertheless saw something outside traditional long jumping. Their picture was of a person running, taking off, remaining in a more or less extended posture and landing; a somersault did not fit. Other coaches and athletes disputed that picture. It was precisely the disagreement that demanded a decision.

An insufficiently articulated line appears here. It concerns not only the board, sand, wind and measurement, but also some officials' image of the event. That image is not identical with every earlier rulebook, nor was it the unanimous view of participants. The dispute exposes a gap between existing permissions and what officials now want to exclude.

The somersault challenged that understanding of the event. In a competition permitting the movement, its distance could be measured by the existing method; a governing body could still decide not to allow it in future. The choice was whether to broaden the interpretation and admit the rotation as long jumping or explicitly exclude it. Contemporary reporting shows the international body chose exclusion. That does not mean all athletes and coaches had previously shared the same boundary.

It chose to defend it. The previously invisible line became a written rule: no somersaults.

This is one way to understand a construct discovering its boundary when crossed. Some decision-makers brought an image of the event that had not been fully articulated. The new movement challenged it and forced them to say whether they would defend or broaden it. That does not mean nobody had considered the question before. Delamere's rotation shows an understanding that had not settled everything becoming an explicit, binding decision.

The title therefore speaks of discovery: a new case makes insufficiently examined expectations visible. Discovery does not exclude drawing something new at that moment. A boundary need not have lain complete and dormant in the shadows; it may take concrete form in the conflict between an inherited image and a new practice. The collision reveals the construct's own power to decide, and forces it to face where the line should now be drawn.

In Essay 8, the 1936 removal of a clause that would have barred the flop was the construct clearing away an old rule it considered unnecessary, without realising that the rule was a door. Here the process is reversed. The construct discovers that it needs a door where none existed and hurriedly builds one. In one case it inadvertently removed a door; in the other it was forced to build one. Both show that it does not know in advance where its boundaries lie. It must wait for someone to reach the boundary before discovering whether a door should be there.

VI. For Another Innovation, the Rules Had Already Left a Door Open

Now consider the opposite case.

Pole-vault poles have changed material several times. World Athletics' own historical overview gives this chronology: the first recorded use of bamboo poles was in 1857; steel poles were introduced in the 1940s; flexible fibreglass poles, followed by carbon-fibre poles, became the modern standard.

The transformation brought by fibreglass was enormous. It was not banned, and none of its records were removed.

The first world-record breakthrough with fibreglass came from Davies in 1961. Uelses followed in 1962. By 1963, fibreglass record-breaking had become routine, and most leading vaulters had changed poles.

The scale can be quantified. A University of Oregon study of innovation summarised it approximately this way: during the bamboo era, from 1899 to 1944, the world record rose by 3 feet 9 inches; after innovations of the fibreglass and related polymer era arrived, it rose by approximately 4 feet 6 inches from 1960 onward. This was a transformation equal to any technical revolution, yet it triggered no reset of the records.

Why? Because the rules had already left the door open.

The rule on pole materials was exceptionally permissive. Current World Athletics rules say that a pole may be made from any material or combination of materials, of any length or diameter, provided its basic surface is smooth. A 1966 historical study of fibreglass pole vaulting said that the IAAF did not legislate against fibreglass because its own rules already allowed poles of any material, length and diameter.

That sentence is decisive. The existing words any material gave fibreglass a clear space of legality. A new material did not automatically cross the boundary. This alone does not establish that officials gave no thought to fairness or safety. But admitting an innovation already within that permission did not require rewriting the pole's material definition first.

Fibreglass also provoked controversy. Here controversy must be separated from adjudication.

On the controversy side, contemporaries called fibreglass poles a gimmick or an unfair mechanical aid, and magazines openly debated the innovation's fairness.

On the adjudication side, the equipment remained legal because it fell within the already open pole rule. No primary evidence has been found of an IAAF decision to establish a separate world-record list for fibreglass users.

The difference between fibreglass and the somersault was not that only one was controversial. Both were. The somersault provoked a dispute about the definition of long jumping and was explicitly excluded; fibreglass fell within a pole rule already written broadly. One boundary was a broad, express permission. The other emerged as a restriction when an inherited image of the event came into dispute. The two boundaries did not have identical origins.

What is easily missed is that fibreglass stayed inside the boundary not because its effect was small. Its part in the development of performances was considerable; the account cited earlier gives a rise of 4 feet 6 inches over the relevant era. A bamboo-only rule would have required consideration of an amendment, an exception or refusal of the new pole. Neither a ban nor a record reset would follow automatically. What matters is not only how radical a technology is, but the space opened by a definition and how the institution uses it.

VII. A Principle Emerging from the Cases

Set these two cases beside several others and a principle can be inferred. First, however, we must be clear that it is not written down anywhere.

No general IAAF or World Athletics provision has been found that states in one place when records are reset and when they are not. World Athletics' record rules describe ratification within compliant competitions and allow its leadership or Council to decide doubtful cases. They do not set out a universal philosophical test for every future technological change.

The following principle is therefore inferred from decisions that actually occurred. It is the best evidence-based synthesis of how those decisions operated, not a discovered doctrine.

The principle is this.

When the construct redefines the legal implement itself, changing the event's conditions of legality, it resets the records and establishes a new series. The men's javelin redesign in 1986 did this, as did the rollback against serrated tails in 1991.

When innovation falls within an already legal definition of equipment, or when the rules merely add prospective certification requirements, it does not reset the records. Fibreglass poles, synthetic tracks and start information systems follow this pattern.

The javelin deserves elaboration because it is the clearest reset case.

World Athletics' own historical account says the men's javelin was redesigned in 1986 because of increasingly frequent flat landings, disputes over validity, and distances potentially dangerous for a stadium infield after Hohn's 104.80-metre record. It explicitly states that the 1986 redesign required a new set of records. The scale was enormous: the men's record effectively reset from 104.80 metres with the old implement to 85.74 with the new, a drop of 19.06 metres. This was not merely a prospective adjustment to approval. It was a new specification accompanied by a new record book.

The javelin also supplies a second reset example. Manufacturers introduced serrated tails, modifying tail drag and recovering some of the lost distance. Those implements were outlawed in 1991, the best marks achieved with them were rescinded, and the record reverted to the best performance with a conventional post-1986 implement.

Now compare the javelin and pole vault side by side. The javelin's records reset in 1986 because the implement itself was redefined and its legal specifications changed. Pole-vault records did not reset because the pole was not redefined: the any-material rule remained unchanged throughout. In both cases equipment changed, but only one produced a reset. The dividing line was whether the construct altered the implement's legal definition.

That distinction has a practical consequence worth identifying. Whether new equipment triggers a reset depends not on how much it improves performance, but on how broadly the old rule happened to be written. Javelin rules are specific, prescribing the centre of gravity and distribution of weight. Changing those parameters creates a new implement and requires a reset. Pole rules are general, allowing any material, so material changes remain within the definition and trigger none. The same technological progress may cause a reset under a precise rule but not under a broad one. Whether records reset depends in substantial part on how narrowly or broadly the original rule-makers expressed themselves.

This principle also explains synthetic tracks and starting blocks. Replacing cinder with synthetic surfaces was a vast change of venue, but it did not reset records. World Athletics did not redefine the events into a narrower class of facility. It required records to be achieved at certified facilities. That is a prospective ratification condition, not retrospective abolition of old records.

VIII. A Line That Was Never Written Down

Let us bring the essay together.

The construct gave opposite answers to related questions, and definition is one boundary worth distinguishing. Safety and the event's character both appeared in public discussion; failure to locate complete injury statistics does not erase the former. Another question remains visible: how an innovation is included in the understanding of an event, or explicitly kept outside it.

The somersault crossed the definition of long jumping. It was too different and might not be traditional long jumping, so it was banned. Redesigning the javelin crossed the definition of the legal implement. The javelins of 104.80 and 85.74 metres were different implements, so the records were reset. Fibreglass did not cross the definition of a pole. The any-material rule already encompassed it, so it was absorbed and the records retained. Cross the definition and the system rewrites; remain within it and the system absorbs.

But something deeper lies within that principle: most of these boundaries were not drawn in advance.

The reporting from 1974 shows an explicit international decision about somersaulting. It does not reconstruct every earlier rulebook. The contrast with the pole appears in the wording: a broad material permission already included fibreglass. That alone does not tell us how far earlier rule-makers had considered future possibilities. The effects of a broad rule can be described without attributing either carelessness or foresight to its writers.

Boundaries appear here in two ways. Pole vaulting had a broad written permission accommodating a new material. In long jumping, a new practice conflicted with an inherited image of the event and led to an explicit restriction. The result alone does not tell us whether earlier thinking was casual or carefully developed. What becomes visible is the contrast between an already broad permission and a decision made urgent by a new case.

This brings us to the essay's remainder.

In Essay 8, the flop was a possibility enclosed by material conditions, emerging once those conditions loosened. The somersault was different. It was not materially blocked. Soft mats already existed, as did sandpits; turning a somersault into a sandpit was physically feasible. What blocked it was not matter but the invisible line defining what the event was. That line could be moved. It was not a law of physics, but a shared understanding, a convention. The construct could have moved it outward and recognised somersaulting as long jumping. It chose not to.

The somersault thus became a particular remainder: a technically feasible possibility with substantial competitive results, later excluded by international rules. It had happened, but that rule system no longer allowed it. Delamere's rotations, other experiments and Stierle's 7.5 metres were traces of its reality. They made it worth taking seriously; they did not establish superiority over conventional technique under controlled conditions. The ban defended one understanding of the event. That choice remains open to examination.

The possibility consequently lost room to develop in international competition. Contemporary reporting also said that domestic competitions could continue unless their governing bodies adopted a ban; experiments in training did not become physically impossible. The further possibilities of twenty-eight or thirty feet remained projections not fully tested in comparable sanctioned competition. Drawing a rule changed how a technical path could continue. We cannot supply history with a result it never established.

A remainder constrained by a decision deserves separate attention. Earlier cases involved names excluded from the ledger, explanations left open, or questions of technical merit outside the institution's remit. Here the institution had choices: it could broaden its understanding or write a restriction, while also assessing risks. It chose prohibition. That choice is different from physical impossibility. Its reasons and alternatives remain open to examination without our first asserting that an old convention was the only cause.

Essay 11 will develop this distinction further. Hohn's 104.80 metres remains a lawful and valid historical performance. After the new specification came into force, the old-specification record series stopped accepting entries. What was closed was the ledger under those comparative conditions, not the possibility that a human body might ever again achieve 104.80 metres.

The ruler has not yet measured accurately. It is still measuring.

traditional_pairs: 这一层第十一篇会讲得更彻底。那里有一个成绩，合法，有效，而且永远不可能被追平，因为投出它的那件器械，已经被这个构亲手取消了。
第十一篇会把这一层讲得更彻底。霍恩的104.80米是合法而有效的历史成绩；新规格实行后，旧规格的纪录序列不再接收新条目。封存的是那套比较条件下的账本，不是宣布104.80米这个距离在人类身体上永远不可达到。
第十一篇會把這一層講得更徹底。霍恩的104.80米是合法而有效的歷史成績；新規格實行後，舊規格的紀錄序列不再接收新條目。封存的是那套比較條件下的賬本，不是宣佈104.80米這個距離在人類身體上永遠不可達到。
到1974年，同样的内容已经出现在全美大学体育协会的规则里:运动员在触及落地区之前的试跳中使用任何形式的空翻。这说明前空翻的禁令在一部有1974年版权的主要规则里已经成文，即便确切的国际田联采纳会议从可查的档案里更难钉死。
1974年的全美大学体育协会规则中，已经有禁止试跳空翻的条款。国际田联这一边，也并非连会议都无法定位：1974年10月5日《Athletics Weekly》的同期报道，把禁令明确放在罗马大会，并记述了技术委员会关于安全与项目性质的理由。同期报道能帮助定位决定，但它还不是原始决议文本。
1974年的全美大學體育協會規則中，已經有禁止試跳空翻的條款。國際田聯這一邊，也並非連會議都無法定位：1974年10月5日《Athletics Weekly》的同期報道，把禁令明確放在羅馬大會，並記述了技術委員會關於安全與項目性質的理由。同期報道能幫助定位決定，但它還不是原始決議文本。

这个档案上的空缺，本身也是这个系列反复出现的东西。可以确定禁令存在，可以确定它1974年前后成文，可以确定此后规则的连续。确定不了的是那个决定是在哪一次具体的会议上，以哪一份具体的决议做出的。这和前面几篇里那些找不到的会议记录，找不到的申请表，找不到的推导过程是同一类空缺。这个构留下了它的结论，那条写在规则里的禁令;没有留下它的过程，那次做出禁令的讨论。后人能看到它禁了，看不到它是怎么决定要禁的。
所以这里的档案空缺应当缩小：可以依据同期报道确定大会和禁令，尚未找到的是原始决议、具体条文的通过记录，以及完整讨论过程。一个决定留下了新闻中的踪迹，不等于它如何形成已经毫无遗漏地呈现在我们面前。这个系列关心的，正是证据能把我们带到哪里，又在哪里停下来。
所以這裡的檔案空缺應當縮小：可以依據同期報道確定大會和禁令，尚未找到的是原始決議、具體條文的通過記錄，以及完整討論過程。一個決定留下了新聞中的蹤跡，不等於它如何形成已經毫無遺漏地呈現在我們面前。這個系列關心的，正是證據能把我們帶到哪裡，又在哪裡停下來。
前两篇讲的是规则的沉默。跳高规则不规定怎么过杆，于是背越式钻进这个沉默里，活了下来。铅球规则不规定用滑步还是旋转，于是两种技术在这个沉默里并存了七十年。这一篇要问的是:规则的沉默什么时候结束。一个构不可能对所有事情永远沉默，总有一刻它要开口。而它开口和不开口的分界线在哪里，这一篇要从这两件相反的事情里找出来。
前两篇讲的是规则的沉默。跳高规则不规定怎么过杆，于是背越式钻进这个沉默里，活了下来。铅球规则不规定用滑步还是旋转，于是两种技术在这个沉默里自1970年代以来并存了半个多世纪。这一篇要问的是:规则的沉默什么时候结束。一个构不可能对所有事情永远沉默，总有一刻它要开口。而它开口和不开口的分界线在哪里，这一篇要从这两件相反的事情里找出来。
前兩篇講的是規則的沈默。跳高規則不規定怎麼過桿，於是背越式鑽進這個沈默里，活了下來。鉛球規則不規定用滑步還是旋轉，於是兩種技術在這個沈默里自1970年代以來並存了半個多世紀。這一篇要問的是:規則的沈默什麼時候結束。一個構不可能對所有事情永遠沈默，總有一刻它要開口。而它開口和不開口的分界線在哪裡，這一篇要從這兩件相反的事情里找出來。
选这两件事来对照，不是随手挑的。它们几乎在所有别的方面都一样，只在结果上相反，这使得那个造成差别的原因容易被隔离出来。两件都发生在这项运动里，两件都是一样能提高成绩的新东西，两件都引来了公平性的质疑，两件都涉及安全的讨论。当这么多条件都相同，而结果相反的时候，那个真正起作用的变量就藏在剩下的那点不同里。这一篇要做的，就是把那点不同找出来，而它最后落在一个词上:定义。
选这两件事来对照，不是随手挑的。它们在几个关键方面相似，却有相反结果：都发生在田径里，都提出了改善成绩的可能，都引来公平与安全讨论。但这种对照不是控制实验，不能把其他差异全部排除。它能帮助我们辨认一个常被安全争论遮住的问题：新东西是否仍被看作原来的项目。沿着这条线，这一篇最后会走到一个词上：定义。
選這兩件事來對照，不是隨手挑的。它們在幾個關鍵方面相似，卻有相反結果：都發生在田徑里，都提出了改善成績的可能，都引來公平與安全討論。但這種對照不是控制實驗，不能把其他差異全部排除。它能幫助我們辨認一個常被安全爭論遮住的問題：新東西是否仍被看作原來的項目。沿著這條線，這一篇最後會走到一個詞上：定義。
先说清楚一件事。这两个相反的答案，不能简单地用安全来解释。禁前空翻式的理由是安全，可是没有找到任何伤害数据支撑这个理由;放行玻璃纤维竿的时候，安全也不是靠禁掉它来处理的。所以安全不是那条分界线。真正的分界线在别处，在这两样东西各自有没有越过一条线上。那条线是这个项目对自己的定义。
先说清楚一件事。这两个相反答案，不能只靠一句“为了安全”就解释完。同期报道既提到前空翻可能伤及颈部，也提到它是否仍符合跳远的精神。现有公开材料没有提供足以核对风险大小的完整统计，但这不证明决策者从未考虑过安全，也不证明安全理由只是借口。这一篇着重追问的是另一个已经被提出的理由：一种革新是否越过了项目对自己的理解。
先說清楚一件事。這兩個相反答案，不能只靠一句“為了安全”就解釋完。同期報道既提到前空翻可能傷及頸部，也提到它是否仍符合跳遠的精神。現有公開材料沒有提供足以核對風險大小的完整統計，但這不證明決策者從未考慮過安全，也不證明安全理由只是藉口。這一篇著重追問的是另一個已經被提出的理由：一種革新是否越過了項目對自己的理解。
这一点是这一篇的核心。在1974年之前，跳远规则里没有关于空翻的禁令。为什么没有，因为在1974年之前，没有人在跳远里翻跟头。规则不去禁一件从来没有人做过的事。所以这条边界，在德拉米尔和那几百个人开始翻跟头之前，是不存在的。它不是本来就画在那里，等着有人去撞;它是在有人撞过来的那一刻，才被匆忙画出来的。
这一点是这一篇的核心，但需要把范围说准。1974年的报道让我们看见，一种正在比赛与训练中尝试的技术，怎样受到国际规则的明确禁止。它不能替我们证明，在此前所有机构、所有年份的规则里，都从未有过相关限制。也不能因为技术新出现，就断言规则不会预先禁止尚未实践的动作。能够看见的是：这种翻转把原先尚未被充分说清的项目边界，推到了必须讨论并作决定的位置。
這一點是這一篇的核心，但需要把範圍說准。1974年的報道讓我們看見，一種正在比賽與訓練中嘗試的技術，怎樣受到國際規則的明確禁止。它不能替我們證明，在此前所有機構、所有年份的規則里，都從未有過相關限制。也不能因為技術新出現，就斷言規則不會預先禁止尚未實踐的動作。能夠看見的是：這種翻轉把原先尚未被充分說清的項目邊界，推到了必須討論並作決定的位置。
背越式钻进了跳高规则的沉默里。1936年那条会挡住它的条款被取消之后，规则对背向过杆保持沉默，而背越式在这个沉默里活了下来，因为恰好有软垫这个物质条件在放行它。前空翻式也钻进了跳远规则的沉默里，1974年之前跳远规则对空翻保持沉默。但这一次结局相反:规则没有继续沉默，它立刻开口，把这个刚冒头的技术禁掉了。
背越式进入了跳高规则没有指定唯一过杆姿势的空间。旧限制的取消与软垫的普及，为它的采用提供了条件。前空翻式也在当时一些比赛和训练里获得了试验空间。但它遇到另一种结果：主管机构明确开口，在国际比赛中把这种动作列为失败。两种革新获得的空间不一样，不能简单当成同一条沉默规则下的两次实验。

这里可以看到扎眼这件事在构的运行里起的作用。一样东西钻进规则的沉默，能不能活下来，一部分取决于它扎不扎眼。悄悄长起来的，等长成了已成事实，构往往就默认了它，因为这时候再去禁它，要面对一大批既得的成绩和既成的习惯。一下子冒出来的，构还来得及在它站稳之前把它按住。所以同样是钻沉默，速度快慢决定了命运。背越式的慢，让它熬过了那个危险期;前空翻式的快，让它撞上了构最警觉的时刻。这不是关于哪个技术更好，是关于哪个技术长得更不动声色。
这里可以提出一个关于显眼程度的解释。一种革新在既有规则没有明确回答的地方出现，能否被接受，也许与它的发展节奏、既成成绩和引起的关注有关。发展久了再禁止，机构需要面对已经形成的使用习惯；刚出现时作决定，阻力可能不同。背越式与前空翻式的遭遇使这种差别值得研究。但它还不是已经排除了安全、动作特征和管理层选择的唯一原因，不能把命运全部归给“谁长得更悄悄”。
這裡可以提出一個關於顯眼程度的解釋。一種革新在既有規則沒有明確回答的地方出現，能否被接受，也許與它的發展節奏、既成成績和引起的關注有關。發展久了再禁止，機構需要面對已經形成的使用習慣；剛出現時作決定，阻力可能不同。背越式與前空翻式的遭遇使這種差別值得研究。但它還不是已經排除了安全、動作特徵和管理層選擇的唯一原因，不能把命運全部歸給“誰長得更悄悄”。

这一点值得和前面几篇连起来看。这个构对成绩的要求极其严格，一个成绩要进纪录，必须有精确的计时，精确的丈量，合规的风速，认证的器材。它对数字的要求高到苛刻。可是当它要禁掉一个技术的时候，它没有拿出任何数字。要求别人拿数字的构，自己在做这个决定的时候，一个数字都没有。
这一点值得和前面几篇连起来看。成绩要进入纪录，通常需要能按具体标准复核的计时、丈量、风速和器材资料。技术禁令则还包含另一层判断：即使没有已经积累的大量事故，机构也可能需要评估潜在风险。这里可追问的是，它提出的风险依据怎样公开、怎样接受检验，而不是因为暂时找不到数字，就认定决定没有任何依据。
這一點值得和前面幾篇連起來看。成績要進入紀錄，通常需要能按具體標準復核的計時、丈量、風速和器材資料。技術禁令則還包含另一層判斷：即使沒有已經積累的大量事故，機構也可能需要評估潛在風險。這裡可追問的是，它提出的風險依據怎樣公開、怎樣接受檢驗，而不是因為暫時找不到數字，就認定決定沒有任何依據。

这个不对称本身是有意味的。它说明这个构对数字的要求，是分场合的。在批准一个成绩的时候，它要求极高的精确，因为那是它的核心业务，是它权威的来源，容不得含糊。而在禁止一个技术的时候，它不要求数字，因为这不是一个测量问题，是一个判断问题。测量需要数字，判断不需要，判断需要的是一个理由，哪怕这个理由只是一种不安。所以同一个构，可以一边在成绩上锱铢必较，一边在技术上凭感觉行事，这两件事在它那里并不矛盾，因为它们本来就是两种不同的活动。
这种差别不使判断免于证据要求。测量通常围绕一个明确的量，安全判断还要比较可能的伤害、不确定性和等待的代价。后者未必能化成同一种精度的数字，却仍需要说明理由、认真对待相反证据，并留下修正的可能。同一个机构可以在不同任务上采用不同标准，但不能因此把感觉本身当成无需解释的结论。
這種差別不使判斷免於證據要求。測量通常圍繞一個明確的量，安全判斷還要比較可能的傷害、不確定性和等待的代價。後者未必能化成同一種精度的數字，卻仍需要說明理由、認真對待相反證據，並留下修正的可能。同一個機構可以在不同任務上採用不同標準，但不能因此把感覺本身當成無需解釋的結論。

背越式得到物質條件的放行，前空翻式則被明確規則追上。這裡有一種值得考慮的差別：發展的節奏。背越式隨軟墊普及，逐漸累積成績與使用習慣；前空翻式在短時間里聚集了試驗、一次與奧運冠軍並列的成績，以及三十英尺的遠大預測。這種關注程度的差異，可能影響決策。但這不等於背越式從未驚動機構，也不等於前空翻式僅僅因為太扎眼就被禁掉。
一个跳远运动员，助跑，起跳，在空中翻一个跟头，落进沙坑。他跳出的距离，按跳远的规则丈量，合规，有效。可是技术委员会的人看着它，觉得这不像跳远了。为什么不像。因为跳远这个项目，在所有人的理解里，是一个人助跑，起跳，在空中保持某种伸展姿势，然后落地的运动。翻跟头不在这个理解里。
一个跳远运动员，助跑、起跳，在空中翻一个跟头，落进沙坑。在允许这种动作的比赛里，距离可以按既有方法丈量。但一些技术委员会成员仍觉得，这不像传统的跳远。他们心里的画面，是人助跑、起跳，在空中保持某种伸展姿势，然后落地，翻跟头不在这个画面里。另一些教练和运动员却不同意这种理解。正是这种分歧，迫使机构作出决定。
一個跳遠運動員，助跑、起跳，在空中翻一個跟頭，落進沙坑。在允許這種動作的比賽里，距離可以按既有方法丈量。但一些技術委員會成員仍覺得，這不像傳統的跳遠。他們心裡的畫面，是人助跑、起跳，在空中保持某種伸展姿勢，然後落地，翻跟頭不在這個畫面里。另一些教練和運動員卻不同意這種理解。正是這種分歧，迫使機構作出決定。
这里出现了一条看不见的线。这条线不是写在规则里的，规则只规定了起跳板，落地区，丈量方式，风速。规则从来没有写过跳远的时候不能翻跟头，因为在1974年之前，不需要写。这条线写在人们对这个项目是什么的共同理解里，写在传统里，写在跳远这个词唤起的那个画面里。
这里出现了一条尚未充分说清的线。它不只关乎起跳板、沙坑、风速与丈量，也关乎一部分管理者心里的项目形象。这个形象不等于此前所有规则的总和，也不是所有参与者一致同意的理解。争论让一种落差显形了：既有的允许空间，与管理者现在想要排除的东西，并不完全重合。
這裡出現了一條尚未充分說清的線。它不只關乎起跳板、沙坑、風速與丈量，也關乎一部分管理者心裡的項目形象。這個形象不等於此前所有規則的總和，也不是所有參與者一致同意的理解。爭論讓一種落差顯形了：既有的允許空間，與管理者現在想要排除的東西，並不完全重合。
这就是构在被越过时才发现边界的意思。那条边界一直在，它在人们对跳远的理解里。但只要没有人越过它，它就一直是隐性的，不需要被写出来，甚至不需要被意识到。是前空翻式的出现，第一次让这个构意识到自己有这样一条边界。它意识到的方式，是有人越了过去。在那之前，如果你问技术委员会跳远能不能翻跟头，他们可能根本没想过这个问题。是德拉米尔的跟头，让这个问题第一次被问出来，也让那条边界第一次被画出来。
构在被越过时发现边界，可以这样理解。一部分决策者带着尚未充分说出的项目形象，新动作向它提出挑战，逼他们表明是守住这个形象，还是把它扩大。这并不意味着此前谁也没想过这个问题。德拉米尔的跟头让我们看见：一种并未预先决定一切的理解，怎样变成具有约束力的明确决定。
構在被越過時發現邊界，可以這樣理解。一部分決策者帶著尚未充分說出的項目形象，新動作向它提出挑戰，逼他們表明是守住這個形象，還是把它擴大。這並不意味著此前誰也沒想過這個問題。德拉米爾的跟頭讓我們看見：一種並未預先決定一切的理解，怎樣變成具有約束力的明確決定。

这就是为什么这一篇叫构在被越过时才发现边界。发现这个词是准确的，不是设立，不是宣布，是发现。这个构不是先想好了自己的边界，再等着执行;它是在被撞的那一刻，才发现原来这里有一条边界。撞之前，那条边界处在一种沉睡的状态，它在人们的共同理解里，但没有被说出来，甚至没有被想到。是越过它的那个动作，把它从沉睡里叫醒，逼着这个构第一次正视它，然后决定是守还是让。边界一直都在，只是它要等到被越过，才被这个构自己看见。
所以题目用了“发现”：一个新案例，让尚未充分澄清的期待显现。但发现并不排斥在当下重新划线。那条边界未必早已完整地沉睡在暗处，它也可能在旧有形象与新实践的冲突中，才取得具体形状。碰撞让构看见自己的决定权，也逼它面对：接下来，这条线究竟要画在哪里。
所以題目用了“發現”：一個新案例，讓尚未充分澄清的期待顯現。但發現並不排斥在當下重新划線。那條邊界未必早已完整地沈睡在暗處，它也可能在舊有形象與新實踐的衝突中，才取得具體形狀。碰撞讓構看見自己的決定權，也逼它面對：接下來，這條線究竟要畫在哪裡。
所以玻璃纤维竿和前空翻式的差别，不在于一个有争议一个没争议，两个都有争议。差别在于，前空翻式越过了跳远的定义那条线，而玻璃纤维竿落在了撑竿规则那条本来就画得很宽的线之内。一个越过了边界，一个没有，尽管这两条边界的宽窄是这个构自己在很久以前就定下的。
所以玻璃纤维竿和前空翻式的差别，不在于一个有争议、一个没有，两个都有争议。差别在于，前空翻式引发了关于跳远定义的冲突，最终被明确排除；玻璃纤维竿则落在撑竿规则早已写得很宽的许可之内。一边是宽泛的明文允许，一边是继承下来的项目形象在争论中被明确成限制，两条边界并不具有同样的来历。
所以玻璃纖維竿和前空翻式的差別，不在於一個有爭議、一個沒有，兩個都有爭議。差別在於，前空翻式引發了關於跳遠定義的衝突，最終被明確排除；玻璃纖維竿則落在撐竿規則早已寫得很寬的許可之內。一邊是寬泛的明文允許，一邊是繼承下來的項目形象在爭論中被明確成限制，兩條邊界並不具有同樣的來歷。

这里有一个容易被忽略的地方。玻璃纤维竿之所以没有越界，不是因为它比前空翻式更温和，更循规蹈矩。玻璃纤维竿对撑竿跳成绩的改变，可能比前空翻式对跳远成绩的改变还要剧烈，它把纪录抬高了四英尺六英寸。它带来的变化一点都不小。它没有越界，纯粹是因为它撞上的那条线，这个构当年画得太宽了。如果撑竿的规则当年写的是撑竿必须用竹子，那么玻璃纤维竿就会立刻越界，就会像前空翻式一样被禁，或者像标枪一样触发重置。它的命运，不取决于它自己有多激进，取决于它撞上的那条线当年被画在了哪里。
容易忽略的是，玻璃纤维竿留在界内，并不是因为影响小。它在成绩发展中作用很大，前面引用的综述把相关时代的纪录增幅记为四英尺六英寸。如果规则只准竹竿，机构就得考虑修改规则、设置例外，或拒绝新竿，并不是禁用或纪录重置会自动发生。决定命运的不只是技术有多激进，还有定义留下了多大空间，以及机构怎样使用这个空间。
容易忽略的是，玻璃纖維竿留在界內，並不是因為影響小。它在成績發展中作用很大，前面引用的綜述把相關時代的紀錄增幅記為四英尺六英吋。如果規則只准竹竿，機構就得考慮修改規則、設置例外，或拒絕新竿，並不是禁用或紀錄重置會自動發生。決定命運的不只是技術有多激進，還有定義留下了多大空間，以及機構怎樣使用這個空間。
跳远不能翻跟头这条线，在1974年之前不存在，是德拉米尔翻了跟头才把它逼出来。这个构并不预先知道自己对跳远的定义到哪里为止，它是在有人走到那条线上的时候，才第一次意识到那里有一条线，然后才把它画出来。而撑竿那条线之所以早就在，不是因为这个构预见到了玻璃纤维竿，恰恰相反，是因为它当年把那条线画得太宽太随意，随意到任何材料四个字，宽到把一切还没出现的材料都无意中包了进去。
1974年的报道让我们看见关于空翻的明确国际决定，却不能替我们重建此前所有规则。与撑竿的差别，可以从文字上看出来：一条宽泛的材料许可已经包容了玻璃纤维。单凭这一点，我们无法知道旧规则的起草者当时把未来想到了多远。说明宽规则的效果，并不需要替他们断言是随意，还是远见。
1974年的報道讓我們看見關於空翻的明確國際決定，卻不能替我們重建此前所有規則。與撐竿的差別，可以從文字上看出來：一條寬泛的材料許可已經包容了玻璃纖維。單憑這一點，我們無法知道舊規則的起草者當時把未來想到了多遠。說明寬規則的效果，並不需要替他們斷言是隨意，還是遠見。
所以这个构的边界，有两种存在方式。一种是像撑竿这样，早就画好了，而且画得很宽，宽到后来的东西撞不到它。另一种是像跳远这样，根本没有画，一直是隐性的，藏在人们对这个项目是什么的共同理解里，直到有人越过它，它才被匆忙地画出来。这两种边界，都不是这个构深思熟虑地设计出来的。宽的那条是随手画宽的，隐的那条是压根没画的。
这里，边界以两种方式出现。撑竿有宽泛的明文许可，可以容纳后来出现的材料；跳远的新实践则与某种继承下来的项目形象冲突，随后形成明确限制。我们不能仅凭这个结果，断言过去的设计未经思考，或已经深思熟虑。能够辨认的是：一种允许早已很宽，另一种决定则被新案例推到了眼前。
這裡，邊界以兩種方式出現。撐竿有寬泛的明文許可，可以容納後來出現的材料；跳遠的新實踐則與某種繼承下來的項目形象衝突，隨後形成明確限制。我們不能僅憑這個結果，斷言過去的設計未經思考，或已經深思熟慮。能夠辨認的是：一種允許早已很寬，另一種決定則被新案例推到了眼前。

这种被约定挡住的余项，和前面几种都不一样，值得单独辨认。被裁定到账外的名字，是构主动排除的;算不清的成因，是构无力分开的;不去裁定的技术优劣，是构不进入的领域。而前空翻式是构本可以接纳，却选择不接纳的东西。它落在构的能力范围之内，构完全有办法把那条定义的线往外推一点，把它纳进来，就像它本可以承认翻跟头也是跳远。它没有这么做，不是因为做不到，是因为它选择守住一个旧的理解。所以这种余项，是一个选择的产物，而不是一个能力的边界。它被挡在外面，是因为构决定把它挡在外面，而这个决定本可以是相反的。
这种被决定限制的余项，值得单独辨认。前面有被排到账外的名字，有尚未解释清楚的成因，有机构不进入的技术优劣问题。这里，机构确实有选择：它可以在评估风险的同时扩大理解，也可以写下限制。它选择了禁止。这样的选择不同于物理上的做不到；它的理由与其他可能方案仍然可以被追问，而不必先断言唯一的原因就是旧约定。
這種被決定限制的餘項，值得單獨辨認。前面有被排到賬外的名字，有尚未解釋清楚的成因，有機構不進入的技術優劣問題。這裡，機構確實有選擇：它可以在評估風險的同時擴大理解，也可以寫下限制。它選擇了禁止。這樣的選擇不同於物理上的做不到；它的理由與其他可能方案仍然可以被追問，而不必先斷言唯一的原因就是舊約定。

edits.before: 这个分别值得再想一层。趋势是可以外推的，因为它是连续的，一年比一年远，画一条线就能看出它往哪里去。意外是不可外推的，因为它是离散的，一个人突然想出一个从来没有人想过的动作，这件事没有先兆，画不出线。所以构面对趋势的时候，可以像看着潮水上涨一样提前筑坝;面对意外的时候，它只能等那件事发生了，才知道有这样一件事，然后才反应。标枪的距离是潮水，前空翻式是一块突然砸下来的陨石。对潮水可以预备，对陨石只能事后清理。这就是为什么同样是这个构，在两件事上一个提前一个滞后。
edits.after: 这个分别值得再想一层。这里可以外推的是距离上限可能扩张的趋势，不是每个赛季都比上一年更远，也不是画一条线就能保证它兑现。对比之下，德拉米尔把前空翻带到比赛中，给规则提出了一个具体而突兀的问题。可以把前者比作涨潮时提前筑坝，后者比作事后才发现需要处理的陨石。这是帮助理解这两个案例的比喻，不是一条“趋势总能预见、意外永远没有先兆”的定律。一个构能不能提前准备，要看它已经掌握了什么线索、能试验什么，以及准备为哪些可能性付出代价。

edits.before:
First, correct the familiar story

Uwe Hohn threw 104.80 metres in 1984, the only official men's javelin mark beyond one hundred metres under the old specification. Popular history often says the implement was redesigned because throws had become dangerously long. World Athletics' own historical account gives a more specific primary problem: increasingly frequent flat landings generated disputes over whether attempts had landed tip first and should be valid.

Safety and stadium geometry were part of the surrounding concern, but the technical committee had been working on implement behaviour before Hohn's throw. His mark dramatized the issue; it did not single-handedly cause the reform.

Moving the centre of gravity

The men's javelin specification changed for 1986. Moving the centre of gravity forward and changing aspects of the tail altered flight so that the implement would descend more clearly and land tip first more reliably. Distances also fell.

This was not the same event with a minor equipment tolerance. The object through which performance was produced had changed systematically. A direct progression would compare throws made by materially different implements while pretending the conversion were neutral.

Close one book, open another

Athletics therefore began a new world-record progression for the redesigned javelin. Hohn's 104.80 did not become false. It remained the old-specification record—valid in a ledger whose conditions had been closed.

The operation is often described as deleting old records. “Archiving” is more accurate. The mark survives historically while losing the possibility of being broken under current rules. It becomes at once permanent and inactive.

The quotation nobody can securely retrieve

Retellings sometimes attach a neat quotation to the redesign—an official line about throws threatening the far end of stadiums or endangering spectators. Such sentences may capture real anxieties, but a memorable quotation should not be treated as an institutional reason unless its document can be located. The official historical account emphasizes flat landings and judging disputes.

This difference between a plausible story and a traceable source is central to record culture itself. Athletics asks an athlete's number to arrive with documentation. Historical writing about athletics owes the decision a comparable chain of custody.

Two truths about 104.80

Hohn's mark can no longer be superseded within the closed old-specification world-record sequence. That does not mean a future athlete could never throw the same distance with a different implement. It remains one of the greatest performances in javelin history. These statements fit together because a record has an address: implement specification, rules, and date.

The new ledger solved an operational problem. It did not provide a formula translating every old throw into a new-specification equivalent. Such a conversion would need to know release speed, angle, wind, individual technique, and the precise aerodynamic response of each implement. The causal interaction is too rich for one subtraction.

Comparability through rupture

Record systems usually preserve authority by presenting continuity. Here the only honest way to preserve comparability was to declare a break. The institution protected the meaning of future comparisons by refusing to assimilate the past.

The old book had to stop accepting new world-record entries so that the new book could compare like with like. Yet the person attached to the old record bears a peculiar cost: his finest mark remains at the head of a closed sequence, not because it proved a human limit, but because current competition uses a different implement. The number survives. What no longer continues is its former route into the record progression.

I. A claim that must first be corrected

Let us first correct a widely repeated claim. If this essay began from that claim, everything that followed would be wrong.

The popular story goes like this: Hohn's 104.80 metres in 1984 is an eternal record, a throw annulled because it went too far. The IAAF struck it out so that other athletes would have a chance of catching up.

Almost every word of that story needs correcting.

Hohn's throw was not annulled. It remains in World Athletics' official archives today, identified as a performance in the old javelin event. It remains a ratified mark, Hohn's personal best, and an entry in the record progression, carrying an old-implement designation. It was never declared illegal. No subsequent technical ruling retrospectively found the javelin he used to be non-compliant.

What restarted was not Hohn's performance but the world-record sequence for a new implement specification. In April 1986 the javelin specification changed, and the construct opened a new record book for that specification. Hohn's throw belonged to the old implement and stayed in the old book. The current men's javelin world record is Železný's 98.48 metres, not Hohn's 104.80.

The precise statement is therefore this: 104.80 metres was the final world record of the old-specification event, not an annulled throw.

No official category called an “eternal record” was found in the formal rules and record material examined here. No IAAF or World Athletics rule, congress resolution, or official record table has been found that calls Hohn's throw eternal, permanent, or unbreakable. That language belongs to popular media, social media, and retrospective videos. The construct's own vocabulary is functional: an old-event designation, a historical progression.

This essay concerns the more accurate, and stranger, fact: a performance can be legal, valid, and fully preserved in history, while the construct itself abolishes the category in which it held current-record status. And it does so not by erasing the performance but by closing the book that contains it.

The previous essay asked how a construct discovers its boundary when that boundary is crossed, and then decides whether to hold it or let it move. This essay asks what holding the boundary costs.

We need to be careful about the word “hold.” In the previous essay, the construct defended a definition of what the long jump was: it refused to admit somersaulting. Here it defended something else: comparability within a record sequence. Every performance in the same sequence had to be comparable with the others. When a new implement made that impossible, the solution was to put old-implement and new-implement performances in separate books. Preserving comparability meant producing incomparability. The sentence sounds contradictory, but it is precisely what this essay will unfold.

II. More than five metres in one step

Hohn threw 104.80 metres in East Berlin on 20 July 1984, at the Olympic Day athletics meeting in the Friedrich-Ludwig-Jahn-Sportpark. World Athletics' account identifies it as his second attempt of the competition.

It exceeded Tom Petranoff's previous world record of 99.72 metres by 5.08 metres. It was the only ratified throw beyond one hundred metres in the old men's event.

Pause over those 5.08 metres.

Before Hohn, the progression had gone from Ferenc Paragi's 96.72 metres in 1980 to Petranoff's 99.72 in 1983. Those two records were three metres apart: progress was already being measured in metres. Hohn added more than five in a single step. This was not a continuation measured in centimetres. It was a leap.

Another common impression must immediately be corrected: javelin distances were not increasing every year throughout the 1980s.

The world-leading marks were 96.72 metres in 1980, down to 92.48 in 1981, back to 95.80 in 1982, then 99.72 in 1983 and 104.80 in 1984. In 1985 Hohn himself led the season with only 96.96 metres, nowhere near his own 104.80.

The accurate account is that aerodynamic development and elite athletes sharply pushed out the upper envelope of performance. That does not mean every season was longer than the last. The upper envelope expanded while individual seasons fluctuated. Hohn's throw was the most extreme point on that expanding envelope, not the summit of a smoothly rising curve.

Several things about that throw cannot now be obtained. Their absence is itself worth recording.

The exact make and model of Hohn's javelin cannot be established. Many later accounts name famous old javelin models, but no implement-control certificate, manufacturer's serial number, or authoritative competition inventory has been found linking a particular model to that particular throw. Treating a brand or nominal distance rating as an established fact would therefore be unsafe.

Precise weather and wind measurements for the attempt are likewise unavailable. Javelin records do not have the two-metres-per-second wind limit applied to sprints and horizontal jumps. But javelin flight depends strongly on wind, air density, angle of attack, and the implement's orientation. No authoritative wind vector, temperature, pressure, or air-density record has been found for Hohn's attempt. Any precise conversion based on assumed weather is therefore speculative.

This is the same predicament as Beamon's jump in Essay 5. An extreme performance occurred at a moment whose conditions were not fully recorded. The surviving evidence is insufficient to separate precisely and cleanly how much came from the person and how much from the day. The difference is that Beamon's wind was within the rules, and altitude was not an exclusion from record eligibility. A federation could not alter the site's altitude, but could decide how high-altitude performances were classified, identified or recognized. In Hohn's case, the institutional response concerned a redefinition of the implement itself.

That distinction matters. With Beamon, the construct chose to recognize the mark within the existing progression rather than create a separate altitude category. The performance, whose causes cannot be exactly disentangled, remained at the top for twenty-three years. That did not mean high-altitude marks were beyond regulation in principle. Hohn's case involved another directly editable object: the javelin itself. An implement's specification can be changed. The difference is not that legislation was possible in one case and impossible in the other, but that different institutional choices were made. The construct could not move the site's altitude; it could regulate record categories, and in javelin it could also alter the implement.

III. The proposal was already on its way

One claim must be rejected because it reverses causation: Hohn's throw single-handedly forced the reset.

It did not.

Bremicker, who participated in the IAAF Technical Committee's work, explicitly rejected that chronology. Changes were underway before the throw. The committee conducted experiments in 1982–83. The proposed construction rules were finalized in 1983, placed on the agenda for the Los Angeles Congress early in 1984, and circulated to member federations in May. Hohn threw 104.80 metres on 20 July, about two weeks before the congress.

His throw could not have generated a proposal circulated months earlier. What it could do was strengthen the case politically and symbolically. The more defensible statement is that 104.80 metres became the enduring public image of a decision whose technical process was already well advanced.

This connects with the previous essay, but the connection must be precise.

In the somersault long jump, the boundary was drawn when it was crossed. Before 1974 the long-jump rules did not prohibit somersaulting. Tuariki Delamere's somersault brought that prohibition into being. There, the boundary genuinely appeared after the crossing.

The javelin was different. Here the boundary was being drawn before it was crossed. The Technical Committee began experimenting in 1982, before Petranoff's 99.72 metres in May 1983 and before anyone had broken one hundred metres. The construct did not react in panic only after Hohn reached 104.80. It had anticipated excessively long distances and begun preparing several years earlier.

What, then, was Hohn's throw in this story? The strongest annotation to a decision already taking shape. It gave a technical discussion an argument everyone could see: more than five metres in one step, 104.80 metres. The number was the best possible exhibit. It was not the cause of the decision but its most powerful evidence, and evidence is not the same as cause.

A different pattern now appears. In earlier essays, the construct often lagged behind events, responding and making rules afterward. Here it acted in advance of the extreme performance. Why? The issue was not only whether a particular new technique was acceptable. It also concerned range and landing problems that could be investigated through sustained testing. The upper range of distances was expanding, and that trend could be extrapolated. No particular throw had to occur before an excessive distance could be anticipated. In these two cases, accumulating range and landing problems supplied grounds for advance testing; the particular somersault prompted a response after it was demonstrated. That does not mean every novel technique must be unforeseeable.

Consider the distinction one step further. Here the extrapolation concerned a potentially expanding upper range, not a guarantee that every season would exceed the last or that a drawn line must come true. Delamere's competitive somersault, by contrast, presented the rules with a concrete, abrupt question. One can picture the former as building a dam against a rising tide, the latter as discovering a meteorite that must be dealt with after impact. The image helps explain these cases; it is not a law that trends are always predictable and surprises never have warning signs. Advance preparation depends on available clues, possible tests and the costs an institution is willing to bear for possibilities.

IV. Making the javelin lower its head

The construct did not restrict the athletes. It redesigned the javelin.

In 1982–83 the IAAF Technical Committee and manufacturers produced test javelins whose centres of gravity were moved forward by two, three, four, and five centimetres. Hundreds of throws followed, mostly from launching machines, with some made by athletes. A three-centimetre shift was judged sufficient to ensure tip-first landings. The committee majority chose four centimetres for a greater reduction in distance and a lower likelihood of another expensive specification change later.

The main dimensional changes were these: the centre of gravity moved four centimetres toward the tip; the minimum permitted diameter of the tail increased, restricting extremely slender, high-lift tail profiles; and the event remained the men's 800-gram javelin. It did not become a lighter implement.

The aerodynamics behind these changes are the only slightly technical part of this essay. They deserve explanation because the logic of the whole affair lies here.

In an old high-performance javelin, the centre of pressure could move relative to the centre of gravity as the angle of attack changed, allowing a positive pitching moment and sustained lift. Put simply, the old javelin could pitch upward in flight, behave like a gliding airfoil, travel far along a shallow trajectory, and land flat. Flat landings created two problems: deciding whether the tip had struck first could be difficult and disputed, and the implement travelled too far.

The new specification moved the centre of gravity forward relative to the aerodynamic forces and, together with shape restrictions, changed the pitching behaviour. Under the relevant positive-angle-of-attack conditions, the javelin tended more strongly toward a nose-down pitching moment. Put simply, it pitched down earlier, spent less time gliding, and was more likely to land tip first. Adjudication became clearer and flight range was restrained. This describes the general effect sought by the design limits, not identical behaviour under every wind and release condition.

The construct addressed flat landings and excessive distance through the same intervention: making the javelin pitch downward in flight. One shift of the centre of gravity dealt with two problems at once.

It is easy to miss that the problems were different in kind. Flat landing was a problem of adjudication: could the construct clearly determine whether a throw was valid? It concerned measurement itself. Excessive distance was a problem of venue: could the stadium contain the throw? It concerned physical space. The problems were not necessarily linked. One was inside the ledger, the other outside it. The changes affected both, but range was not an unconsidered side-effect. Bremicker's committee account explicitly identifies clear, measurable landings as the primary goal, while explaining why range and future redesign costs favoured four centimetres. This is not a complete record of every discussion, but it is direct testimony about the priorities.

Its cost is the subject of this essay. The new and old javelins were different implements. Their flight physics differed: one could lift and glide, the other would pitch down. Performances produced by them could not simply be compared within one continuous record sequence.

V. One ledger closes; another opens

The chronology is clear: the construction rules were finalized in 1983, circulated to member federations in May 1984, accepted by the Los Angeles Congress in 1984, and took effect on 1 April 1986. The interval of almost two years allowed competitions, athletes, and manufacturers to make the transition.

At the moment of implementation, this is what happened.

Performances achieved with the two implements ceased to be treated as interchangeable members of a single world-record progression. On 21 September 1986 Klaus Tafelmeier threw 85.74 metres with the new specification. It became the first ratified record in the new sequence.

Hohn's 104.80 metres was not the target Tafelmeier had to surpass.

That sentence is the centre of this essay. Tafelmeier's 85.74 did not challenge Hohn's 104.80, although 104.80 is numerically much larger. The implement categories behind the two numbers had become materially different. After the old sequence closed, Tafelmeier's mark supplied the starting point for a new one.

“Starting from zero” needs qualification. The first new record of 85.74 metres was obviously not a throw of zero metres. It was already a very long throw. Zero describes its position in the record sequence: no earlier ratified record stood before it in that new book. It was the first. The construct opened an empty first page, and Tafelmeier wrote its first line. Between that line and the larger figures in the old ledger, 99.72 and 104.80, lay not a record deficit but the boundary between two books. 85.74 is less than 104.80, yet 85.74 was a current record for the new specification and 104.80 no longer was, because they belonged to different ledgers.

An unusual situation resulted. World Athletics now makes three mutually consistent arrangements: Železný's 98.48 metres is the current men's javelin world record; Hohn's profile lists 104.80 under the old javelin event; and the official historical progression retains old performances with an old-implement designation.

This is closure and separation of a record sequence, not destruction of the underlying historical line.

The distinction must be clear. Legality and current-record status are different judgments. Hohn's throw remains legal and historically ratified, while the event category on which its world-record status depended has been superseded. Similar things happen when a governing body replaces an event distance, a scoring table, a weight class, or an implement category. Earlier performances can remain official without governing the records of the successor event.

The decathlon tables in Essay 7 are a relative of the same principle. There, a new conversion table left Thorpe's ten performances unchanged but changed his total. Here, a new javelin left Hohn's distance unchanged but changed the record sequence to which it belonged. In both cases the event itself did not move; the construct's placement of it did. The difference is that old and new decathlon totals can be set alongside one another because they calculate the same competition. Old and new javelin performances cannot be directly compared in that way because they were produced with different implements.

VI. The original wording cannot be obtained

One limitation must be acknowledged honestly: the original text deciding this reset has not been obtained.

Among the sources consulted, no publicly accessible scan of the complete 1984 congress motion, roll-call vote, amendment history, or verbatim record-reset clause was found. The effective date and substantive decision are strongly established by Technical Committee testimony and subsequent IAAF practice. But without the original record, no particular verb supposedly used by the congress, whether “invalidate,” “abolish,” “close,” “archive,” or “transfer,” should be put in quotation marks as its exact wording.

World Athletics' later phrase about a new set of records accurately describes the institutional result. It should not be presented as a quotation from the 1984 congress itself.

This gap has appeared repeatedly in the series. Here it falls in a particularly revealing place.

Essay 2 could not locate the earliest original record-application form. Essay 3 could not locate Thorpe's original admission letter. Essay 4 found no clause-by-clause record of the 1928 debate over removing the event. In Essay 10, contemporary reporting locates the somersault ban at the Rome Congress, but the original resolution and full deliberative process have not been obtained. Now the original clause resetting the status of one of this sport's most famous performances is unavailable.

Each instance has the same shape: the construct preserved its conclusion, the closed ledger and the new record sequence, while the available material does not let us reconstruct the complete discussion that led to it. Here the contrast is especially sharp. The affected performance, 104.80 metres, is one of the sport's most discussed numbers. A performance recalled countless times has no readily accessible original record of the moment its status changed. The result is widely known; this essay has not obtained a complete original decision-making record.

The recurring pattern permits a provisional conclusion. The construct produces judgments that enter rules, record tables and archives. In this inquiry, those outcomes have often been easier to obtain than a complete account of their formation. Discussions, disputes, trade-offs and votes cannot always be joined together from the public material. To borrow a factory image, we can see the product without yet having the records needed to reconstruct every operation. That is not a claim that every factory or institution discards its process records. The gap is between executing a published judgment and being able to retrace how it arose. A public conclusion does not automatically place every step of its reasoning before the reader.

Another related item is missing. No contemporary motion, federation proposal, athletes' petition, or congress amendment has been found expressly proposing that Hohn retain the title of old-implement world-record holder while a new list opened. Nor has documentary evidence been found that such a proposal was formally rejected, or that the IAAF issued reasons for rejecting it.

That is interesting because the outcome actually achieved was very close to that hypothetical preservation proposal. The old progression remained in official record history, and Hohn's mark continued to be classified under the old event. During the women's javelin transition in 1999, an IAAF spokesperson used clearer language: the old marks would be identified as having been achieved under different conditions. That archival arrangement resembles the supposed preservation proposal, except that the old performances no longer receive the unqualified title of current world record.

The construct therefore did not erase all old performances to preserve comparability, as the popular story suggests. In an important sense it did the opposite: it declared the two implements incomparable within a single current-record sequence while preserving the old progression as history. “Erasure” is defensible only as a metaphor for the loss of current-record status. It is not a literal description of the statistical archive.

VII. A number that can no longer be caught, and its two truths

Return now to the most striking question, and the easiest to get wrong: can 104.80 metres never be equalled?

The answer must be divided in two. Neither half amounts to the popular “eternal record.”

First: 104.80 metres has ended its life as a current world record. It is no longer the target anyone must surpass. The current men's world record is Železný's 98.48 metres. A new performance challenges that number, not Hohn's. In current-record terms, 104.80 has withdrawn into the old-event archive.

Second: no sports institution can establish as a fact that the numerical distance 104.80 metres will never be reached again. A future athlete could theoretically throw that far with the current implement, though no one has yet done so and 98.48 remains the present maximum. A recognized historical-implement competition could reproduce the distance without changing the current-specification world record. Permanence is a prediction, not a ratification category.

The phrase “eternal record” conflates two things: the end of 104.80 as a current record, and the impossibility of reproducing the number. The former is true. Its current-record status has ended. The latter cannot be established. No one can guarantee that the numerical distance will never again be attained in any form.

Separating these claims matters because combining them produces a conclusion that is both inaccurate and, oddly, diminishing. “Eternal record” sounds like praise, an imperishable monument. Yet the error obscures what is genuinely strange. The strange thing is not that the number can never be reached, but that the conditions under which it entered this record sequence no longer exist. “Eternal record” directs attention to the number when it should be directed to the javelin. The central fact is not the number's size. It is that the construct withdrew the implement that produced it.

The accurate and unusual statement is this: Hohn threw with an implement that no longer exists as an authorized implement of the current event. After April 1986, the old-specification javelin was no longer legal for that competition. In ordinary current competition, nobody can use it to produce another performance because the implement itself has left the event.

This is the remainder of the essay, in one of the sharpest forms encountered in the series.

Earlier remainders were names omitted from lists, causes that could not be calculated, techniques left unadjudicated, and actions that could have been admitted but were not. Each fell outside the ledger in its own way. Hohn's throw is not outside it. It is openly present in the official record progression, clearly designated and available to anyone who looks. It is legal, valid, and preserved.

But it is no longer commensurable within the same record sequence as later performances. It cannot be placed in one continuous progression with new-javelin throws because the implements are materially different. It is a legal, valid, fully preserved performance that cannot be made equivalent to its successors within that progression.

This remainder is cleaner than the others because no defect in the performance itself explains its exclusion. It was not removed through a finding of unfairness, cheating, excessive wind, or ineligibility. It is intact within its own book. The only problem is that the book has closed. It closed not because the performance was wrong but because the construct had to stop adding entries to the old book if the new one was to remain internally comparable.

A ledger closed without losing a single thing inside it. Hohn's throw remains clearly on the page. But nobody can write another entry there, because the pen, the javelin that wrote 104.80, has been taken away by the construct. The book is open for everyone to read and simultaneously closed to anything new.

VIII. No conversion is available

What, then, would Hohn's throw amount to with a new javelin?

The old distance alone supplies no uniquely determined answer. The kind of absence involved is the final subject of this essay.

Consider the numbers people calculate. Apply a ten-percent reduction and the result is 94.32 metres. Apply twelve to thirteen percent and it becomes approximately 92.22 to 91.18. Subtract the reported average elite reduction of seven metres and it becomes 97.80.

Those results range across more than six metres, from 91.18 to 97.80. None is an official conversion. None incorporates the unavailable wind conditions and release parameters specific to Hohn's attempt, or his adaptation to a new implement.

The technical reasons are extensive. Aerodynamic coefficients differ by model. Centres of pressure move differently as angle of attack changes. Wind alters relative air speed and effective angle of attack. Release velocity, orientation, pitch, yaw, and spin interact rather than contributing independently. Historical tests found differences of more than ten metres between brands under nominally identical launch and atmospheric conditions. Athletes also change their technique when implements change.

Together these reasons show why the old distance alone cannot be multiplied by one universal factor to yield an equivalent new-javelin mark. The implements differ across interacting dimensions, while wind and release conditions have not been fully preserved. Those conditions cannot be collapsed into a single multiplier. This does not rule out conditional aerodynamic models. Models can state assumptions and produce estimates; they cannot turn missing conditions into known ones or recover a uniquely determined counterfactual from 104.80 alone.

This rules out the most tempting claim: that 104.80 proves Hohn was intrinsically 6.32 metres better than Železný.

That claim subtracts 98.48 from 104.80 and treats the resulting 6.32 metres as the difference between the men's throwing ability. But the distances came from different implement systems. They establish who threw farther in raw metres, not an implement-neutral ranking of ability. Modern biomechanics has supplied no accepted scalar correction that settles the comparison.

Even whether Hohn himself would have surpassed Železný with the new javelin cannot be determined. His ability with the old implement, his physique, and the release that produced 104.80 do not determine how he would have adapted technically over several seasons. His career ended before a meaningful long-term comparison with the new implement could be established. Conversely, Železný's 98.48 cannot reliably be converted into a claim about how far he would have thrown Hohn's javelin.

The essay therefore ends with a double impossibility.

First, 104.80 cannot be caught within its old record sequence because the implement that produced it has been withdrawn. This is the boundary on the implement side.

Second, 104.80 cannot be converted into a uniquely equivalent new-javelin performance because no valid general conversion exists. This is the boundary on the comparability side.

Together these boundaries define the performance's position: later marks cannot enter the closed old-specification sequence, nor can they be treated as equivalent to it without stating conditions. It remains the longest throw in that old book. “Cannot be caught” means that the sequence no longer continues, not that the physical distance of 104.80 metres can never be reached. “Cannot be converted” means that no trustworthy universal conversion exists, not that every qualified historical comparison is forbidden.

The construct can measure how far the throw travelled, 104.80 metres, to the centimetre. It cannot say what that throw is worth in today's javelin system. The old distance alone does not define one uniquely equivalent value. Conditional modelling remains possible, but it cannot recover an unstated, uniquely determined counterfactual from that number alone.

The previous essay ended by saying that when the construct draws a line, it simultaneously crosses out a path it could have taken. Here that claim acquires a more thorough form. To keep the new javelin book internally comparable, the construct closed the old one. It destroyed nothing inside. Hohn's throw remains intact. It merely stopped the ledger. Once the book stopped, its largest number hung there: legal, valid, no longer catchable within that sequence, and without a universal conversion, like something sealed in amber, plainly visible but impossible to touch or take out.

Amber captures both sides of this remainder. What it contains is perfectly preserved: a feather or insect whose every detail may remain visible millions of years later. That corresponds to the throw's legality, validity, and complete preservation. Yet what amber contains is also isolated. It is there, separated from the present by a transparent, uncrossable layer. One can see it but cannot restore it to the living world. That corresponds to the closed progression and the absence of a universal conversion. The construct did not destroy the performance. It did something stranger: it sealed it, leaving it perfectly preserved and isolated on the final page of a closed ledger. Preservation and separation are two sides of the same act.

The ruler has not yet measured accurately. It is still measuring.

在霍恩之前，紀錄的推進是這樣的:帕拉吉1980年的九十六米七二，彼得拉諾夫1983年的九十九米七二。這兩條紀錄相差三米，已經是在以米為單位推進。而霍恩一步加了五米多。這不是釐米級的延續，是一次跳躍。
这一点和第五篇里比蒙那一跳是同一种处境。一个极端的成绩，发生在一个没有被完整记录下条件的时刻，于是它到底有多少来自那个人，有多少来自那一天，永远算不清。区别在于，比蒙那一跳的条件里没有一个可以立法处理的东西，风是合规的，海拔是地理。而霍恩这一投触发的，是对器械本身的重新定义。
这一点和第五篇里比蒙那一跳是同一种处境。一个极端的成绩，发生在一个没有被完整记录下条件的时刻，现存资料还不足以把这个成绩中人的表现与当天条件的贡献精确、干净地拆开。区别在于，比蒙那一跳的风在当时规则内，海拔也没有被设为排除纪录的条件。机构不能改变当地海拔，却可以决定怎样分类、标注或认定高海拔成绩。而霍恩这一投所在的故事，涉及的则是对器械本身的重新定义。
這一點和第五篇里比蒙那一跳是同一種處境。一個極端的成績，發生在一個沒有被完整記錄下條件的時刻，現存資料還不足以把這個成績中人的表現與當天條件的貢獻精確、乾淨地拆開。區別在於，比蒙那一跳的風在當時規則內，海拔也沒有被設為排除紀錄的條件。機構不能改變當地海拔，卻可以決定怎樣分類、標注或認定高海拔成績。而霍恩這一投所在的故事，涉及的則是對器械本身的重新定義。
这个区别很关键。比蒙那一跳，构没有任何可以立法的抓手，它只能把那个算不清的成绩原样收下，放进纪录表，让它在最高处挂了二十三年。而霍恩这一投，构有一个抓手，就是那支标枪本身。标枪是一件器械，器械是可以被重新规定的。所以面对一个太远的成绩，构在比蒙那里无能为力，在霍恩这里却能出手，不是因为它对霍恩这一投的成因了解得更清楚，而是因为这一次它找到了一个可以动的东西。它动不了海拔，它动得了标枪。

这个区别很关键。比蒙那一跳，构当时选择在既有纪录序列中承认，没有另开海拔类别。那个成因算不清的成绩留在最高处二十三年，并不是因为机构原则上不能为高海拔成绩立规则。霍恩这一投所涉及的，是另一个可以直接改动的对象：标枪本身。标枪是一件器械，器械的规格可以重新规定。两例的差别，不是一个有立法权、另一个没有，而是已经采用的制度选择不同。构动不了当地的海拔，能动的却包括纪录类别；在标枪这里，它还动得了那件器械。

這個區別很關鍵。比蒙那一跳，構當時選擇在既有紀錄序列中承認，沒有另開海拔類別。那個成因算不清的成績留在最高處二十三年，並不是因為機構原則上不能為高海拔成績立規則。霍恩這一投所涉及的，是另一個可以直接改動的對象：標槍本身。標槍是一件器械，器械的規格可以重新規定。兩例的差別，不是一個有立法權、另一個沒有，而是已經採用的制度選擇不同。構動不了當地的海拔，能動的卻包括紀錄類別；在標槍這裡，它還動得了那件器械。

標槍這裡不一樣。這裡的邊界，在被越過之前就已經在畫了。技術委員會1982年就開始做實驗；九十九米七二要到1983年5月才出現，那時仍沒有人突破一百米。這個構不是等到霍恩投出一百零四米八零才慌忙反應，它在此之前幾年就已經預見到距離會變得太大，已經在準備了。

这里可以看到一个和前面几篇不同的模式。前面几篇里，构常常是滞后的，它在事情发生之后才反应，才立规则。这里构是提前的，它在极端成绩出现之前就在准备了。为什么这一次它提前了。因为这一次的问题不是一个技术好不好的判断问题，是一个物理上的趋势问题。距离在往上走，这个趋势是可以外推的，不需要等到某一个具体的成绩出现，就能预见到迟早会有一个太大的距离。构对趋势可以提前，对单个的意外只能滞后。而距离的增长是一个趋势，前空翻式的出现是一个意外。

這裡可以看到一個和前面幾篇不同的模式。前面幾篇里，構常常是滯後的，它在事情發生之後才反應，才立規則。這裡構是提前的，它在極端成績出現之前就在準備了。為什麼這一次它提前了。因為這一次面對的，不只是某個新動作可否接受的判斷，還包括能夠持續試驗的射程與落地問題。距離在往上走，這個趨勢是可以外推的，不需要等到某一個具體的成績出現，就能預見到遲早會有一個太大的距離。在這兩個例子里，距離和落地問題的累積給了構提前試驗的線索；前空翻式則在具體動作被展示後，迫使它作出回應。這不是說所有新動作都必然無法預見。

这个分别值得再想一层。趋势是可以外推的，因为它是连续的，一年比一年远，画一条线就能看出它往哪里去。意外是不可外推的，因为它是离散的，一个人突然想出一个从来没有人想过的动作，这件事没有先兆，画不出线。所以构面对趋势的时候，可以像看着潮水上涨一样提前筑坝;面对意外的时候，它只能等那件事发生了，才知道有这样一件事，然后才反应。标枪的距离是潮水，前空翻式是一块突然砸下来的陨石。对潮水可以预备，对陨石只能事后清理。这就是为什么同样是这个构，在两件事上一个提前一个滞后。

这个分别值得再想一层。这里可以外推的是距离上限可能扩张的趋势，不是每个赛季都比上一年更远，也不是画一条线就能保证它兑现。对比之下，德拉米尔把前空翻带到比赛中，给规则提出了一个具体而突兀的问题。可以把前者比作涨潮时提前筑坝，后者比作事后才发现需要处理的陨石。这是帮助理解这两个案例的比喻，不是一条“趋势总能预见、意外永远没有先兆”的定律。一个构能不能提前准备，要看它已经掌握了什么线索、能试验什么，以及准备为哪些可能性付出代价。

新的重量分布把压力中心移到了重心的后面，在正攻角上产生一个负的俯仰力矩。说得直白些，新标枪在飞行中会自己把头往下压，而不是继续滑翔或者平落。它扎着头落地，尖头先着地，判罚清楚了;而且因为它不再滑翔，它飞得近了。
新规格使重心相对于气动力的作用位置前移，并配合外形限制，改变了飞行中的俯仰特性。在相应的正攻角条件下，标枪更倾向于产生使尖头向下的俯仰力矩。说得直白些，新标枪更早低头，滑翔阶段缩短，更容易尖头先着地，判罚因而更清楚，飞行距离也受到抑制。这不是说所有风况与出手姿态都相同，而是在解释这些设计限制希望获得的总体效果。
新規格使重心相對於氣動力的作用位置前移，並配合外形限制，改變了飛行中的俯仰特性。在相應的正攻角條件下，標槍更傾向於產生使尖頭向下的俯仰力矩。說得直白些，新標槍更早低頭，滑翔階段縮短，更容易尖頭先著地，判罰因而更清楚，飛行距離也受到抑制。這不是說所有風況與出手姿態都相同，而是在解釋這些設計限制希望獲得的總體效果。

这里有一个容易被忽略的地方，就是这两个问题的性质其实不一样。平落是一个判罚问题，它关乎这个构能不能清楚地判定一次投掷有效还是无效，这是一个关于度量本身的问题。距离太大是一个场地问题，它关乎体育场装不装得下，这是一个关于物理空间的问题。这两个问题本来没有必然联系，一个是账本内部的，一个是账本外部的。而重心前移这一个改动，恰好同时压下了它们。这有点像运气，一个为解决判罚而设计的改动，顺带解决了场地。但也正因为它同时解决了两个问题，后来关于这次改动到底主要是为了哪一个的争论，才一直没有定论。

edits.before: 这里可以看清这个构在面对不确定时的一种典型选择。它本可以承认，人的反应下限我不确定，所以我在判罚时留出足够的余地，把疑点留给运动员。它没有这样做。它选择了划一条确定的线，而划线就必须选一个具体的数，选了这个数，就等于宣布线那边的一切都不成立。这是一个用确定性换真实的交易:它得到了一条清楚的，可执行的线，代价是把那些落在线外的真实，当成了不存在。对一个必须在赛场上当场做出判罚的构来说，这个交易也许是不得不做的，因为它没有办法在每一次起跑后都停下来，去争论人到底能多快反应。它需要一个当场能用的数。可是需要一个当场能用的数，和这个数是真的，是两回事。它用一个当场能用的定义，替换了一个它并不掌握的真相。

edits.after: In the 2022 world championship 110-metre hurdles final, Devon Allen registered 0.099 seconds and was disqualified. The number marked a detected change in force after the gun; it did not by itself establish when the movement began or whether the gun caused it. Under the rule, a reading below 0.100 triggers a possible-false-start alert, followed by recall and the starter's examination of times and other available information. The alert alone is not an automatic disqualification.
edits.reason: Corresponding approved source correction
edits.before: In the 2022 world championship 110-metre hurdles final, Devon Allen registered a reaction time of 0.099 seconds and was disqualified. The difference between legal and illegal was one thousandth of a second. Nothing about the sensor reading suggested he had moved before the gun in ordinary language. Under the rule, a reaction below 0.100 counted as a false start.

edits.after: Allen's sanction and the physiological interpretation of his recorded interval are distinct questions. Showing that some humans can react faster than the threshold would justify reviewing the rule. It would not, without evidence about this particular start and its measurement, establish that Allen's sanction was wrong.
edits.reason: Corresponding approved source correction
edits.before: The verdict did not say that the apparatus had failed. It said that a movement recorded too soon after the signal could not be recognized as a legitimate human response.

edits.after: The threshold rests on a physiological proposition: auditory reaction plus the force required to register a start was assumed not to occur legitimately below about one tenth of a second. New evidence can challenge that proposition. Once incorporated into a rule, however, changing the number requires a formal revision, not an official's spontaneous response to one study. A binding rule is not thereby a scientifically proven or unrevisable truth.
edits.reason: Corresponding approved source correction
edits.before: The threshold began from a physiological proposition: auditory reaction plus the force required to register a start was assumed not to occur legitimately below about one tenth of a second. If kept as an assumption, new evidence could weaken confidence in it. Once incorporated into the rule, the number became a definition. A sub-0.100 result was not merely suspicious; it generated the legal status.

edits.after: No start rule can eliminate the remainder. A fixed threshold offers consistency but risks excluding some genuine fast reactions; a lower threshold may admit more anticipation, and individual visual judgment brings its own inconsistencies. These are risks to assess, not proof of what happened in Allen's case. A workable line distributes uncertainty. It must not pretend to have resolved every physiological and causal question on either side.
edits.reason: Corresponding approved source correction
edits.before: No start rule can eliminate the remainder. A fixed line yields consistency and spectacle at the cost of edge cases. Individual visual judgment might rescue some edge cases at the cost of unequal decisions. The impossible real movements—responses that occurred but cannot be credited—are the price of making every lane answer to one start.

edits.before: 可以查到的是，直到1990年，用的是一个一百二十毫秒的标准，而一百毫秒此后成了国际田联的标准，一些后来的记述把它出现在规则里的时间定在1991年前后。但找不到任何一份数字化的国际田联代表大会记录或者技术委员会决议，既说采用零点一零零秒，又指认一个具体的实验作为它的证据基础。
edits.after: 佩因和希布斯2007年的研究回顾说，1990年以前使用的是一百二十毫秒，后来采用一百毫秒；另一些后来的记述把这个变化放在1991年前后。但本篇还没有找到一份原始的国际田联大会记录或技术委员会决议，同时写明首次采用零点一零零秒，并列出具体实验依据。后人的回顾是一条线索，还不能替代那份决定本身。
