In this essay
  1. I. A contrast that must first be dismantled
  2. II. A real advantage that has been exaggerated
  3. III. The forty-millimetre line has no published derivation
  4. IV. Vienna: a performance that was never a record
  5. V. Swimming retained its records too
  6. VI. Both sides have a case
  7. VII. Why there is no adjudication here
  8. VIII. A conclusion chosen, not compelled

I. A contrast that must first be dismantled

This essay was originally going to present a clean contrast: running shoes kept their records, swimsuits had theirs annulled. Two structurally identical equipment disputes, two opposite decisions.

That contrast is wrong. It must first be dismantled, or the whole essay will rest on sand.

Here is what actually happened. World records set in the polyurethane swimsuits of 2009 were not annulled. FINA retained them, provided they had been achieved in recognized competitions while the suits remained approved. Most of the forty-three world records set at the Rome World Championships remain in the historical progression.

Running shoes were treated similarly. World Athletics retained eligible road performances achieved in shoes later restricted or superseded by new rules. It did not delete performances achieved in thick-soled, carbon-plated shoes.

What about Kipchoge's 1:59:40.2 in Vienna? It is often described as an annulled world record. But it was never a world record. It was a specially arranged attempt, announced and understood beforehand to be ineligible for record recognition. The reasons it could not enter the record book were independent of the shoes.

The neat contrast therefore fails. It was not retention in one case and annulment in the other. Both retained their records. The real question is not why the construct gave opposite answers to the same problem, but why it chose not to annul the performances, when the opposite choice was available.

The preceding two essays concerned a construct rewriting rules and resetting records when an implement definition was crossed. The 1986 javelin change closed the old-specification ledger and opened a new one. Here we encounter the reverse: faced with equipment that similarly crossed an established boundary, the construct declined to reset the records and kept old performances and new technology in the same book. That choice is defensible, just as the opposite javelin choice was defensible. Its opposite would also have been defensible.

This essay has no answer. It is the first in the series, so far, that genuinely has none. That absence is its subject.

Why this essay in particular? Earlier technical questions retained a factual core. How much of Beamon's jump came from altitude? There is no answer, but it is at least a question about facts, even if their contributions cannot be calculated. The question here concerns value. Retain or annul is not something more data can settle. No amount of experimental evidence tells us whether a legal but non-comparable performance ought to count, because “ought” is not something data can answer. For the first time, the distinction between fact and value becomes the centre of an entire essay. And value is precisely where the construct is least capable of achieving closure.

II. A real advantage that has been exaggerated

First establish the facts about running shoes, since both sides begin there.

Thick-soled, carbon-plated shoes do produce a measurable advantage. Repeated controlled experiments have demonstrated it. The earliest advanced shoes generally reduced submaximal metabolic cost by approximately two to four percent relative to conventional racing shoes.

That is a population average. It is real.

But two qualifications must immediately be added, or the number will be misread.

First, a four-percent reduction in metabolic cost does not mean a four-percent faster race. Racing involves fatigue, turns, gradients, surfaces, weather, fuelling, and tactics. A four-percent oxygen saving does not mechanically become a four-percent faster marathon. Observational studies have estimated marathon-time effects between 0.6 and 2.8 percent, depending on sex and modelling assumptions, generally smaller than the laboratory's four percent.

Second, individual differences are enormous, and they are observed differences, not merely hypothetical ones. In one controlled experiment with world-class Kenyan runners, laboratory running-economy responses across the seven Kenyan runners and tested shoe models ranged from an 11.3-percent detriment to an 11.4-percent benefit. The same shoe could be a substantial help to one person and a burden to another. Some athletes respond strongly; others improve hardly at all; some use more energy at the fixed test speed in a particular model.

Keep this second point in mind. It will become one of the weightiest elements of the argument.

The two sides disagree over whether the advantage constitutes a discontinuity or ordinary footwear improvement. One calls it a rupture: unusually resilient foam could be used in much larger volumes because the plate and geometry stabilized the platform, producing a metabolic effect several times larger than the marginal differences usually observed between traditional racing shoes. The other calls it continuous innovation: every racing shoe modifies cushioning, stiffness, traction, and geometry. There is no motor or external energy source. The benefit still depends on the athlete.

Another popular claim should be dismantled: that the carbon plate alone returns enough energy to explain the whole advantage. That does not hold. Removing or reducing longitudinal bending stiffness in an otherwise similar shoe did not eliminate its economy benefit. The plate's isolated contribution is not the system's total effect. The advantage arises from interactions among foam energy return, stack height, rocker geometry, mass, and altered joint mechanics, not from the plate alone.

This connects with Beamon's jump in Essay 5. Several interacting factors combine to produce an effect, and one cannot simply isolate a single factor and assign it a definite contribution. The carbon plate is not a motor, just as altitude was not the sole cause of Beamon's jump.

III. The forty-millimetre line has no published derivation

From 2017 to 2019, road performances accelerated unusually sharply, coinciding with the rapid spread of advanced footwear.

A study spanning 2001–2019 and including 11,400 top-one-hundred performances found that 2017–2019 was the three-year window with the greatest average improvement in almost two decades. Those three years accounted for approximately forty-four percent of the improvement in women's marathon performance since 2001 and thirty-five percent of the men's.

The acceleration is real. Its cause is disputed.

The shoe-centred explanation points to mutually reinforcing evidence: timing, adoption patterns, laboratory effects, changes within athletes, and the exceptionally sharp three-year jump. The multifactor explanation points to faster courses, a deeper East African field, improved pacing and fuelling, weather selection, appearance fees, training, and the preferential adoption of new shoes by runners who were already faster. Shoe allocation in observational data was not random.

Without long-term randomized assignment, confounding in observational data needs careful treatment. The evidence supports a footwear contribution without uniquely and exactly apportioning the entire acceleration between shoes and other influences. This does not invalidate all causal research or rule out better estimates. Again we encounter Essay 5's structure: an effect cannot simply be divided into independent contributions.

World Athletics responded on 31 January 2020. Road-shoe soles could be no thicker than forty millimetres and could contain no more than one embedded rigid plate.

The January 2020 announcement examined here supplied no complete quantitative derivation uniquely fixing the limit at forty millimetres.

World Athletics cited its internal Assistance Review Group's assessment of independent research that had found sufficient cause for concern and announced a working group to guide further research, certification, and long-term regulation. But the January 2020 announcement published no formal evidence table, model, threshold-validation study, or calculation explaining why the limit was forty rather than thirty-five, thirty, or forty-five millimetres.

Legal analysis characterized the line as regulatory and precautionary, not as a result directly demonstrated by a particular experiment.

The connection with earlier essays is especially clear. In Essay 7, the public material located here did not fully reconstruct the development of the decathlon coefficients. Here the January 2020 announcement supplied no quantitative derivation uniquely fixing forty millimetres. It did publish policy reasons: protecting competition integrity, pausing more radical designs and allowing further research. Lacking a unique experimental derivation is not the same as lacking justification. A line can be precise to the millimetre while readers still need to ask how those reasons support it, and how it compares with other possible limits.

A further point matters. The forty-millimetre limit separates acceptable from unacceptable shoes, but a benefit does not naturally change from reasonable to unreasonable at precisely forty millimetres. Height, foam and geometry interact; adjacent numbers need not mark a difference in kind. Experiments can inform the consequences of forty, thirty-nine or other limits, and a rule can explain its trade-offs. An experiment alone cannot turn a changing effect into the one boundary that ought to be adopted. Having to decide is not the same as having to decide arbitrarily. A choice can be reasoned and contestable without being uniquely compelled by the data.

Other information is also unavailable. Was a stricter proposal, such as thirty millimetres or a complete ban, formally put forward and voted down? No meeting record has been located. A complete named membership list for every phase of the working group is also unavailable. The gaps have a familiar shape: the conclusion and some reasons are public, while the available material does not reconstruct the full proposal and deliberation process. The initial Assistance Review Group membership was published; lacking a complete roster for every phase does not mean no names were ever released.

IV. Vienna: a performance that was never a record

Now consider the most frequently misdescribed performance: Kipchoge's 1:59:40.2 in Vienna.

The familiar version says that he broke two hours and set a record, only for World Athletics to annul it because of his shoes.

Every link in that story is wrong.

It was not an annulled record because it was never an eligible record. The obstacle was not the footwear but the organization of the attempt.

More than forty elite pacemakers were arranged in rotating teams. A group ran around Kipchoge in an aerodynamic formation, changing approximately every 4.8 kilometres. Computational fluid dynamics and wind-tunnel research informed the formation. Drinks were handed to him from a moving bicycle rather than collected by him at fixed stations. A lead vehicle projected visual pacing guidance.

Together these arrangements made a specially organized attempt that did not meet ordinary marathon record conditions; that does not make every favourable condition a violation in itself.

World-record recognition requires a genuine competition, properly arranged, advertised, authorized, and conducted under the rules. The Vienna arrangement, with rotating helpers who were not competitors in the race, did not meet the usual conditions for world-record ratification; having one runner as the target is not by itself a separate violation. Legal pacemakers are competitors who start the race and remain subject to its rules. Assistance by people who are not competing, who leave and re-enter, or who are stationed to pace an athlete without being competitors in that race is prohibited. Rotating fresh teams in and out is fundamentally different from ordinary legal pacing.

Vienna was ineligible for reasons independent of the shoes. Rotating non-competing pacemakers and moving refreshments raised the assistance and feeding problems that made this specially organized attempt ineligible under ordinary record conditions. Ideal pacing, a suitable course and favourable weather are not each a violation merely because they help; the actual competition, course and assistance conditions matter. Whatever the precise legal status of the footwear, it would not turn the attempt into a ratifiable record.

An honest qualification must also be added about the shoes themselves. The exact engineering specifications of the Vienna prototype are unavailable. No complete manufacturer's specification or public destructive inspection of Kipchoge's actual Vienna shoes has been located. The later retail model was publicly described as having one full-length carbon plate, but that does not prove the prototype had the same construction. Media widely speculated about stack heights above forty millimetres and as many as three plates. Those remain unconfirmed claims.

The accurate description is therefore this: a real and extraordinary performance, an attempt explicitly understood beforehand to be ineligible for record recognition, excluded because it failed competition and assistance conditions independent of the unresolved details of its shoe construction.

Calling Vienna an annulled record merges two separate matters: the performance's ineligibility and the controversy over the shoes. The first does not depend on the second. Even perfectly compliant footwear would not have made Vienna record-eligible.

V. Swimming retained its records too

Swimming likewise did not annul the records, despite the popular story.

In 2008, a suit combined densely woven elastane fabric, polyurethane panels, body compression, a water-repellent surface, and ultrasonically welded seams. Development testing claimed roughly twenty-four percent less skin-friction drag than older fabric. That was a manufacturer's development-test claim, not an independently verified twenty-four-percent improvement in race performance.

In 2009, competing suits intensified impermeable polyurethane coverage, compression, trapped-air effects, and buoyancy effects. Some leading designs were effectively all-polyurethane full-body suits, rather than textile suits with limited panels.

The Rome World Championships produced forty-three world records.

To appreciate how unusual that was, set it against the ordinary scale. A few world records at one championship would already be remarkable. Forty-three meant broad sections of the record book being rewritten within days. Retrospective studies estimated gains of several percentage points in certain events, an extraordinary quantity in a sport decided by hundredths of a second. The number's abnormality became one of the strongest arguments for annulment: a technological change accompanying forty-three world records is difficult to describe as merely routine equipment evolution.

FINA then acted. On 24 July 2009 its congress approved a return to textile suits and limits on body coverage. For existing records, however, it chose no retrospective cancellation. On 31 July it confirmed that the old approved list would remain valid through 31 December, with new requirements applying from 1 January 2010.

On this point FINA and World Athletics did the same thing: restrict the future without rewriting the past. Earlier records stayed in the progression and remained current until surpassed.

FINA's public reason was that the records had been set under the rules and conditions applicable at the time, and it would not reconsider them.

Another popular explanation must be dismantled: that FINA judged the records fair because everyone had equal suits.

That was not its claim. The formal public reason was narrower: the performances were legal under the rules then in force. Access was not literally equal. Contracts, national-team arrangements, supply, fit, approval timing, and model performance differed. The construct declared legality, not fairness, still less universal equality. Legality and fairness are separate judgments. It made only the former.

VI. Both sides have a case

The real question is now clear. Running shoes and swimsuits did not receive opposite treatment. Both retained their records. That choice can be strongly opposed and strongly defended. This section presents both cases. The essay will not adjudicate between them.

Begin with the strongest case for retention.

First, legality and institutional responsibility. Athletes are entitled to rely on governing bodies' rules and approved lists. FINA approved the suits and kept those approvals effective through 31 December. World Athletics permitted compliant carbon-plated shoes in recognized road races. Retrospectively penalizing athletes would transfer the regulator's delay or error onto competitors who followed the rules at the time.

Second, records have never been technologically pure. Tracks, pools, timing, lane ropes, starting blocks, training science, nutrition, bicycles, rackets, and shoes continually change. A record measures the best performance under conditions recognized on its date, not an abstract constant of unaided humanity. Retrospectively drawing a line at polyurethane or thick foam requires a defensible explanation of why those innovations differ in kind from every previously accepted improvement. That explanation is difficult to give.

Third, no scientifically valid subtraction exists. Average effects cannot be subtracted from individual performances. Shoe responses range from disadvantages to double-digit laboratory benefits. Suit effects vary with fit, body shape, stroke, and distance. An individual record cannot reliably be converted into a hypothetical textile-suit or traditional-shoe performance. Here the enormous individual differences from Section II matter. If the same shoe affects different runners so differently, there is no fixed bonus that can be assigned to everyone wearing it and then deducted.

Fourth, selective annulment would rest on uneven evidence. Photographs and surviving product records cannot conclusively identify every shoe or suit variant. Prototypes changed; customized fit varied; approval status evolved rapidly. Annulment limited to clearly identified users might leave equally assisted but unidentified performances untouched, producing a less accurate record book.

Together these four arguments make a strong case for retention. The opposing case is comparably strong.

Consider the strongest arguments for annulment or reclassification.

First, a record is an institution of comparability, not merely a legal competition result. A championship determines who won under the day's rules. A record claims a best performance across history. A governing body could preserve medals and places while declining to make a technologically discontinuous performance the benchmark for athletes obliged to use materially slower equipment.

Second, governing bodies can correct their own category errors, and have done so. Cycling's hour record supplies a precedent. The UCI moved technologically assisted performances into a “Best Human Effort” category and reinstated an earlier benchmark achieved with conventional equipment. Retrospective reclassification is institutionally possible even when the performances were celebrated at the time. This matters because it establishes that non-annulment is not an incapacity. The opposite can be done and has been done. Retention is a choice.

Third, the performance discontinuity was exceptionally large. Rome produced forty-three world records; retrospective studies estimated gains of several percentage points in certain events. The top-one-hundred running acceleration of 2017–2019 was the largest three-year improvement in the two-decade dataset. Such synchronized jumps can be read as evidence that the record category had materially changed before the rules caught up.

Fourth, formal legality is insufficient when the approval process itself is defective. FINA repeatedly revised its 2009 approvals and struggled to measure buoyancy, permeability, and material composition. World Athletics' earlier rules prohibited unfair assistance without an operational advance test. Provisional regulatory approval does not necessarily establish that the resulting records belong to the same historical category.

Fifth, unequal access was intrinsic rather than incidental. Early advanced shoes went first to selected sponsored athletes. Access to polyurethane suits depended on contracts, federations, supply, and last-minute approvals. When a technology has substantial benefits, exclusive or unstable access affects both competition between contemporaries and the hierarchy of records.

Together these five arguments also make a strong case for annulment.

Like the retention case, this is not necessarily an extreme position indifferent to athletes. It rests on an equally serious principle: records mean something because they are comparable. A record that cannot be compared with successors loses its central function. On this view, a mark that later athletes in compliant equipment could never approach would cease to be a monument worth aspiring to and become an impassable wall. It would hold everyone below a height partly produced by something they were no longer permitted to use. The annulment side defends the principle that records should be comparable human benchmarks, not equipment's unreachable residue. That principle is as legitimate as non-retroactivity.

Both sides have a case. How they have one is the heart of the essay.

VII. Why there is no adjudication here

These are not a correct side and an incorrect side, one defensible and one indefensible. Both are defensible, but they stand on different ground.

Retention rests on contemporaneous legality and finality. On that foundation, a performance achieved in compliant equipment at an official competition is a valid record, and retrospectively changing its status is unjust.

Annulment rests on longitudinal comparability within a record category. On that foundation, a performance that prevents meaningful comparison between generations should not be their benchmark, even if it was entirely legal when achieved.

Both foundations are real, and they point in opposite directions. Which one is chosen depends less on proving one uniquely correct than on what the construct prioritizes: legality and finality at the time, or long-term comparability of the category.

That is why this essay offers no answer. It is not a problem that more evidence alone would automatically dissolve. The record still has gaps; even a fuller account would require an explanation of how contemporaneous legality and long-term comparability should be weighed. The available material does not uniquely exclude every other reasonable option. Primary records establish three institutionally coherent options: prospective restrictions with retention, retrospective reclassification, and parallel records for equipment eras. They supply no rule demonstrating that one is universally more legitimate.

Other sports give different answers, which is precisely the point. Golf and tennis tend toward prospective rules preserving earlier legal achievements. Cycling reclassified records when equipment fundamentally changed the historical test. Archery maintains parallel, technically defined record categories: compound-bow records do not replace recurve records simply because both are archery. Three approaches, with no cross-sport principle establishing which alone is right.

This connects with Essay 9. There the construct declined to decide whether glide or rotation was superior because no universal optimum had been established. Here it did decide: it retained the records. But no objective standard uniquely compelled that decision. It could have chosen the opposite. Essay 9 concerned a construct declining to adjudicate; here the adjudication hangs between two defensible foundations.

The difference deserves another look. Facing glide and rotation, the construct did not intervene because it lacked a single scale that could rank the techniques universally. Its silence acknowledged that absence. Here it intervened and chose retention. But contemporaneous legality, the foundation it chose, had no demonstrably superior claim over longitudinal comparability. The decision was therefore not uniquely grounded by an objective rule. It selected one of two equally available grounds. It could have selected the other. Silence and choice reveal something in common: without an objective standard, silence honestly refrains from choosing, while choice selects a ground that could have been otherwise. Neither is the sort of reproducible judgment compelled by a shared criterion.

Essay 7 offers another connection. The decathlon scoring table faced incompatible definitions of fairness, so even the proper question was not unique. Here retention and annulment both work because they express different reasonable understandings of a record. One sees it as the best competition result under the conditions of its time. The other sees it as a comparable benchmark across eras. Like the definitions of fairness in Essay 7, neither can be demonstrated to be the uniquely correct understanding.

VIII. A conclusion chosen, not compelled

Bring the essay together.

Running shoes and swimsuits generated structurally similar equipment disputes. Both combined interacting features rather than relying on one magical component. Both produced measurable average improvements with large individual differences. Both spread rapidly after early competitive success. Both governing bodies initially operated with broad, qualitative fairness or equipment rules, then adopted numerical or material restrictions. Both applied the new restrictions prospectively and retained performances achieved in recognized, compliant competitions.

Faced with these similar cases, the construct made the same choice: retention.

But the choice is contestable. It is not the only correct course, not a conclusion forced by evidence, not a decision with no alternative. The construct selected one of several defensible possibilities. Opposite retention stood comparably strong reasons for annulment or reclassification, and an actual precedent for the contrary choice: cycling's hour record.

This joins the essay to its two predecessors.

In Essay 10, the construct discovered a boundary when it was crossed and decided whether to defend it or open it. I noted that the decision could have gone the other way. In Essay 11, redefining an implement reset the records and closed the old javelin ledger. Both involved choices, though they could appear natural or almost compelled. This essay turns “it could have been otherwise” from a side remark into its whole subject. It shows clearly that structurally similar equipment disputes can lead either to a reset, as in javelin, or to retention, as with shoes and swimsuits. Both have complete arguments and precedents. The construct chose the latter.

The remainder takes another new form.

Earlier remainders were excluded names, unquantifiable causes, unadjudicated techniques, actions that might have been admitted, and legal but non-comparable performances. Here the remainder is the unchosen option itself. Annulment, reclassification, parallel era records: these were workable possibilities with precedents. The construct chose retention, leaving them as paths not taken. They were not wrong. They were unchosen.

This remainder is especially difficult to identify because it does not appear in the ledger at all. It is another form the entire ledger could have taken. Had the construct chosen annulment, today's record book would look different. Rome's forty-three records would carry different designations or occupy a separate era sequence. That alternative book was a real possibility. It failed to materialize not because it was unworkable, but because the construct took the other road.

There was no signpost at the fork. No single principle supplied by these materials excluded every other reasonable direction. It chose retention with a complete set of reasons; it could have chosen annulment with another complete set. Both roads led to coherent record institutions, but different ones. One was selected. The other remained across the fork, equally defensible but untravelled.

To see how unusual this remainder is, place it beside the others. An omitted name can be spoken. Unquantifiable causes can still be recognized as present. An incomparable javelin performance can be seen in the old book. Each has an object one can point to. This remainder has none. It is a record book that never happened, the book that would exist today had the construct chosen annulment. Nothing in the actual world can be identified as that book, precisely because it is the unrealized version. It is an absent road, a choice's reverse side, a possibility diverted away. Of all the things the construct cannot close, this is the lightest, too light even to enter the ledger. Yet it is also the most comprehensive, because it is another possible form of the whole ledger.

The construct can measure a shoe's energy saving, a swimsuit's drag reduction, and a performance to the hundredth of a second. It cannot measure whether those performances ought to count. “Ought” is not a measurable quantity. It is a judgment that must be chosen, with no uniquely correct answer.

The ruler has not yet measured accurately. It is still measuring.

edits.before: 这个规则平时不显眼，因为大多数案子的证据不是势均力敌的，总有一边更强，裁决跟着更强的那边走，举证责任落在谁身上并不改变结果。举证责任真正起作用的，恰恰是证据两边持平，无法判定的时候。而假肢这类案子，由于中心的那个反事实无法被观测，证据几乎注定是无法判定的。所以在这个领域里，那个平时不显眼的规则，变成了决定性的。一个在别处只在边角起作用的规则，在这里走到了舞台中央，因为这里的核心事实，恰恰是那个永远无法被观测，因而证据永远无法真正压向一边的东西。
edits.after: 这个规则在证据未能达到标准时格外显眼。假肢案件的中心反事实不能被直接观测，研究因而必须依赖比较、估计和模型，不确定性很难完全消除。但不能直接观测，不等于证据注定永远持平。后面的利珀案恰好说明，间接证据仍可能使一方达到平衡概率的证明标准。举证责任分配的是证明不足的后果，而不是宣布所有这类案件都只能靠默认规则决定。
edits.reason: Directly unobservable counterfactual does not force evidence to remain balanced: Leeper VI is an internal counterexample; official WA2020 statement confirms burden met.

edits.before: 也就是说，皮斯托瑞斯赢的，只是皮斯托瑞斯，那副假肢，那次比赛。它没有为假肢装置创造一个一般的豁免。
edits.after: 也就是说，皮斯托瑞斯赢的，只是皮斯托瑞斯与案中审查过的那副假肢。它没有为假肢装置创造一个一般的豁免。
edits.reason: Specific athlete/prosthesis limitation is not one-meeting-only eligibility; new English already correctly omits the meeting limitation.

edits.before: 要公道地看，把举证责任压给运动员，当时有它自己的道理，不是纯粹的刁难。国际田联的立场是，运动员掌握着对那个装置的使用权，掌握着它的配置，训练历史和相关的个人成绩数据;让一个申请例外的人来承担举证，被认为可以保护竞争的完整，而且在行政上可操作。这个理由不是没有分量。一个人要求一个例外，由他来证明这个例外无害，在很多别的场合是合理的。问题在于，这个特定的场合有一个别处没有的特征:他要证明的那个东西，依赖于一个无法被观测的反事实。于是一个在别处合理的举证分配，在这里变成了要求一个人去证明一件在物理上无法被证明的事。
edits.after: 要公道地看，把举证责任压给运动员，当时有它自己的道理，不是纯粹的刁难。国际田联的立场是，运动员掌握着对那个装置的使用权，掌握着它的配置，训练历史和相关的个人成绩数据;让一个申请例外的人来承担举证，被认为可以保护竞争的完整，而且在行政上可操作。这个理由不是没有分量。一个人要求一个例外，由他来证明这个例外无害，在很多别的场合是合理的。问题在于，这个特定的场合有一个别处没有的特征:他要证明的那个东西，依赖于一个无法被观测的反事实。于是一个在别处合理的举证分配，在这里变成了要求一个人对一个无法直接实验检验、只能依靠间接证据评估的命题承担证明不足的风险。
edits.reason: Keep reason for criticizing allocation, without claiming legal proof physically impossible.

edits.before: 到这里，举证责任在这项运动里已经翻转了三次。
edits.after: 到这里，举证责任经历了三个阶段、两次方向翻转。
edits.reason: Three positions federation→athlete→federation contain two changes, not three. Remove draft source commentary in English.

edits.before: 三次翻转，对应三个不同的结果。而这三个结果的差别，很大程度上不来自科学的进展，来自举证责任的方向。这是这一篇要说的核心:在一个决定性事实无法被观测的领域里，裁决的实际内容，是举证责任的分配，而这个分配是一个规则性的选择，它可以被措辞或者裁决翻转，翻转之后结果随之翻转。
edits.after: 三个阶段，对应不同的结果，其中有两次举证方向的翻转。这显示举证责任能怎样改变不确定性的法律风险，却不能把三个不同运动员、不同装置与不同证据的案子，当成同一份证据只换规则的实验。皮斯托瑞斯和雷姆的对照让分配的分量可见，利珀的实体败诉则提醒我们：责任分配很重要，实际证据仍然能决定结果。
edits.reason: Pistorius/Rehm/Leeper do not have identical evidence; Leeper merits finding must not be erased by burden narrative.

edits.before: 举证责任的规则，决定的是当证据势均力敌的时候谁输。它不规定一个科学方法，不规定一个最低样本量，不规定一个被接受的比较对象，也不规定一个把优劣聚合起来的算法。平衡概率这四个字，只告诉你在天平持平的时候往哪边倒，它不告诉你天平该怎么称。
edits.after: 举证责任决定谁承担证明不足的后果；平衡概率则要求所主张的事实更可能成立，而不是不成立。两者相关，却不是同一件事。它们都不会自动给出科学方法、最低样本量、比较对象，或把各种优劣加总的算法。当天平持平时，负担责任的一方会输；但在到达这个结果之前，还要判断证据有没有达到那个概率标准。
edits.reason: Separate burden allocation from standard of proof. Balance of probabilities requires more likely than not, not merely a tie-breaking formula.

edits.before: 这个区分很重要，因为它划出了举证责任能做什么，不能做什么的边界。举证责任能做的，是在证据无法判定的时候给出一个结果，它保证案子总能有一个裁决，不会因为科学说不清就永远悬着。举证责任不能做的，是告诉你科学该做到什么程度才算说清了。一个更好的研究方法，一个更合适的比较对象，一个把各阶段优劣加总的算法，这些是科学和政策要回答的问题，举证责任回答不了。所以举证责任是一个兜底的规则，它在真相无法抵达的地方，替裁决兜住底;但它不是通往真相的路，它恰恰是在承认那条路走不通之后，才被启用的东西。
edits.after: 这个区分很重要，因为它划出了举证责任能做什么，不能做什么的边界。举证责任能做的，是在证据无法判定的时候给出一个结果，它保证案子总能有一个裁决，不会因为科学说不清就永远悬着。举证责任不能做的，是告诉你科学该做到什么程度才算说清了。一个更好的研究方法，一个更合适的比较对象，一个把各阶段优劣加总的算法，这些是科学和政策要回答的问题，举证责任回答不了。所以举证责任是一个兜底的规则，它在真相无法抵达的地方，替裁决兜住底;但它不是通往真相的路，它从审理开始就分配证明责任，只是在证据仍不足时，其兜底作用显得格外清楚。
edits.reason: Burden is assigned throughout adjudication, not first activated after truth declared unreachable. Retain fallback metaphor in bounded form.

edits.before: 这就是这个构在这里的处境。它面对一个无法被观测的事实。它没有办法判定这个事实，因为那个有生物肢体的运动员不存在。于是它退到一个更前面的位置，不再试图判定真相，而是分配谁承担无法判定真相的代价。而即便是这个退后的位置，它也没有一个客观的依据来决定该往哪边分配。把责任给国际田联，还是给运动员，这本身是一个价值和法律的选择，而这个选择，三次被作出，三次不同。
edits.after: 这就是这个构在这里的处境。它不能直接观察那个拥有生物肢体的运动员，只能用间接证据评估反事实，并在证据仍不足时分配后果。科学本身也不会自动指定责任该给联合会还是运动员；这还涉及法律上的公平、可操作性与风险分配。前面三个阶段作过两种方向的选择，其中一次又改回原方向。证据的判断和证明不足的代价，必须分开看。
edits.reason: Do not infer cannot judge from no directly observable intact-limb body; three stages not three mutually different allocations.

edits.before: 面对一个不存在的事实，构做不到判定。它能做的，是退后一步，不判定真相，而分配谁承担无法判定真相的代价。

edits.before:
A question the stopwatch cannot see

Oscar Pistorius ran on carbon-fibre prostheses and sought to compete in events governed for athletes without such devices. The stopwatch could rank the performances. It could not answer the prior question: did the prostheses provide an overall competitive advantage prohibited by the rules?

That question is invisible at the finish line. It requires comparison between a real athlete using prostheses and a counterfactual version of the same athlete with biological lower legs. The second body has never existed. No experiment can observe it directly.

Three questions that must remain separate

The public debate often collapsed three issues. First, do the prostheses differ mechanically from biological legs? Clearly. Second, do some differences create local advantages, such as energy return or lower distal mass? Evidence can investigate that. Third, do the combined differences produce an overall advantage in the competitive task? That conclusion does not follow automatically from the first two.

A device may assist one phase and impose costs in another. Starts, acceleration, top speed, curves, stability, fatigue, and fitting belong to the total performance. Selecting one measurable advantage as decisive risks mistaking a component for the whole.

Who must prove the advantage

World Athletics' predecessor initially ruled Pistorius ineligible on the basis of commissioned testing. In 2008 the Court of Arbitration for Sport overturned that decision. The CAS award did not establish that prostheses could never provide an advantage. It held that the federation had not proved that these particular prostheses gave Pistorius an overall net advantage under the applicable rule and evidence.

Burden of proof determined the practical outcome. Under uncertainty, the rule had to decide who would lose if the evidence remained inconclusive. Assign the burden to the athlete and uncertainty excludes; assign it to the regulator and uncertainty permits.

A study that declined to deliver a verdict

Subsequent scientific work continued to find unusual combinations of advantages and disadvantages. Researchers disagreed over which variables were decisive and how to compare them. That disagreement was not scientific failure. It reflected a target—overall advantage relative to an unobservable body—that no single laboratory measure could fully represent.

Science could narrow claims: energy storage differs; limb mass differs; acceleration and swing dynamics differ. The legal construct still had to decide how those findings map onto eligibility.

Rule revision changes the direction

Later rules governing mechanical aids placed greater responsibility on athletes seeking to use non-standard devices to show that the aid would not provide an overall competitive advantage. The substantive uncertainty remained, but its institutional direction changed.

This demonstrates why “follow the science” is incomplete in classification disputes. The same unsettled evidence can produce admission or exclusion depending on the procedural allocation of risk. Science informs the decision; burden of proof decides what happens when science runs out.

A body without a stable address

The category system wants to place every entrant into a rule-defined relation with a reference athlete. Pistorius' body resisted that operation. It was neither an ordinary unassisted body nor a separable machine attached to an otherwise comparable body. Athlete, device, training history, and movement had developed together.

The institution could admit or exclude him. What it could not do was make the counterfactual comparison fully observable. The remainder is not missing data waiting for one better study. It is the absent body the question itself requires.
edits.after:
In this essay
  1. I. A question that cannot be observed
  2. II. Three steps that must remain separate
  3. III. Who bears the burden of proof?
  4. IV. An amendment that reversed the direction
  5. V. A study that declined to decide
  6. VI. A decision that reversed the direction again
  7. VII. Choosing a direction does not specify how much uncertainty is tolerable
  8. VIII. A body the construct cannot accommodate

I. A question that cannot be observed

First make the question precise. The whole essay hangs on it, and it cannot be answered directly.

An athlete who runs on carbon-fibre prostheses seeks admission to open competition against athletes without prostheses. The governing body must decide whether his prostheses give him an overall competitive advantage over athletes who do not use them.

The standard form of that judgment is counterfactual: if this athlete had intact biological limbs instead of prostheses, how fast would he run in the same event?

That question cannot be observed directly.

The version of him with intact biological limbs does not exist. His lower legs are absent. No experiment can give him biological lower legs, have him run, and compare the result with his prosthetic performance. For an athlete with absent limbs, that state of the world can never be experimentally observed.

Pause over this, because it differs from every earlier uncertainty in the series. Altitude's contribution to Beamon's jump existed in principle but was entangled with other factors. That was a difficulty of separation. A shoe's energy saving can in principle be measured, though individual differences are large. That is a difficulty of variation. Here the difficulty is more fundamental: the object required for comparison is not in the world. It is not hidden or too small to measure. It has never been produced. Once a biological lower leg is absent, the performance it might have produced is absent from the observable world too. The construct's reference point is a vacancy.

Researchers can only approach it indirectly: compare the athlete with others, change his prosthetic configuration, simulate, reconstruct through anthropometry, make statistical predictions, or combine these methods. In the Leeper case, the Court of Arbitration for Sport made the limitation clear: a prediction of an athlete's intact-limb performance is necessarily an informed estimate rather than a scientifically verifiable fact, and includes uncertainty that cannot be eliminated.

This therefore differs from the essays that precede it.

Earlier problems retained some observable factual core. The altitude contribution to Beamon's jump could not be disentangled, but the variables existed and had been measured. Whether advanced shoes should count in Essay 12 was a value question, but both sides relied on observable data. Here the problem is not merely an unresolvable calculation or a value judgment. The fact to be judged does not physically exist and cannot be seen.

How does the construct adjudicate when a fact cannot be observed?

This is a wall every system of measurement will eventually encounter. A construct devoted to measurement bases its authority on what can be seen and weighed, yet some things it must judge fall beyond that reach. Earlier invisible things were still approachable: a lost original document, an entangled cause, an unchosen option. Here the invisible thing is a body that never existed. When the construct's central powers, seeing and measuring, fail because there is no object to see or measure, it must either acknowledge its inability or find a way to decide without observing that object. The burden of proof supplies that way.

That is this essay's subject. The answer is surprising but entirely intelligible: when truth cannot be determined, adjudication retreats to a prior question. Who bears the cost of not being able to determine it? Allocating the burden of proof answers that question. Where the evidence remains unresolved, that allocation becomes the decision.

II. Three steps that must remain separate

Before discussing Pistorius, establish a discipline. This essay is easiest to misunderstand at precisely this point. Three things must be kept separate.

First, a laboratory measures a mechanical or physiological difference.

Second, a governing body calls the difference an advantage.

Third, a tribunal decides whether the governing body has proved an overall competitive advantage under a particular rule.

These are three different propositions. Measuring a difference does not establish that it is an advantage. Calling it an advantage does not legally prove that it is an overall advantage.

Ordinary discussion almost always collapses the distinctions. People hear that a prosthesis returns more elastic energy than a biological ankle and intuitively conclude that it must confer an advantage, and therefore that its user must benefit unfairly. But greater elastic-energy return is an isolated mechanical fact. To establish an advantage, one must show that its benefits over the whole event exceed accompanying disadvantages such as lower force production, slower acceleration, or poorer stability. To establish an overall advantage legally, positive and negative factors must then be weighed against a standard of proof. Between additional joules returned and an overall competitive benefit lie two wide gaps. The unobservable counterfactual runs through both.

Take Pistorius. In 2007 the IAAF commissioned Brüggemann's team at the German Sport University Cologne to conduct tests. One bilateral below-knee amputee, Pistorius, and five non-amputee sprinters ran sixty metres on an indoor straight. The study identified lower mechanical work during stance, a substantially different distribution of work among the prosthetic ankle, knee, and hip, lower limb mass, and a high ratio of mechanical energy returned to energy absorbed by the blades. The researchers inferred that the prostheses might permit the same sprint performance at a lower metabolic cost.

That is the first step: measurement and inference. The researchers themselves described the measurements as leading to a hypothesis. A hypothesis, not a conclusion. It was an inference from mechanical work, not a direct experimental reconstruction of the nonexistent athlete with biological limbs.

The IAAF's official summary went further, stating that Pistorius used approximately twenty-five percent less energy than runners without prostheses at the same speed. That is the second step: interpreting the measured difference as an advantage.

The disputed question was not whether mechanical differences had been measured. They had. It was whether those measurements established an overall race advantage after starts, acceleration, bend running, fatigue, force-production limits, and all disadvantages were included.

That third step is legal adjudication, not laboratory measurement. Keeping the three apart is the foundation of the essay.

They must remain separate because each supports a different degree of certainty. Measurement can establish mechanical numbers. Calling the difference an advantage is already an interpretation that places it within a complete race. Deciding whether overall advantage has been proved is a legal act weighing evidence in both directions against a proof standard. Collapsing the steps commonly lends the certainty of the first to the third: because the mechanical difference is established, people assume the overall advantage is established too. In fact, certainty diminishes along the route from a definite mechanical difference to a disputed advantage to an overall net advantage that cannot be directly observed.

III. Who bears the burden of proof?

On 14 January 2008, the IAAF Council found that Pistorius's Cheetah prostheses violated Rule 144.2(e) and declared him ineligible to compete under IAAF rules while using them.

This was an eligibility decision, not merely a scientific statement.

Pistorius appealed to CAS. On 16 May 2008, following a two-day hearing, CAS upheld his appeal, immediately revoked the IAAF Council's decision, and declared him eligible to compete in IAAF-sanctioned events using the prostheses examined in the case.

The crucial point was not that CAS found the prostheses conferred no advantage. It did not make that finding. The crucial point was who bore the burden of proof.

The 2007 Rule 144.2(e) prohibited devices that provided an advantage. Grammatically and legally, the prohibited fact was the existence of advantage. Excluding Pistorius therefore required proving that advantage existed. The party asserting it, the IAAF, had to provide the proof.

The award records that the IAAF accepted the burden of proof, a point the tribunal did not need to discuss further.

That is the essay's first pivot.

Accepting the burden meant the IAAF had to establish an overall net advantage. It failed to do so. CAS observed that the Cologne protocol concentrated on straight-line running at specified speeds without sufficiently incorporating starts, acceleration, bend running, and all countervailing disadvantages. The evidence did not establish overall advantage to the required standard. Under the burden-of-proof rule, the party making the claim lost.

Notice what happened. CAS did not say that the prostheses had no advantage. It said that the party alleging advantage had not proved it to the required standard. Those are entirely different statements. One asserts a fact; the other adjudicates proof. Because the central counterfactual could not be directly observed, the tribunal could make the latter judgment without establishing the former.

The standard was the civil standard, usually called the balance of probabilities. When the evidence is evenly balanced, the party bearing the burden loses.

The rule becomes especially visible when the evidence does not meet the required standard. Prosthesis cases rely on comparison, estimates and models because the central counterfactual cannot be directly observed, leaving uncertainty difficult to eliminate. But unobservability does not condemn the evidence to an eternal tie. Leeper’s case below shows that indirect evidence can still satisfy the balance of probabilities. The burden allocates the consequences of insufficient proof; it does not declare every such case decidable only by default.

Pistorius therefore won not because his prostheses were proved to confer no advantage, but because the IAAF bore the burden and failed to establish advantage on the balance of probabilities. The burden's direction determined who bore the consequences of the unresolved factual question. Those consequences were the decision itself.

IV. An amendment that reversed the direction

CAS expressly limited the decision's scope. It did not apply to another athlete or another prosthesis. Later cases had to be assessed on their own facts.

Pistorius's victory therefore concerned Pistorius and the specific prostheses examined. It created no general exemption for prosthetic devices.

That narrowness later mattered greatly, because the rule changed.

In 2015, after controversy concerning Rehm and legal advice, the IAAF revised the provision. New Rule 144.3(d) prohibited mechanical aids unless the athlete established, on the balance of probabilities, that the aid would not provide an overall competitive advantage over athletes not using it.

That sentence reversed the direction completely.

Under the old rule, the prohibited fact was the existence of advantage, and the IAAF had to prove it. Under the new rule, the condition for permission was the absence of advantage, and the athlete seeking permission had to prove that absence.

Not one laboratory measurement changed. The science remained the science. The counterfactual remained unobservable. Only the consequences of inconclusive evidence changed. Under the old rule, insufficient evidence meant the IAAF lost and the athlete could compete. Under the new one, insufficient evidence meant the athlete lost and could not compete.

The same unresolved fact could therefore yield opposite outcomes under two rules. No new scientific discovery was required. Reversing the burden of proof was sufficient.

Here the essay's central proposition appears in full: where the decisive fact cannot be observed, the practical content of an inconclusive adjudication is an allocation of the cost of not knowing. A change in a rule's wording can reverse that allocation, leading the same evidence toward the opposite outcome.

The 2015 rule assigned the legal risk of uncertainty to the athlete. Uncertain evidence meant the exception had not been established, so the athlete could not compete.

Fairness requires acknowledging that placing the burden on the athlete had its own rationale. It was not simply obstruction. The IAAF's position was that the athlete controlled the device's use and configuration and possessed the relevant training history and personal performance data. Requiring an applicant for an exception to prove the case was considered administratively workable and protective of competitive integrity. That reasoning has weight. In many contexts, a person seeking an exception can reasonably be asked to show that it is harmless. The problem was this context's unusual feature: what had to be proved depended on an unobservable counterfactual. A burden allocation reasonable elsewhere could here become a demand to prove something that could never be directly tested.

V. A study that declined to decide

To see the rule's force, consider its effect on a particular study.

Before Rio 2016, Rehm and German sports bodies commissioned a multi-institutional investigation. It tested three below-knee-amputee long jumpers, including Rehm, and seven experienced non-amputee jumpers. It found effects pointing in opposite directions.

One direction was disadvantage. The amputee group's average maximum sprint and approach speeds were lower, although Rehm's own speed fell within the non-amputee group's range.

The other was favourable mechanics. The amputee jumpers lost less horizontal velocity at take-off, and their prostheses returned more elastic energy than the comparison group's joints below the knee.

The study therefore did not point to one answer. Some findings worked against Rehm and others in his favour. They were measured in different units and could not simply be added.

The authors then did something crucial: they explicitly declined to adjudicate.

The researchers said that, at that stage, they could not determine whether Markus Rehm’s prosthesis did or did not give him an overall advantage.

That is stronger than saying no advantage was found. It does not report an unsuccessful search. It says the study could not determine either proposition. The authors explained that something favourable to one technique could be unfavourable to another, while the limiting factors of the different techniques could not yet be fully identified.

Now place that inconclusive study inside the rule assigning the burden to the athlete.

The rule requires proof of no advantage. The study cannot determine whether an advantage exists. The athlete has therefore not discharged the burden, because uncertainty is not proof of absence. Under that rule, admission is denied.

The direction of the burden directly affects the outcome. If the federation must prove advantage, the same inconclusive study leaves it unable to do so and the athlete may compete. If the athlete must prove no advantage, the study leaves him unable to do so and he is excluded. The study itself favours neither side. It honestly acknowledges uncertainty. Opposite burden allocations turn that neutral uncertainty into admission or exclusion.

The parties read the study in opposing ways. At a press conference on 30 May 2016, Rehm said that no advantage from the prosthesis could be established and treated that as support for continuing his Olympic bid. Critics, including Beckmann and colleagues, stressed that inability to establish advantage did not prove its absence under the applicable rule. The research team's own position was that neither proposition had been established.

Three parties, three formulations, one study. The difference was not the measurements but each party's position relative to the burden of proof.

The example brings the proposition into sharp focus. Disagreement over an honestly inconclusive study concerned not what it measured but who should bear its inconclusiveness. Rehm, seeking to compete, understood uncertainty as insufficient reason for exclusion. Critics defending the rule understood it as failure to establish the exception. The researchers stated that neither proposition had been established, and stopped there. The study left judgment to others. Their judgments depended on the burden's allocation.

That year the IAAF president said Rehm had not, at that stage, demonstrated the absence of advantage. After discussions with the IAAF, Rehm confirmed that he would not pursue qualification for Rio 2016.

VI. A decision that reversed the direction again

The burden later moved back, this time through adjudication.

In 2020 Leeper's case reached CAS. Leeper, a bilateral below-knee-amputee sprinter, sought recognition of his prosthetic performances alongside those of athletes without prostheses.

CAS did two things that must remain separate.

First, it addressed the burden. It held the 2015 clause placing the burden on the athlete unlawful and invalid because of its differential effect on disabled athletes. The reversal was neither necessary nor proportionate, especially when the neighbouring general technology rule placed the burden on the federation. Paragraph 359 invalidated the rule insofar as it required the athlete to establish the absence of overall competitive advantage. CAS severed that clause rather than deleting the entire mechanical-aid prohibition. Following severance, paragraph 362 placed the burden on the IAAF to prove that Leeper, or another disabled athlete seeking to use prostheses, obtained an overall competitive advantage from the particular prostheses concerned.

On burden allocation, the direction returned to the 2008 position: the federation must prove advantage, rather than the athlete prove its absence. Leeper won on that point.

Second, CAS addressed the merits. It found that World Athletics had, on the specific evidence, established an overall competitive advantage from Leeper's particular prostheses, especially their height and resulting leg length, which enabled him to run faster than his estimated intact-limb counterpart. Leeper lost on that point. His appeal succeeded only in part.

Keeping these decisions separate prevents the essay's proposition from collapsing into a simplistic slogan.

The burden determines the starting point and who bears inconclusive evidence. It does not independently determine the destination. In Leeper's case, the burden was assigned to World Athletics, but World Athletics met it on the balance of probabilities. Even with the federation bearing the burden, the athlete lost.

The direction of proof is therefore not the only determining factor. It is a decisive default when evidence remains balanced. When one side genuinely proves its case to the applicable standard, the merits prevail over that default. Leeper's prosthetic-height issue was a case in which the evidence did not remain evenly balanced but met the standard.

Height itself deserves attention because it was one of the more tangible features in this otherwise counterfactual field. A bilateral amputee sprinter's prosthetic height directly determines standing height and leg length; other things being similar, longer legs imply a longer stride. Actual prosthetic dimensions and ordinary anthropometric relationships provide something that can be estimated without wholly reconstructing the absent biological body. In Leeper's case, this relatively tangible feature helped World Athletics satisfy the standard. It illustrates the converse of the earlier argument: when something can be estimated with sufficient confidence, the burden's default recedes and substantive evidence takes over.

A tribunal can therefore reject a federation's burden-allocation rule and still uphold exclusion under a lawfully reassigned burden. Proof allocation and merits are distinct decisions. Leeper's case demonstrates the separation particularly clearly.

VII. Choosing a direction does not specify how much uncertainty is tolerable

By this point, the burden of proof has passed through three stages and two reversals.

The 2007 rule prohibited devices providing advantage, with the burden on the IAAF. In Pistorius, the IAAF accepted that burden but did not meet it, and the athlete was admitted.

The 2015 rule required the athlete to demonstrate no advantage. Rehm faced a study that declined to decide, did not discharge the burden, and did not proceed to Rio.

The 2020 Leeper award severed the athlete-burden clause and restored the federation's responsibility. Under that restored burden, World Athletics nevertheless established the advantage of Leeper's particular prostheses, and the athlete lost on the merits.

The three stages produced different outcomes and included two reversals of the burden. They show how allocation changes the legal risk of uncertainty. But three athletes, devices and evidentiary records are not an experiment in which identical evidence was merely placed under different rules. Pistorius and Rehm make the allocation’s importance visible; Leeper’s loss on the merits reminds us that evidence can still decide the outcome.

A limitation must be added, or the proposition goes too far.

The burden determines who bears insufficient proof; the balance of probabilities asks whether the proposition is more likely true than not. They are related but distinct. Neither automatically supplies a scientific method, minimum sample size, comparator or algorithm for combining benefits and disadvantages. If the evidence is evenly balanced, the burdened party loses. Before that outcome, however, the tribunal must decide whether the probability standard has been met.

This marks the boundary of what the burden can do. It can ensure an outcome when evidence is inconclusive, preventing a case from remaining unresolved indefinitely because science cannot settle it. It cannot specify how good the science must be to settle the question. Better methods, more appropriate comparators, and ways to aggregate effects across phases of an event are matters for science and policy. The burden is a fallback for adjudication when truth cannot be reached, not a route to that truth.

Moving the burden can change a legal result without changing any laboratory measurement. It cannot determine how much scientific uncertainty is acceptable. The deeper question, which method, comparator, and aggregation procedure should establish a prosthesis's net advantage, remains unanswered. The burden merely allocates the cost when that question cannot be resolved.

This is the construct’s predicament. It cannot directly observe the athlete with biological limbs; it must assess the counterfactual through indirect evidence and allocate the consequences if proof remains insufficient. Science alone does not assign the burden to federation or athlete: legal fairness, workability and risk allocation also matter. Across the three stages, the burden took two directions, eventually returning to the earlier one. Assessing evidence and assigning the cost of insufficient proof must remain distinct.

VIII. A body the construct cannot accommodate

Bring the essay together.

The construct assumes that performances can be compared and that comparison requires a common basis. Among athletes without prostheses, that basis is the biological body. Bodies differ, but they are of the same broad kind: muscles, tendons, and bones working under nervous control. That shared category makes comparison possible.

An athlete running with prostheses disrupts the category. Part of the interface producing movement is non-biological. A running prosthesis is primarily passive. Its stiffness, geometry, alignment, and loading govern how it stores and returns energy, while it changes limb mass, lever arms, and the distribution of joint work. It is not the same kind of thing as a biological leg.

The construct therefore confronts a body its comparison framework cannot readily place. To admit it into comparison with non-prosthetic bodies, it asks whether the prosthesis provides an overall advantage. That question calls for the unobservable counterfactual athlete with biological limbs.

This is the remainder, in another new form.

Previous remainders included omitted names, unquantifiable causes, unadjudicated techniques, unchosen options, and legal but non-comparable performances. They fell outside the ledger in different ways, but pointed toward something that existed or could be identified. Here the remainder is a physically nonexistent fact: this athlete running with biological limbs. That version has never existed and cannot be observed. What the construct seeks to judge is not merely outside the book. It is absent from the world.

Faced with a counterfactual it cannot directly observe, the construct can still assess indirect evidence. If that evidence fails to meet the standard, it must also decide who bears the cost of insufficient proof.

This is a sharp version of a recurring movement in the series. When causes remain unresolved, record the result; when a performance table cannot choose a technique for each person, leave judgment partly to practice; when science supplies no unique answer about what ought to count, choose among defensible arrangements. Here the absent comparative body requires evidence and models. The burden does not cancel that assessment: it specifies the consequences if it remains insufficient. Overall advantage was not established against Pistorius, but was established to the legal standard against Leeper. Two reversals show that allocation may change an unresolved result even without new measurements. They do not show that evidence can never distinguish the cases.

Care is essential: this essay is not a conclusion about which athlete should win. Pistorius, Rehm, and Leeper have each articulated their own positions. Pistorius sought a fair opportunity for disabled athletes to compete against non-disabled athletes. Rehm argued that an inconclusive study should not be treated as proof of advantage. These are normative positions, not scientific evidence. The essay does not adjudicate between them, just as the tribunals could not directly observe the underlying counterfactual bodies.

Athletes with limb differences have entered open competition before. Natalie du Toit competed in open-water swimming; George Eyser won gymnastics medals with a wooden leg. These are histories of inclusion, but not adjudicated precedents for carbon-fibre prostheses under an overall-net-advantage test. They show that limb difference alone need not exclude someone from open competition. They do not determine who bears the burden when a required mechanical aid may alter an event's mechanics and the central comparison cannot be observed.

The construct can measure elastic-energy return, horizontal velocity lost at take-off and distance to the centimetre. It cannot directly measure how fast this same person would run with biological limbs. That absence requires estimates and leaves uncertainty. Estimates can nevertheless meet a legal proof standard; when they do not, the burden assigns the consequences. Three stages and two reversals leave us not with universal undecidability, but with a distance that cannot be skipped between direct measurement, assessment of evidence and allocation of risk.

The ruler has not yet measured accurately. It is still measuring.

edits.before: 前面第十三篇讲的是，构面对一个物理上不存在的事实，那个有生物肢体的运动员，退到了分配举证责任。这一篇讲的是一件相邻，但不同的事。这一篇里，构面对的不是一个不存在的事实，是一个必须被作出的分类，而它分类所依据的那个判据，落在一个连续的，重叠的，由多种因素共同决定的生理现实上，无法被干净地划开。
edits.after: 前面第十三篇讲的是，构无法直接观察那个拥有生物肢体的反事实身体，仍须评估间接证据，并在证明不足时分配风险。这一篇讲的是一件相邻，但不同的事。这一篇里，构面对的不是一个不存在的事实，是一个必须被作出的分类，而它分类所依据的那些判据涉及不同层次的生理特征：有的是类别标志，有的是连续数值，也有发育史与功能反应；它们与项目表现的关系不能由一个标志完全说明。
edits.reason: Sequence presence is categorical; hormone quantities/developmental effects are not the same variable. English already appropriately qualifies. Root review amendment: align13 indirect evidence; measurements do not by themselves fix unique norm, without declaring justification impossible.

edits.before: 它不裁定谁对。它不给出女性的真正定义，因为这不是一篇文章能给出的，也不是任何一个仲裁庭给出过的。它要做的，是记录一件确凿的事:六十年来，回答"谁可以进入女子组"这个问题的判据，被换过至少七次，而每一次更换，都不是把上一个判据测得更准，是换了一个完全不同的东西来测。
edits.after: 它不裁定哪一方对，也不试图给出女性的终极定义。它记录的是近六十年里，女子参赛资格曾采用多种判定方法。下面按七组历史节点整理，其中涉及不同组织，也包含某些判据的回归与组合；不是同一机构整齐地把一条标准连续换了七次。重要的是，不少变化改变了所检查的对象，而不只是把同一个对象测得更准。
edits.reason: The list groups seven historical approaches, repeats genetic testing and mixes IOC/IAAF regimes; not seven successive wholesale replacements.

edits.before: 这件事本身，不涉及立场。无论一个人在这个问题上站哪一边，判据换过七次，是一个可以核对的历史事实。而这个事实，恰恰是这一篇要讲的构的处境。
edits.after: 这些历史变化可以查证，但怎样把它们分组，仍是一种整理方式。无论读者站在哪一边，都可以检视每次采用的标准、所属组织与适用范围；这一篇要观察的是这些变化显示的制度处境，而不是让一个整齐的次数替代具体历史。
edits.reason: Do not assert seven changes as a verified neutral count after grouping seven nodes.

edits.before: 把这一点先立住，是因为这一篇的分寸全在这里。一个人可以坚定地认为女子组必须有明确的边界，也可以坚定地认为现行的边界划错了地方，这两种立场，以及它们之间的许多种立场，都不在这一篇的裁断范围里。这一篇要观察的，不是哪一条边界是对的，而是这个构在划任何一条边界时，共同面对的那个困难:它必须给出一个清楚的，赛前就能执行的二元判定，而它用来判定的每一个依据，都取自一个本身并不清楚地分成两半的生理现实。这个困难，对每一种立场都成立。
edits.after: 把这一点先立住，是因为这一篇的分寸全在这里。一个人可以坚定地认为女子组必须有明确的边界，也可以坚定地认为现行的边界划错了地方，这两种立场，以及它们之间的许多种立场，都不在这一篇的裁断范围里。这一篇要观察的，不是哪一条边界是对的，而是这个构在划任何一条边界时，共同面对的那个困难:它必须给出一个清楚的，赛前就能执行的二元判定，而它用来判定的各类依据，并不直接给出每个具体运动员的项目优势，更不会自动决定怎样的优势应当成为排除理由。这个困难，对每一种立场都成立。
edits.reason: Keep difficulty of inference to eligibility, not blanket denial of categorical markers.

edits.before: 外观，性染色质，某条性染色体的特异序列，血清睾酮，特定性发育差异，男性青春期，再到那段基因序列。七个判据，测的是七个不一样的东西。
edits.after: 外观、性染色质、特定基因序列、睾酮与雄激素敏感性、特定性发育差异、青春期史，再到基因筛查。这是七组便于回顾的历史节点，不是七种彼此完全不同、从不重复的单一测量。它们显示的是资格制度怎样更换、组合或重新采用不同依据。
edits.reason: Some entries repeat the same marker and several combine multiple features.

edits.before: 这里必须点出一件容易被忽略的事。这不是同一个测试的七次改良。一次比一次更准地测量同一个东西，那叫改良。而这里，每一次更换，被测量的那个东西本身变了。外观和染色质不是一回事，染色质和睾酮不是一回事，睾酮和青春期史不是一回事。所以"女子分类一直存在"这句话是真的，但它不等于"女子资格的科学定义始终相同"。分类一直在，判据一直在换，而换的不是精度，是对象。
edits.after: 这里不只是同一个测试的连续改良。有些变化确实调整了旧阈值，有些保留并组合了已有条件，还有些换了被检测的对象。外观、染色质、睾酮与青春期史不是同一个量。所以“女子分类一直存在”不等于“资格判据始终相同”；但判据有变化，也不能一概说成每一步都完全改换了对象。
edits.reason: Avoid exact seven-replacement premise. Includes related correction:2023 threshold adjustment is refinement of an existing variable, not a wholly new measured object.

edits.before: 这个区别有一个实际的后果，值得点出来。如果七次更换是同一个东西越测越准，那么最新的那个判据，应该是前面所有判据的一个改进版，它测的还是那件事，只是测得更好。可事实不是这样。最新的那道基因筛查，测的不是更精确的睾酮，也不是更精确的染色质，它测的是一个和睾酮，和染色质都不同的东西，一段基因序列的有无。它不是睾酮判据的改良，它是对睾酮判据的替换。这意味着，如果将来某一天，判据从基因又换成别的东西，那也不会是对基因判据的改进，而是又一次替换。这个构不是在一条路上越走越远，它是在反复地换路。
edits.after: 这个区别有实际后果。最新的基因筛查并不是把睾酮或染色质测得更精确，而是采用了另一种标志；但这不妨碍某些规则同时保留发育与功能方面的条件。将来若更换依据，也需要分别问：是改进旧测量、调整阈值，还是换了代理标准？构有时沿原路细化，有时换路。不能把所有变化预先说成科学进步，也不能一概判成只是来回折返。

edits.before: 四处地方，四条精确的线，而每一条都划在一个说不出它为什么划在这里的位置上。这不是某一个机构的疏忽，是这类边界的共同处境:它要划分的那个东西，是连续的，没有一个自然的断点，在那里一切突然从可接受变成不可接受。既然那个东西是连续的，任何一条线都必然是切出来的，而切出来的线，可以被解释，可以被辩护，但无法被证明。

edits.before:
A decision required before the race

Athletics separates many elite events into male and female categories. The competition cannot begin without assigning entrants. Whatever philosophical uncertainty surrounds sex, development, identity, and advantage, the entry system requires a decision by a deadline.

That operational demand explains both the persistence of classification and the instability of its criteria. Over roughly six decades, international sport has relied at different times on physical examination, chromatin tests, chromosome analysis, hormone thresholds, legal or identity status, rules for differences of sex development, and rules governing transgender participation. Each criterion promised a workable proxy for the protected category. None measured “fairness” directly.

The current rule changed in 2025

Any account written before September 2025 is now historical. World Athletics merged its approach to gender-diverse eligibility and introduced a once-in-a-lifetime SRY gene test for athletes seeking access to the female category at covered elite competitions. Under the implementation rules approved in December 2025, a negative SRY result permits entry; a positive result triggers further medical assessment, with limited transitional provisions.

SRY is a highly accurate proxy for the presence of Y-linked male development in most cases, not an oracle that resolves every variation of sex development. The regulations themselves need follow-up procedures because biology does not guarantee that one marker will classify every individual without exception.

Seven criteria, seven mismatches

The historical sequence should not be read as steady approach toward a final essence. Anatomical examination could not reliably capture chromosomal or developmental variation. Barr-body screening used a proxy that misclassified some individuals. Chromosome tests encountered mosaics and differences between genotype and phenotype. Testosterone thresholds converted continuous and context-dependent values into a legal line. Legal sex and gender identity answered social recognition without directly measuring competitive advantage.

Each method observed something real. The mismatch lay between the thing observed and the larger judgment assigned to it.

A line through a continuum

Many traits relevant to performance—height, muscle mass, haemoglobin, response to testosterone, limb proportions—vary within and across categories. Population differences can be large while individual distributions overlap. An average cannot assign a particular person a precise quantum of advantage.

Rules nevertheless need a boundary. A threshold at one hormone concentration or a binary response to a genetic test turns complex variation into an administrable status. The discontinuity belongs to the rule, not to the underlying continuum.

Evidence and jurisdiction

Legal challenges have moved through internal bodies, national courts, the Court of Arbitration for Sport, and human-rights review. These forums do not ask identical questions. One may examine whether a sporting rule is proportionate to its aim; another may review procedural fairness or fundamental rights; another may defer to a federation's expertise.

Apparently conflicting judgments can therefore coexist because they address different jurisdictions and standards. “The science won” or “the athlete won” compresses several levels of review into one imagined tribunal.

Classification is productive

A category does not merely describe bodies already arranged by nature. It creates an entry pathway, a protected field, a testing bureaucracy, privacy risks, appeals, medical burdens, and new forms of uncertainty. It makes competition possible while distributing the cost of being difficult to classify.

There is no location for the line that leaves every value intact. Move it and different athletes become eligible, different risks become acceptable, and different understandings of the category prevail. The institution must choose because it must stage the race. Calling the result natural only hides who chose and what the choice was meant to protect.
