I. A decision that must precede the race

Before a women's event begins, something must already have happened. The organizers must have decided who may enter the category.

The decision cannot wait until afterward. Entry, call-room procedures, record ratification, and medal allocation all depend on it. Before the starting gun sounds, everyone on the line has already been judged eligible to stand there. The women's category is, first of all, an eligibility classification: a binary, enforceable decision that must be made before competition.

This essay concerns that decision, and the repeated replacement over sixty years of the line on which it rests.

Essay 13 concerned a construct unable to observe the counterfactual body with biological limbs directly. It still had to assess indirect evidence and allocate the risk of insufficient proof. Here the problem is adjacent but different. The construct faces not an absent fact but a classification it must make. The physiological reality from which its criteria are drawn is continuous in some respects, overlapping, and jointly determined by multiple factors; it cannot be divided cleanly by a single proxy.

The essay's purpose and limits should be clear.

It does not decide which side is right or offer an ultimate definition of womanhood. It records several approaches to women’s eligibility over roughly sixty years, organized below into seven historical groupings. They involve different governing bodies and include returning or combined criteria, not seven neat, successive replacements by one institution. The important point is that many changes altered what was examined, rather than merely measuring the same object more accurately.

The historical changes can be checked, while their grouping remains an editorial arrangement. Whatever the reader’s position, each criterion, governing body and scope can be examined. The essay concerns the institutional predicament shown by those changes, not a tidy count standing in for the history itself.

This distinction governs the essay's restraint. Someone may firmly believe that the women's category needs a clear boundary, or firmly believe that the current boundary is misplaced. Those positions, and the many between them, are not adjudicated here. The subject is the difficulty shared by attempts to draw any such boundary: a clear, enforceable, pre-competition eligibility decision must be derived from physiological traits that are not all reducible to one perfectly separating measurement. That difficulty confronts every position.

II. Seven different criteria

First set out the sequence on which the essay rests.

Around 1966, some international competitions introduced physician-conducted visual, physical, or gynaecological examinations. The criterion was bodily appearance.

In 1967 international athletics began sex-chromatin screening, the Barr-body method. Cells from the lining of the mouth were examined for chromatin associated with an inactivated sex chromosome. The criterion shifted from appearance to a cellular chromosome marker.

In the 1990s the IOC adopted polymerase chain reaction testing for sequences specific to a sex chromosome, commonly targeting a sex-determining gene sequence or other specific DNA. The criterion shifted from sex chromatin to a particular genetic sequence.

In 2011 the IAAF introduced eligibility regulations for women with hyperandrogenism. The criterion shifted to serum testosterone together with assessment of androgen sensitivity.

In 2018 the rules targeted particular differences of sex development. The conditions included specified bodily conditions, testosterone at or above a threshold, and sufficient androgen sensitivity. The criterion narrowed from high testosterone generally to a particular group of bodily conditions.

In 2023 the testosterone ceiling was lowered further, and regulated events expanded from selected middle distances to all world-ranking competitions. The parallel transgender rules ceased to depend only on years of testosterone suppression and instead considered whether the athlete had undergone male puberty. Developmental history entered the criteria.

In 2025 World Athletics introduced a one-time genetic-sequence test in place of the previously separate DSD and transgender eligibility regimes. The sequence was SRY. The criterion had come back to a genetic sequence, this time as a unified preliminary screen.

Appearance, sex chromatin, a particular genetic sequence, testosterone with androgen sensitivity, specified DSD conditions, pubertal history, and genetic screening again: seven useful historical groupings, not seven entirely different, non-repeating single measurements. They show how eligibility systems replace, combine or return to different bases.

This history is not merely refinement of a single test. Some changes adjusted an existing threshold, some retained or combined conditions, and others changed what was examined. Appearance, chromatin, testosterone and pubertal history are not the same quantity. The continued existence of the category does not establish unchanged eligibility criteria; neither does change mean that every step replaced the object entirely.

The distinction has practical consequences. The new genetic screen does not measure testosterone or chromatin more precisely; it uses another marker. Regulations may nevertheless retain developmental or functional conditions alongside it. A future change therefore calls for separate questions: does it improve an assay, adjust a threshold or replace a proxy? The construct sometimes refines a route and sometimes changes it. Not every change is automatically scientific progress, nor is every change merely retracing its steps.

This connects with the decathlon table in Essay 7, but more sharply. There, the same question, how to convert performances across events, had received five different answers. Here, the eligibility question had been approached through the historical criteria set out here. The table altered a conversion rule. These changes alter the basis of a person's entrance into competition.

III. No criterion directly measures its intended object

The scientific limits reveal a recurring feature: none of these criteria directly measures the complete object the rule seeks to judge.

As supporters of the regulations formulate it, that object is whether an athlete has a sufficiently large, event-specific competitive advantage arising from androgen effects associated with male puberty.

Each criterion measures something else.

The Barr-body test identifies visible chromatin associated with an inactive sex chromosome. It measures neither athletic ability, gonadal function, nor androgen action. Some women without Barr bodies could fail an initial screen, while some individuals with Barr bodies who had experienced substantial androgen effects could pass. It was neither a reliable standalone test of womanhood nor a test of athletic advantage. A 1991 paper estimated that such screening might unjustly exclude approximately one in 504 female athletes.

PCR identifies a particular genetic sequence. It is more direct in that analytical sense, but cannot alone determine whether the sequence functions normally, whether the body responds to androgens, what phenotypic changes occurred at puberty, or the size of any advantage in a particular event. Greater sensitivity for detecting DNA does not settle how the result should translate into eligibility. At Atlanta 1996, 3,387 women athletes were screened; eight initial results required review, and all eight athletes were ultimately allowed to compete. Detection of chromosome-specific material did not automatically mean ineligibility.

Testosterone appears closer to the physiological mechanism, but remains an incomplete proxy. It does not directly measure muscle response to androgens, pubertal development, or event performance. An analysis of post-competition samples from 693 elite athletes found overlapping male and female testosterone distributions under particular measurement conditions and thresholds. That challenges the absolute proposition that no male and female single serum values can ever overlap. It does not establish each person's androgen responsiveness, pubertal history, or performance advantage within the overlapping range.

The latest genetic criterion makes the separation from individual advantage particularly visible. The first gate asks whether the target sequence is detected, rather than measuring current testosterone or estimating personal competitive advantage. A test can answer the sequence-presence question with high analytical accuracy without estimating athletic performance with equal accuracy. The rules themselves need an exception for complete androgen insensitivity, demonstrating that a genetic marker and functional androgen action do not correspond one to one.

The criteria therefore share a property. They measure identifiable traits, appearance, chromatin, genes, hormones, while none directly measures the full event-specific advantage at issue. Each is a proxy: a measurable substitute for something harder to measure. A gap remains between proxy and target.

That gap is not simply a temporary deficiency in science. It has a structural source. A sufficiently large advantage in a particular event is not a single quantity captured by one measurement. It results from interacting factors: pubertal development, muscle response to hormones, skeletal and cardiopulmonary structures, and the conversion of those features into performance in a specific event. A criterion based on appearance, genes, or hormones can capture only part of that chain. Using one link as a proxy for the whole necessarily omits others. A better assay alone cannot remove a gap rooted in the target's composite nature.

IV. The line was not calculated from an effect size

During the testosterone-based period, the gap took a concrete form: how was the threshold chosen?

The 2011 regulations did not convert a fixed percentage advantage into one publicly derived numerical cutoff. They used the normal male range as a basic boundary, supplemented by androgen sensitivity. The threshold came from clinical reference ranges and category concepts, not a calculation of how many seconds each additional unit of testosterone would produce.

The 2018 rules specified a number. The IAAF described it as an enforceable boundary clearly above the levels of the great majority of women without DSD and below the usual male range, allowing room for measurement error and individual fluctuation. In the arbitration evidence, experts described a low range for women without polycystic ovary syndrome and a much higher male range. The chosen number was neither the arithmetic midpoint nor a mathematical output of the event study's effect sizes.

That is the section's central point. No public dose-response model demonstrated a necessary minimum percentage advantage above the cutoff and its absence just below. The applicants' experts expressly challenged this in arbitration. The institutional response relied principally on reference ranges, androgen physiology, and administrative workability. The threshold can therefore be described as a normative and clinical boundary, but not as a precise calculation from the reported effects of roughly one to four percent.

The number was lowered in 2023. Official explanations placed the new standard closer to the upper end of the usual female reference range. The published rules specified obligations and time limits but supplied no calculation mapping the new value to a particular percentage change in competition performance. Nor did a public model explain why identical hormone values should apply across every athletics event.

With the 2025 genetic criterion, the same issue continued in another form. The assay's accuracy is analytical: it answers whether the sequence is present. It does not establish a quantitative relation between sequence detection and an individual's advantage in a particular event. A continuous hormone value became a presence-or-absence genetic screen, without filling the missing derivation of performance effect.

The same line runs through earlier essays. Essay 7 found no complete public derivation of decathlon coefficients. Essay 12 found none for the forty-millimetre shoe limit. In Essay 13, overall net prosthetic advantage was a legal standard applied to evidence, not a directly measured variable. Here the testosterone thresholds were not calculated from a demonstrated event effect size.

Four precise boundaries, none uniquely located by the kind of derivation one might expect. This is not simply one institution's oversight. It is the common condition of boundaries imposed on continuous effects without a natural point at which everything changes from acceptable to unacceptable. Such lines can be explained and defended without being proved uniquely necessary.

V. A population difference that cannot be assigned to an individual

The essay offers no final verdict. That does not mean withholding the strongest arguments on either side. This section and the next set them alongside one another without deciding between them.

Begin with a fact both sides recognize but use differently.

Across many strength, speed, and endurance events, adult elite male and female performances differ by roughly ten to twelve percent. Supporters of the rules identify puberty-related testosterone effects on muscle mass, haemoglobin, skeletal development, and cardiopulmonary systems as major mechanisms. This population-level gap supplies a central empirical rationale for the women's category.

The shared starting point has an important limitation: the overall gap does not directly establish a ten-to-twelve-percent advantage for any particular woman.

Populations and individuals are different objects. A twelve-percent average difference does not imply that every member of one group is twelve percent faster than every member of another. Individuals vary and distributions can overlap. Moving from a population difference to the advantage of a particular person requires a further step the aggregate number cannot itself supply.

Consider how each side uses that limitation.

Supporters argue that precisely because no accurate individual-percentage test is available for every athlete, a manageable category rule is necessary. Eligibility requires an enforceable pre-competition decision, while scientific variables are often continuous, overlapping, and imperfect. Every boundary produces borderline cases. The institution therefore argues that it need not prove an identical advantage for every affected athlete in every race; it must show that the category-level proxy is reasonable, the evidence adequate, and the procedure consistent.

Opponents argue that the general male–female gap cannot simply be assigned to particular women. Serum testosterone is not a complete proxy for muscle responsiveness, pubertal development, or event performance. Athletes with DSD form a very small sample, and key studies are observational or conducted in populations without DSD. The rule should demonstrate that the regulated characteristic produces an advantage sufficiently large, event-specific, and reproducible to justify exclusion, rather than infer it from general male data.

Both arguments begin with the same population gap and the same limit on assigning it to individuals. They reach opposite conclusions. One says: because individual advantage cannot be measured accurately, categories are necessary. The other says: because individual advantage cannot be measured accurately, categories inferred from group data should not exclude individuals.

The essay does not decide which response is correct. Both are responses to the same limitation.

Why does that matter? Their dispute is not primarily over whether the overall gap exists. It concerns what should happen when a well-established population fact cannot be allocated precisely to individuals. One response retreats to categories as administratively workable. The other rejects category-based exclusion where an individual's circumstances may differ greatly from the average. These are attitudes toward uncertainty, not merely conflicting factual measurements. The disagreement arises where scientific description has ended and a decision is still required. No higher measurement automatically resolves that choice.

VI. Evidence and coverage that do not line up

Disagreement over the specific science is equally clear. One mismatch is particularly concrete.

A central study supporting the regulations was published in 2017. It analysed more than two thousand athlete observations from two World Athletics Championships, grouped male and female athletes separately by free testosterone, and compared performances. In several women's events, the higher-testosterone group performed approximately one to four percent better than the lower group.

This was observational competition-data analysis, not a randomized experiment. It attracted several kinds of criticism.

One concerned data quality. Researchers checking public data identified duplicate records, impossible or erroneous performances, and opaque revisions. Arbitration evidence also recorded substantial overlap of athletes between the championships, some samples that could not be classified, and the absence of separate analysis of doping effects. Researchers supporting the rules corrected some errors but denied that they overturned the overall relationships.

Another criticism deserves particular attention.

The study's significant findings included certain middle-distance events, hammer throw, and pole vault. The 2018 regulations covered events from 400 metres to one mile but excluded hammer and pole vault. Conversely, the original study did not report corresponding significant differences for 1,500 metres and the mile, both covered by the rule.

The study said to support the rule and the events actually regulated did not line up. Some events showing an effect were excluded; some included events lacked a corresponding significant result in that study.

This was not only an external allegation. The arbitral tribunal recorded the concern. The majority upheld the regulations but specifically questioned the evidence for 1,500 metres and the mile. Supporters said event coverage also reflected physiology, adjacent distances, and other evidence. Critics argued that this retrospective selection weakened any claim that the rule followed directly from the study.

This connects with Essay 11, with its qualification intact. A participant in the javelin committee identified clear landings as the primary goal, while distance reduction also shaped the specification; one change serving several purposes does not leave every motive unknowable. Likewise, a mismatch in event coverage does not by itself refute the eligibility rule’s reasons. It identifies choices between research findings and regulatory scope that still require explanation.

The gap need not mean deception. More plausibly, a rule rarely follows in a straight line from one study. General physiology, analogy with neighbouring events, administrative convenience, and negotiation also shape it. Research is one input. A mismatch need not show deliberate distortion; it may show that the rule was never research's direct product, despite presentations suggesting otherwise. The decathlon coefficients in Essay 7 offered a similar lesson: something precise and scientific-looking may have more mixed origins than its surface reveals. The appearance of precision can conceal the gap precisely where an exact justification is most needed.

Other evidence remained contested. A randomized trial gave non-elite young women testosterone for ten weeks and found improved running time to exhaustion, but no significant between-group difference in some strength and power measures. Supporters regarded randomization as stronger causal evidence than observational work. Critics noted the small sample, non-elite participants, short intervention, use of time to exhaustion rather than race time, and inability of short-term administration to healthy women to reproduce the lifelong development of athletes with DSD.

The competing evidence stands side by side. Neither side has completely displaced the other. This essay does not supply an adjudication the evidence has not itself supplied.

VII. Four judicial stages, different questions

Semenya's case passed through four judicial stages. Understanding what each considered helps explain why this essay does not pronounce on the ultimate category question.

The first was CAS. In 2019 its majority held that the 2018 regulations were discriminatory but, on the evidence then available, necessary, reasonable, and proportionate to protecting the women's competitive category. It dismissed the challenge. At the same time, it expressed serious concerns about fair implementation, athletes' ability to maintain the threshold, medication side effects, confidentiality, and the evidence for 1,500 metres and the mile.

Be clear about what it did. It asked whether the available evidence justified upholding this rule. It did not establish that every affected athlete necessarily had the same advantage, or offer a formula converting personal testosterone values into seconds. It expressly allowed that implementation proving impossible or excessively difficult could change the proportionality assessment. It adjudicated a particular regulation under the evidence before it, not a universal definition of womanhood.

The second stage was the Swiss Federal Supreme Court. In 2020 it dismissed the application to set the award aside. Its review was exceptionally narrow. The question was not a fresh assessment of all scientific evidence but whether the award violated Swiss public policy under a demanding threshold. It confirmed that the award could not be annulled on the limited grounds available under Swiss arbitration law. It did not independently verify every scientific conclusion.

The third and fourth stages were the European Court of Human Rights. In 2023 a Chamber found, by four votes to three, that Switzerland had violated the Convention. The Swiss government's referral request was accepted, so the Chamber judgment did not become final.

On 10 July 2025 the Grand Chamber delivered its final judgment. By fifteen votes to two it found a violation of Article 6 §1, the right to a fair hearing. Semenya had effectively been compelled to accept CAS's exclusive jurisdiction; the dispute implicated fundamental personal and bodily rights; and the Swiss court's exceptionally narrow public-policy review had not provided adequate safeguards.

This stage is especially easy to misread.

The Grand Chamber found a fair-hearing violation by Switzerland. It also held the discrimination, private-life, and effective-remedy complaints inadmissible for lack of territorial jurisdiction. That was a jurisdictional ruling, not a merits finding that the DSD rule was non-discriminatory. The Grand Chamber did not annul the CAS award, invalidate the athletics regulations, or directly grant Semenya eligibility for women's events.

The stages therefore addressed different questions. CAS considered the rule's validity on the evidence before it. The Swiss court considered whether the award could be set aside. The final Strasbourg judgment considered whether Switzerland's judicial procedure was fair. None supplied an abstract, final answer to who ought to be eligible for the women's category. A procedural victory is not the same as a substantive invalidation. The ultimate classification question remained without the kind of final universal judgment the essay is asking about.

This division of work reveals a broader feature. Each institution confined itself to a narrower question within its authority: this regulation, this arbitral award, this judicial procedure. The largest question remained outside that limited adjudication. This is not necessarily evasion. A legal or arbitral body cannot resolve the category's meaning once and for all. Each addresses the portion within its competence while the broader issue remains open.

VIII. A line drawn through complex physiological variation

Bring the essay together, still without supplying a final answer.

The construct faces a task it must perform but cannot perform without difficulty. Before competition, it must decide who is eligible for the women's category. Competition requires an enforceable binary eligibility outcome. Yet appearance, chromatin, genes, hormones, and pubertal history each capture only part of a multifactorial physiological reality.

This is the remainder, different from every preceding form.

Earlier remainders included omitted names, unresolved causes, techniques not decided by a performance table, unchosen arrangements and unobservable counterfactual bodies. Here it is what a single criterion leaves unanswered about bodies, development and athletic effects. A genetic sequence can yield a categorical presence-or-absence result; hormone levels, functional responses and performance are different variables. Connecting them to eligibility requires evidence and an explanation of the institutional choice.

These changes are not merely successive approaches to one waiting eligibility line. They also concern institutional goals, proxies, enforcement and consequences for individuals. A clear categorical test result does not finish the justification of eligibility; repeated changes do not prove that every boundary lacks empirical grounds either. What no single assay decides is why the boundary ought to fall at this particular place.

This extends the argument of Essay 12. There, continuous footwear advantages did not contain a natural forty-millimetre boundary. Here, the relationship between physiological traits and eligibility likewise does not yield a uniquely compelled cutoff. The difference is the weight of the consequence. A shoe boundary determines whether equipment-related performances count. This boundary affects a person's body, career, dignity, identity, and ability to compete as she understands herself. Moving it carries far greater weight than changing an implement specification.

Precisely because the stakes are so high, restraint matters. The essay could easily become a declaration of allegiance in an already noisy dispute. That is not the series' purpose. It observes what the construct does when closure fails, rather than supplying the judgment the construct cannot finally settle. Here its movement is clear: it must classify; it cannot scientifically derive a uniquely justified eligibility boundary; it repeatedly changes criteria, gives reasons, and faces challenges without reaching an uncontested endpoint. Observing that movement and taking a side are different activities. This essay undertakes the former.

Keep the discipline established at the start: this essay does not decide where the eligibility boundary should fall. It reviews seven historical groupings across organizations and periods. Each approach requires reasons and remains open to questions about evidence, procedure and individual consequences. That history is not seven tidy replacements, and its count supplies no final judgment for either side.

When discussing particular people, the essay relies only on what they have publicly said. One athlete described routine genetic screening in her own 2005 article as an additional barrier to women's entry into sport. Another emphasized in arbitral testimony that she was a woman, not a man. Another argued that her natural body should not exclude her without adequate evidence of advantage. These are publicly expressed positions and experiences, not medical information disclosed by institutions. The essay does not reproduce any medical record the athletes themselves have not made public, just as the tribunals did not reduce the whole question to an answer readable from a single test.

Organizations use differing eligibility arrangements: pubertal history, genetic screening, open categories or continuing revisions. That shows the absence of an agreed institutional answer in practice. It does not logically prove that no uniquely better arrangement could exist. The defensible point is that assays and empirical research do not automatically make every choice among institutional aims, rights and risks.

The construct can measure a person's testosterone, detect a genetic sequence, and estimate a population's average performance gap. It cannot measure the single point at which the women's eligibility boundary ought to be placed. That point is not simply a measurable fact. It is a boundary that must be chosen, whose unique normative justification cannot be established merely by a single assay or by historical changes. Across roughly sixty years, the history above follows several forms of that choice.

The ruler has not yet measured accurately. It is still measuring.

edits.before: 停下来看这一个。跟腱能解释百分之三十的跑步经济性。而跑步经济性，解释了那个样本里约等于零的实际成绩。所以这个性状，能解释一个中间的实验室变量，却解释了那个样本里几乎为零的实际成绩变异。一个真实的百分之三十，和成绩之间，隔着一个几乎为零。
edits.after: 停下来看这个区别。跟腱力臂与跑步经济性的关联，解释了样本中约百分之三十的经济性变异；经济性与该研究的成绩指标却几乎不相关，相关系数是负零点零一。因此不能把前一个百分之三十搬成成绩的百分之三十。但这也不能反推跟腱特征与成绩本身的关系一定为零：相关并不沿着三项变量自动传递。这里缺的是从这项中间指标，到具体成绩乃至群体成功的证据。
edits.reason: r(X,economy) plus r(economy,performance)≈0 does not determine r(X,performance) or causal contribution. Preserve30% and−0.01.

edits.before: 这个故事说，牙买加人有一个普通人没有的短跑基因。而可以确证的是，那个常被提到的α辅肌动蛋白3的某个基因型，在牙买加的低频率，并不是牙买加冠军独有的。牙买加对照约百分之二，非裔美国对照约百分之四，肯尼亚人和尼日利亚人也测得了很低的频率。也就是说，几乎所有的牙买加普通人，都共享这个所谓的群体优势，而其中只有极小一部分成为精英。一个几乎人人都有的东西，不能解释为什么只有极少数人成功。
edits.after: 这个故事说牙买加冠军有普通人没有的短跑基因。研究看到的却是，ACTN3的XX基因型在运动员和对照中都很少见：牙买加对照约百分之二，运动员约百分之三；非裔美国对照约百分之四，运动员约百分之二。牙买加与美国各自的运动员—对照比较，都没有发现显著的基因型分布差异。广泛共享的是很少出现XX这一群体分布，不是几乎人人都拥有那个低频基因型。这不能单凭自身解释，为什么只有极少数人成为精英；也不等于证明这个变体没有任何生理作用。
edits.reason: Original study identifies rare XX genotype, with Jamaican controls2% /athletes3%, UScontrols4% /athletes2%. Commonality is absence of XX, not possession of rare genotype; name variant.

edits.before:
Two real concentrations

Elite distance running includes a remarkable concentration of athletes from particular Kenyan regions and communities, while global sprinting has repeatedly featured Jamaican excellence. These patterns are not inventions. The mistake begins when a distribution of selected elite results becomes a property attributed to an entire people.

Narrative closes that gap quickly. “Kalenjin endurance” and “Jamaican speed” sound like descriptions of bodies. They are actually composites of competition results, regional recruitment, school systems, coaching, economic incentives, migration, altitude, cultural prestige, and selective attention.

A true statistic used as another statistic

The share of finalists or champions from a population can be calculated. It does not tell us the average capacity of every member of that population, much less the cause of the elite concentration. The numerator is visible because the athletes reached international sport. The denominator—everyone who never entered the pathway, trained for another event, lacked access, or stopped early—is usually absent.

This is selection on top of selection. Families and regions notice where success is possible; talented young athletes choose events with models and infrastructure; scouts and coaches look where previous champions have trained. The pathway amplifies a real initial cluster without revealing its origin.

Every story is narrower than its evidence

Genetic explanations identify variants or ancestry patterns that may influence traits relevant to performance. Environmental accounts emphasize altitude, childhood activity, diet, or morphology. Institutional accounts point to school competition, coaching density, national trials, professional opportunity, and peer effects.

No single layer can claim the whole result. Elite performance is produced at the intersection of many rare conditions. A statistically meaningful biological trait need not explain a national system, while a strong training culture need not imply that bodies are interchangeable.

Chronology resists essence

If a timeless national body caused dominance, the dominance should be comparatively timeless. In reality, international success rises, clusters, shifts among regions and coaching groups, and responds to changes in opportunity and event prestige. Jamaica's modern sprint system and Kenya's global distance-running economy have histories.

The body does not change at the speed of institutions. Rapid changes in medal concentration therefore place an upper limit on simple genetic stories, even if inherited traits remain one part of the field.

The strongest claims on both sides

The strongest biological argument does not say that a nationality contains one sprint or endurance gene. It says that population history may alter the frequency of many traits and that elite selection magnifies uncommon combinations. The strongest institutional argument does not say biology is irrelevant. It says that capacities become visible only through pathways that train, select, reward, and export them.

These claims can coexist. Their coexistence is less satisfying than a single explanation because it leaves causal shares unresolved. But unresolved shares are more accurate than a national essence.

The people outside the measurement

Record books contain the tiny fraction of people who reached sanctioned elite competition. They do not contain those who trained and failed, those who chose football, those excluded by gender or class, or those whose talent never met a pathway. Any story drawn only from finalists turns institutional visibility into biological prevalence.

Narrative is therefore another construct. It selects variables, assigns causal weight, and gives a population a readable form. A good narrative can illuminate a system. A closed narrative compresses the system into the body and then presents its own compression as nature.

I. Two real concentrations

Two things are real, and official performances can be used to check them.

One is in East Africa. Since 1964, Kalenjin athletes from Kenya's Rift Valley have accumulated an exceptionally dense concentration of middle- and long-distance achievements. One researcher-coded analysis counted men's Olympic medals, World Championship medals, and annual top-twenty-five marathon performances from 800 metres through the marathon. It assigned Kalenjin athletes fifty-four Olympic medals, seventy-seven World Championship medals, and 206 top-twenty-five marathon performances. Within Kenya, Kalenjin athletes accounted for approximately eighty-four percent of major track medals.

The other concentration is in the Caribbean. Since the 2008 Beijing Olympics, Jamaica has accumulated an equally striking concentration in sprinting: men and women, 100 and 200 metres, championship after championship. The Jamaican α-actinin-3 paper itself noted that Jamaicans won seven of Beijing's twelve individual sprint medals.

Both concentrations are real. They are too prominent to dismiss as anecdotes. This essay neither denies nor intends to deny them.

It asks something else: how do people explain them?

Explanations have grown around both concentrations, and they share a form. They begin with something observable: running barefoot to school, altitude, a gene, a school. They turn it into a cause sufficient to account for the whole phenomenon. The subject of this essay is that these explanations are themselves constructs.

The constructs of the previous fourteen essays were visible in rules, scoring tables, record books, and thresholds dividing people into categories. This one operates less visibly. It exists not in a rulebook but in the causal language used to narrate performances. A bodily characteristic is presented as the cause of a population-level phenomenon. Like every earlier construct, that narration seeks closure and cannot fully achieve it.

Its position needs clarification, because the essay could be mistaken for either of two extremes. It does not say that bodies are irrelevant or biological variation nonexistent; that would be as inaccurate as determinism. Nor does it say every proposed explanation is prejudice and should be discarded. Its claim is narrower: these explanations contain a common logical leap, turning a genuine observation into an unproved causal assertion. The leap, not the observation, is being challenged. Many observations are real. The leap is the construct.

II. A distinction that must come first

Understanding what goes wrong requires a distinction that forms the essay's foundation.

Two different questions are often treated as one.

First: within the Kalenjin population, what makes some people faster than others?

Second: what accounts for Kalenjin athletes' much greater concentration of international middle- and long-distance achievements relative to other populations?

These are separate questions. The first can examine factors differentiating faster and slower individuals within the population: genes, Achilles tendons, training. The second asks what produces differences between populations. Its answer cannot simply be read from the answer to the first.

Within-population heritability does not identify the causes of between-population differences. That is the key sentence of this essay.

An example makes the distinction clear. Suppose a tendon characteristic explains some variation in running ability among Kalenjin individuals. That is possible. It does not establish how much of the international performance difference between Kalenjin athletes and other populations is caused by that characteristic. Geography, economics, schools, recruitment, and training systems also differ between groups and are entangled with ancestry. Within-group and between-group variation operate at different analytical levels. Transferring an answer from one to the other is a basic error.

The distinction immediately exposes a problem. Many genetic and environmental explanations answer only the first question, or measure an intermediate trait, before being presented as answers to the second. For the between-population concentration that actually needs explaining, the source reports no identified percentage contribution from any single proposed factor.

This distinction is repeatedly missed because it cuts against intuition. If something creates differences between individuals, surely it also creates differences between groups? That does not follow. Groups differ in factors that may scarcely vary within the local population being studied. Differences between two children in one Kalenjin village might mainly reflect locally varying factors such as individual aptitude and training. Comparing that population with a northern European country also introduces economics, school density, role models, agents' networks, and the whole system turning running into an international profession. These may vary enormously between populations while varying little within the local sample. Between-population outcomes could therefore depend heavily on factors invisible to a within-population comparison.

The answer must be explicit. How much of the population-level achievement difference has been causally apportioned? The defensible answer offered here is that it remains unknown, with the separate contribution of each proposed factor unidentified.

III. One real number standing in for another

The explanations are particularly persuasive when they carry a real number. The number may be genuine while measuring something other than the claim it is used to support.

Consider several examples.

Research on an angiotensin-converting-enzyme variant found that it could explain up to twenty-four percent of circulating enzyme activity. That is a substantial figure. But the same research found no significant association between the variant and Kenyan elite-athlete status. Twenty-four percent therefore describes enzyme activity in blood, not a proportion of Kenyan sporting success.

A study of α-actinin-3 found that it explained 2.3 percent of variation in forty-metre sprint times among Greek adolescent males. In Jamaica, genotype differences between athletes and controls were not significant. The 2.3 percent came from Greek adolescents' sprint variation, not the achievements of Jamaican Olympic sprinters.

The tendon example is especially revealing. A study of thirty-two Kenyan runners found that an Achilles-tendon moment-arm measurement explained thirty percent of variation in running economy within the sample. Thirty percent sounds substantial. Yet in that same study, running economy was almost unrelated to the performance measure used: the correlation coefficient was −0.01.

Pause over the distinction. The tendon moment arm accounted for about thirty percent of running-economy variation in the sample, while economy was almost uncorrelated with the performance measure, at −0.01. The former percentage therefore cannot be relabelled as thirty percent of performance. Nor does this prove that the tendon trait’s own relationship with performance must be zero: correlations do not automatically transmit through three variables. Evidence is still needed to connect the intermediate measure to performance and then to population success.

That is the numerical substitution, whether intentional or not. A percentage associated with an intermediate phenotype is relabelled as a percentage of national or ethnic achievement. “The tendon explains thirty percent of running-economy variation” becomes “the tendon explains thirty percent of Kalenjin success.” The first was measured. The second was not. The link supposedly joining them, economy to performance, was precisely the link absent in that study.

This continues an earlier theme in a new form. Essay 7 found no public derivation of scoring coefficients. Essay 12 found none for the forty-millimetre shoe line. Essay 14 found that testosterone thresholds were not calculated from performance effect sizes. There the problem was precision without the required derivation. Here a genuine number exists, but measures the wrong object for the explanation being offered. A real but non-equivalent statistic stands in for the missing causal statistic.

The substitution is difficult to detect because it satisfies the desire for a concrete number. A precise percentage makes a complicated phenomenon feel quantified and understood. Listeners often do not ask what the percentage actually describes. “The tendon explains thirty percent” sounds like an explanation of thirty percent of sporting success, though it may concern an intermediate variable with almost no performance association in the sample. Numerical specificity conceals the mismatch between the measured object and the explained object. A true number in the wrong place can mislead more effectively than a vague assertion because it carries the authority of quantification.

IV. Every story is narrower than its claim

Place the familiar deterministic stories against that standard, and each reveals its limits.

The first is running barefoot to school.

The story says Kalenjin children develop their ability by running long distances to school every day. What has been established is an association. In a survey of 404 elite runners and controls, approximately twenty-two percent of controls, seventy-three percent of national-level runners, and eighty-one percent of international-level runners reported running to school as children.

The association is real. But it permits two directions of explanation. The study's authors acknowledged that their design could not determine whether distance running made the children stronger or whether children who already found running easier were more likely to run. Selection into running and the effect of running were not separated. Earlier interviews also found that fourteen of twenty elite runners had not regularly run long distances to school. The evidence therefore supports a higher prevalence of running to school among the sampled elites, not a claim that every Kalenjin champion ran ten kilometres barefoot, still less that this commute caused later success.

The second story is that altitude makes champions.

Parts of the Rift Valley lie around two thousand metres above sea level, and altitude has genuine physiological effects. But altitude is neither sufficient nor universally necessary for championship success. Tibetans and Andean populations live at much greater elevations and show established physiological adaptations without producing Kenya's concentration of international distance champions. Altitude adaptation is widespread; industrial-scale production of elite distance runners is not. This does not establish that altitude contributes nothing. It shows that altitude alone does not determine international outcomes. Classic Kenyan studies also found that sedentary boys living at altitude did not automatically have high maximal oxygen uptake. Activity and training sharply differentiated the groups.

The third story is the sprint gene.

The story gives Jamaican champions a sprint gene ordinary people lack. The study found instead that the ACTN3 XX genotype was rare in both athletes and controls: about two percent in Jamaican controls and three percent in athletes, four percent in African-American controls and two percent in US athletes. Neither population’s athlete–control comparison showed a significant genotype-distribution difference. What was widely shared was the low prevalence of XX, not near-universal possession of the rare genotype. That pattern cannot by itself explain why only a few become elite; it does not prove that the variant has no physiological effect.

The fourth story is that one person made everything happen.

A missionary coach, a school championship, or a club is credited with producing the national phenomenon. Chronology directly challenges that account. The next section considers it.

Each story begins with a real correlate, school travel, altitude, genotype frequency, or an institution, then turns it into a sufficient cause without an identified counterfactual. That is the recurring recipe: take a genuine association, omit the missing comparison, and declare causation.

V. Chronology refuses

The claim that one person or institution created everything encounters a particularly hard obstacle: the order of events.

Begin with Kenya. St Patrick's High School in Iten and its coach, Brother Colm O'Connell, became important nodes in Kalenjin running. But O'Connell arrived in Iten only in 1976, eight years after Keino's 1968 Olympic victory and twelve years after Kenya's first Olympic athletics medal.

He therefore cannot explain the initial breakthrough of the 1960s, which preceded his arrival. His contribution concerns later reproduction of success, continuity of coaching, and international visibility. Origin and reproduction are different questions. His own account emphasizes creating an environment in which athletes could develop, consistent with selection, guidance, and continuity, rather than a coach creating innate ability.

Jamaica's chronology is clearer still.

The inter-school championships began in 1910. The particularly visible intensification of Jamaican sprint dominance dates to Beijing 2008, about ninety-eight years later. A school competition that had existed for nearly a century cannot alone explain why dominance intensified at that particular moment.

What about the later clubs? MVP Track & Field Club was founded in 1999, about nine years before Beijing, offering a possible developmental stage for athletes leaving school. It addressed a concrete bottleneck: enabling athletes and coaches to develop in Jamaica rather than all having to leave for the United States. Another club led by Mills had a coaching lineage preceding Bolt’s breakthrough, but its formal 2009 relaunch came after Beijing.

Together these chronologies challenge two kinds of single-cause account. They challenge institutional sufficiency: the school championships existed for almost a century, much of it without comparable dominance. They also challenge an account relying solely on changes in population genetics: international achievements rose over decades, faster than a population's allele frequencies would plausibly change enough to explain that rise. A gene pool did not have to transform over three or four generations to produce it.

The temporal argument needs precision. A long-stable genetic distribution alone does not explain why achievements changed over a few decades; one must also explain why more people entered training, were discovered and reached international competition then. Markets, coaching, migration and incentives can change quickly. That does not show inherited variation contributed nothing: an existing predisposition may gain different opportunities for expression in a new environment. Chronology challenges a closed single-cause story; it does not settle the division between genes and environment in advance.

Nor did Jamaica become a sprint nation in 1999. It had a major Olympic tradition long before the club, from the 1948 generation through Quarrie and Ottey. Any story making one later institution the absolute beginning collides with achievements that preceded it.

VI. The strongest arguments on both sides

This essay does not declare genetics or institutions the principal cause. It presents the strongest versions of both. Its target is the deterministic narrative form, not either field of explanation as such.

Begin with the strongest genetic argument.

It is not a single speed gene. It argues that the concentration is geographically narrow enough to resist easy explanation through national policy or altitude alone; elite performance is an extreme, highly polygenic phenotype; even samples of several hundred elite athletes may lack power to identify combinations of thousands of small effects; α-actinin-3 demonstrates that performance-relevant functional variation exists; and a genetic contribution need not change during the historical growth period. An already existing distribution may become more visible when markets, coaching, and migration routes allow more people to express it.

The strongest version acknowledges its limit: it establishes plausibility, not a quantified causal share. It is a gene–environment interaction hypothesis awaiting sufficiently powerful genomic, developmental, and institutional evidence from African and Caribbean populations.

Now consider the strongest institutional and selection argument.

International achievement rose within decades, faster than substantial allele-frequency change. Successful regions developed dense, self-reinforcing systems: visible children's competitions, specialist schools, camps, coaching lineages, role models, agents, travel networks, and very large international rewards. Those systems repeatedly selected from thousands of participants. Extreme performers can emerge from a large, intensively selected pool without requiring a large initial difference in population means. Jamaican athlete–control genetic comparisons yielded null findings for the prominent variants, and multinational endurance genomics produced weak results. The best-known variants do not reliably distinguish champions from their local populations.

This argument also has a limit. Institutions tend to concentrate where success already exists, creating reverse causation. No study has randomly assigned an Iten- or Jamaica-equivalent system to a matched population for a generation.

Both arguments are defensible, and both have honest limits. The essay does not adjudicate between them because the evidence needed to partition their causal shares is unavailable.

Neither argument is the target. The target is the move that turns either into determinism. Whether genetic effects are large or small, whether institutional effects are primary or secondary, a probabilistic tendency is not an inevitable outcome. Even a real average tendency does not predetermine every individual's fate, nor establish a phenomenon's only cause. Determinism's mistake is not choosing genes rather than institutions. It is turning “more likely” into “destined.”

That is the balance the essay must preserve. Criticizing biological determinism does not require claiming that everything is environmental and bodies irrelevant. That would merely replace one determinism with another, compressing a complex system into a different single cause. Bodies matter, environments matter, institutions matter. Their separate causal contributions have not been established here. No one can therefore declare one factor decisive on the strength of the evidence presented. Whatever its flavour, determinism pretends that the causal allocation is already known when it is not.

VII. The people who were not measured

Deterministic narratives share a particularly damaging structure hidden in the direction of inference.

They begin with successful athletes, identify a characteristic, and narrate that characteristic as the cause of success.

The direction is reversed.

The problem is reasoning backward from the selected outcome while failing to measure adequately the people who share the characteristic without achieving the outcome.

Thousands of children run to school barefoot; very few become international runners. Certain tendon traits are not exclusive to East African champions, and not everyone with them becomes one. The ACTN3 XX genotype is rare in Jamaican athletes and controls alike, yet most controls are not Olympians. Many features narrated as sufficient causes are also found among people who do not achieve elite success.

These people are not necessarily absent from research: athlete–control comparisons have already appeared above. What leaves them out is the closed story that turns the successful athletes’ shared feature into a sufficient cause.

The narrative reads a feature from the successful, calls it the cause, and stops. It does not examine the unsuccessful people who share it. That comparison would immediately defeat the claim of sufficiency: if most people with the characteristic do not succeed, the characteristic cannot be a sufficient cause of success. The deterministic story depends on not making that comparison.

This is the remainder, in a new form.

Earlier remainders were omitted names, unquantifiable causes, performances belonging to different progressions, counterfactual bodies unavailable for direct observation, and bodily differences not exhausted by one criterion. Here the remainder consists of people who share the narrated feature but did not succeed and consequently never entered the story's field of observation. They are the comparison group the narrative must neglect to close itself.

Earlier constructs failed to close because their objects would not fit, causes could not be calculated, or no unique answer existed. Here the narrative can appear complete precisely because it excludes the people who would defeat its sufficiency claim. It achieves closure not by solving the problem but by looking away from the comparison group. A construct tells a closed story by systematically neglecting those who would open it again.

The structure is widespread. It is an extreme form of survivorship bias: observe the successful, identify shared features, and call them the secrets of success while overlooking unsuccessful people with the same features. The error is familiar in other fields, but particularly persistent in narratives about bodies and ancestry. A visible bodily feature feels intuitively causal. Slender lower legs or an apparently running-suited physique are easy to cast as explanations. People with the same slender legs who never reach a final disappear from photographs, samples, and stories of champions.

This also explains the weakness of slavery-based narratives. One version claims that selection in the slave trade, survival on plantations, or a particular West African source population biologically produced modern Jamaican sprinters. It lacks a demonstrated chain from historical selection pressures to measured allele-frequency changes and then to present sprint performance. It retrospectively fits history to an outcome rather than establishing population genetics. Structurally it resembles the other deterministic stories, merely moving the proposed cause several centuries backward while leaving the intervening links unmeasured.

VIII. A story that compresses the system into the body

Bring the essay together.

Three things are established, and this essay denies none of them. First, the Kalenjin and Jamaican elite concentrations are real. Second, measured biological variation is real: genotype frequencies, limb morphology, tendon geometry, altitude adaptation, and running economy can differ. Denying variation is no more accurate than turning it into destiny. Third, institutional differences are real. Iten's schools and camps, international agents, Jamaican school championships, clubs, and coaching networks affect who trains, for how long, with what support, and who reaches international competition.

One thing remains unresolved: causal shares. No research cited here establishes a percentage of Kalenjin or Jamaican dominance attributable to genes, morphology, altitude, running to school, school championships, camps, clubs, economic incentives, or training-related migration. Percentages attached to intermediate phenotypes must not be relabelled as percentages of national or ethnic achievement.

The fuller picture is therefore not a bodily trait single-handedly causing a population phenomenon. It is a recursive system: small or unknown individual differences can be amplified through recruitment, training, economic competition, migration channels, coaching knowledge, and repeated selection. The individual starting difference is uncertain and may be small. The system can amplify it into a visible concentration.

The deterministic narrative compresses that whole system into the body.

“Born to run,” “natural sprinters,” “a gifted tribe,” “the speed gene”: such phrases reduce a multistage selection system to one bodily feature. They turn a decades-long process spanning schools, camps, markets, and migration into something a person supposedly possessed at birth. That compression loses the system, loses time, and loses the people who share the feature but never pass through the whole process.

That is narrative as construct. Like a rule, table, or threshold, it seeks closure. It wants one bodily feature to close the explanation of an entire phenomenon. It cannot, because the causal contribution connecting feature to phenomenon has not been identified. It substitutes the outcome needing explanation for a cause, substitutes a genuine intermediate statistic for a missing causal one, and turns probability into necessity. Its apparent completeness depends on overlooking the people who would challenge that story.

The construct can measure a tendon, a genotype frequency, and a medal count. It cannot, on the evidence presented, allocate those medals among the tendon, the gene, the schools, the camps, the agents, and decades of selection. That allocation has not been established. In its place, a narrative quietly inserts an answer shaped like a body. The body is real and its variation real. But the population-level causal chain connecting it to the concentration has not been measured as a complete explanation. The narrative skips that chain, joins the endpoints, and says: look, it is this body.

Here the essay connects more deeply with the series. The previous fourteen constructs operated institutionally: deliberately created rules, tables, books, and thresholds. This one operates cognitively, through causal stories people almost involuntarily construct to understand the world. An unexplained phenomenon is difficult to tolerate, so an explanation is made. The easiest places the cause in something visible, a body. Like an institutional construct, it seeks to settle what remains open. Yet closure fails because the chain it assumes has not been established. It seems real because both endpoints are real: a body and a concentration of achievement. Between them lies a causal chain not yet fully identified by these measurements. It may not hold in the proposed form, yet the narrative treats it as self-evident. This is the series' quietest construct. It is written in no rulebook. It lives in the confident tone of the sentence: they succeed because they were born that way.

The ruler has not yet measured accurately. It is still measuring.

这里可以补一层，说明为什么这样的线几乎必然没有推导。四十毫米这个边界要做的，是把可接受的鞋和不可接受的鞋分开。可是鞋的优势是连续的，它随着堆叠，泡沫，几何的变化平滑地增减，并不存在一个自然的断点，在那里优势突然从合理跳到不合理。既然优势是连续的，任何一条分界线都必然是人为切的，切在四十和切在三十九，并没有本质的不同。所以这条线不可能有一个实验来证明它，因为它要划分的那个东西本身没有一个自然的界限。它是一个必须被划，又无法被证明的线，而这样的线，构只能靠决断给出，给不出推导。

这里可以再补一层。四十毫米的边界要把可接受与不可接受的鞋分开，但鞋的优势并没有在四十毫米处天然地从合理跳到不合理。厚度、泡沫与几何会共同影响效果，相邻数值间也未必存在性质上的断裂。实验能够帮助评估四十、三十九或其他限制的后果，规则也可以公开说明为什么采用某种取舍；但实验本身不能把效果的变化，直接变成唯一应当采用的界线。需要作决定，不等于只能任意作决定。决定可以有依据、可以受质疑，却不一定是由数据唯一强制出来的。

这个规则平时不显眼，因为大多数案子的证据不是势均力敌的，总有一边更强，裁决跟着更强的那边走，举证责任落在谁身上并不改变结果。举证责任真正起作用的，恰恰是证据两边持平，无法判定的时候。而假肢这类案子，由于中心的那个反事实无法被观测，证据几乎注定是无法判定的。所以在这个领域里，那个平时不显眼的规则，变成了决定性的。一个在别处只在边角起作用的规则，在这里走到了舞台中央，因为这里的核心事实，恰恰是那个永远无法被观测，因而证据永远无法真正压向一边的东西。
这个规则在证据未能达到标准时格外显眼。假肢案件的中心反事实不能被直接观测，研究因而必须依赖比较、估计和模型，不确定性很难完全消除。但不能直接观测，不等于证据注定永远持平。后面的利珀案恰好说明，间接证据仍可能使一方达到平衡概率的证明标准。举证责任分配的是证明不足的后果，而不是宣布所有这类案件都只能靠默认规则决定。
這個規則在證據未能達到標準時格外顯眼。假肢案件的中心反事實不能被直接觀測，研究因而必須依賴比較、估計和模型，不確定性很難完全消除。但不能直接觀測，不等於證據注定永遠持平。後面的利珀案恰好說明，間接證據仍可能使一方達到平衡概率的證明標準。舉證責任分配的是證明不足的後果，而不是宣佈所有這類案件都只能靠默認規則決定。
也就是说，皮斯托瑞斯赢的，只是皮斯托瑞斯，那副假肢，那次比赛。它没有为假肢装置创造一个一般的豁免。
也就是说，皮斯托瑞斯赢的，只是皮斯托瑞斯与案中审查过的那副假肢。它没有为假肢装置创造一个一般的豁免。
也就是說，皮斯托瑞斯贏的，只是皮斯托瑞斯與案中審查過的那副假肢。它沒有為假肢裝置創造一個一般的豁免。

要公道地看，把举证责任压给运动员，当时有它自己的道理，不是纯粹的刁难。国际田联的立场是，运动员掌握着对那个装置的使用权，掌握着它的配置，训练历史和相关的个人成绩数据;让一个申请例外的人来承担举证，被认为可以保护竞争的完整，而且在行政上可操作。这个理由不是没有分量。一个人要求一个例外，由他来证明这个例外无害，在很多别的场合是合理的。问题在于，这个特定的场合有一个别处没有的特征:他要证明的那个东西，依赖于一个无法被观测的反事实。于是一个在别处合理的举证分配，在这里变成了要求一个人去证明一件在物理上无法被证明的事。

要公道地看，把舉證責任壓給運動員，當時有它自己的道理，不是純粹的刁難。國際田聯的立場是，運動員掌握著對那個裝置的使用權，掌握著它的配置，訓練歷史和相關的個人成績數據;讓一個申請例外的人來承擔舉證，被認為可以保護競爭的完整，而且在行政上可操作。這個理由不是沒有分量。一個人要求一個例外，由他來證明這個例外無害，在很多別的場合是合理的。問題在於，這個特定的場合有一個別處沒有的特徵:他要證明的那個東西，依賴於一個無法被觀測的反事實。於是一個在別處合理的舉證分配，在這裡變成了要求一個人對一個無法直接實驗檢驗、只能依靠間接證據評估的命題承擔證明不足的風險。

三次翻转，对应三个不同的结果。而这三个结果的差别，很大程度上不来自科学的进展，来自举证责任的方向。这是这一篇要说的核心:在一个决定性事实无法被观测的领域里，裁决的实际内容，是举证责任的分配，而这个分配是一个规则性的选择，它可以被措辞或者裁决翻转，翻转之后结果随之翻转。
三个阶段，对应不同的结果，其中有两次举证方向的翻转。这显示举证责任能怎样改变不确定性的法律风险，却不能把三个不同运动员、不同装置与不同证据的案子，当成同一份证据只换规则的实验。皮斯托瑞斯和雷姆的对照让分配的分量可见，利珀的实体败诉则提醒我们：责任分配很重要，实际证据仍然能决定结果。
三個階段，對應不同的結果，其中有兩次舉證方向的翻轉。這顯示舉證責任能怎樣改變不確定性的法律風險，卻不能把三個不同運動員、不同裝置與不同證據的案子，當成同一份證據只換規則的實驗。皮斯托瑞斯和雷姆的對照讓分配的分量可見，利珀的實體敗訴則提醒我們：責任分配很重要，實際證據仍然能決定結果。
举证责任的规则，决定的是当证据势均力敌的时候谁输。它不规定一个科学方法，不规定一个最低样本量，不规定一个被接受的比较对象，也不规定一个把优劣聚合起来的算法。平衡概率这四个字，只告诉你在天平持平的时候往哪边倒，它不告诉你天平该怎么称。
举证责任决定谁承担证明不足的后果；平衡概率则要求所主张的事实更可能成立，而不是不成立。两者相关，却不是同一件事。它们都不会自动给出科学方法、最低样本量、比较对象，或把各种优劣加总的算法。当天平持平时，负担责任的一方会输；但在到达这个结果之前，还要判断证据有没有达到那个概率标准。
舉證責任決定誰承擔證明不足的後果；平衡概率則要求所主張的事實更可能成立，而不是不成立。兩者相關，卻不是同一件事。它們都不會自動給出科學方法、最低樣本量、比較對象，或把各種優劣加總的算法。當天平持平時，負擔責任的一方會輸；但在到達這個結果之前，還要判斷證據有沒有達到那個概率標準。

这个区分很重要，因为它划出了举证责任能做什么，不能做什么的边界。举证责任能做的，是在证据无法判定的时候给出一个结果，它保证案子总能有一个裁决，不会因为科学说不清就永远悬着。举证责任不能做的，是告诉你科学该做到什么程度才算说清了。一个更好的研究方法，一个更合适的比较对象，一个把各阶段优劣加总的算法，这些是科学和政策要回答的问题，举证责任回答不了。所以举证责任是一个兜底的规则，它在真相无法抵达的地方，替裁决兜住底;但它不是通往真相的路，它恰恰是在承认那条路走不通之后，才被启用的东西。

这就是这个构在这里的处境。它面对一个无法被观测的事实。它没有办法判定这个事实，因为那个有生物肢体的运动员不存在。于是它退到一个更前面的位置，不再试图判定真相，而是分配谁承担无法判定真相的代价。而即便是这个退后的位置，它也没有一个客观的依据来决定该往哪边分配。把责任给国际田联，还是给运动员，这本身是一个价值和法律的选择，而这个选择，三次被作出，三次不同。
这就是这个构在这里的处境。它不能直接观察那个拥有生物肢体的运动员，只能用间接证据评估反事实，并在证据仍不足时分配后果。科学本身也不会自动指定责任该给联合会还是运动员；这还涉及法律上的公平、可操作性与风险分配。前面三个阶段作过两种方向的选择，其中一次又改回原方向。证据的判断和证明不足的代价，必须分开看。
這就是這個構在這裡的處境。它不能直接觀察那個擁有生物肢體的運動員，只能用間接證據評估反事實，並在證據仍不足時分配後果。科學本身也不會自動指定責任該給聯合會還是運動員；這還涉及法律上的公平、可操作性與風險分配。前面三個階段作過兩種方向的選擇，其中一次又改回原方向。證據的判斷和證明不足的代價，必須分開看。

面对一个无法直接观测的反事实，构仍可评估间接证据；证据没有达到标准时，它还必须决定，谁承担证明不足的代价。
面對一個無法直接觀測的反事實，構仍可評估間接證據；證據沒有達到標準時，它還必須決定，誰承擔證明不足的代價。

这个退后，是这个构在整个系列里一个反复出现的动作的极端版本。前面很多篇里，构在无法闭合的时候，都会往后退一步:算不清成因，就只记结果不记成因;裁不了技术优劣，就只管成绩不管过程;定不了该不该算数，就在两个都成立的选项里挑一个。每一次退后，都是放弃一个它够不到的东西，守住一个它够得到的东西。而这一篇是退得最远的一次。它连那个要被判定的事实本身都够不到，因为那个事实不存在。于是它退到了最后一道防线:既然真相无法抵达，那就至少决定，谁来承担真相无法抵达的后果。这是构在面对一个彻底的空缺时，唯一还能站住的位置。这就是举证责任。而举证责任，是这个构在无法闭合的时候，能够抓住的最后一样东西。它不能说清那个假肢到底有没有优势，因为那个比较对象不存在；但它可以说清，当这件事说不清的时候，谁来承担说不清的后果。裁决从判定真相，退到了分配代价。而分配代价的方向，三次翻转，说明连这个退后的位置，也没有一个客观的落脚点。

停下来看这个区别。跟腱力臂与跑步经济性的关联，解释了样本中约百分之三十的经济性变异；经济性与该研究的成绩指标却几乎不相关，相关系数是负零点零一。因此不能把前一个百分之三十搬成成绩的百分之三十。但这也不能反推跟腱特征与成绩本身的关系一定为零：相关并不沿着三项变量自动传递。这里缺的是从这项中间指标，到具体成绩乃至群体成功的证据。

这个故事说，牙买加人有一个普通人没有的短跑基因。而可以确证的是，那个常被提到的α辅肌动蛋白3的某个基因型，在牙买加的低频率，并不是牙买加冠军独有的。牙买加对照约百分之二，非裔美国对照约百分之四，肯尼亚人和尼日利亚人也测得了很低的频率。也就是说，几乎所有的牙买加普通人，都共享这个所谓的群体优势，而其中只有极小一部分成为精英。一个几乎人人都有的东西，不能解释为什么只有极少数人成功。

这个故事说牙买加冠军有普通人没有的短跑基因。研究看到的却是，ACTN3的XX基因型在运动员和对照中都很少见：牙买加对照约百分之二，运动员约百分之三；非裔美国对照约百分之四，运动员约百分之二。牙买加与美国各自的运动员—对照比较，都没有发现显著的基因型分布差异。广泛共享的是很少出现XX这一群体分布，不是几乎人人都拥有那个低频基因型。这不能单凭自身解释，为什么只有极少数人成为精英；也不等于证明这个变体没有任何生理作用。

这个来自时间的反驳，是这一整篇里最难被绕过的一个，值得单独强调它的力量。生物的改变有一个速度上限。一个群体的基因构成，要发生能够解释成绩巨变的改变，需要许多代人的选择。而卡伦金和牙买加的国际成绩，是在几十年，也就是一两代人里爆发的。这个时间尺度，对一个纯粹的遗传解释是致命的，因为基因来不及在这么短的时间里改变这么多。它不否认已经存在的遗传差异，但它否认遗传差异是那个爆发的原因，因为那个爆发太快了，快到只有那些能够在几十年里改变的东西，市场，教练，迁移，激励，才可能是它的直接推手。凡是变化快的，原因就必须也是变化快的，而基因不是。
这个时间上的反驳需要说准。几十年里的成绩变化，不能只凭一个长期稳定的基因分布就得到解释；还必须说明，为什么更多人在这个时期进入训练、被发现并到达国际赛场。市场、教练、迁移与激励是可能快速变化的条件。但不必由此推出遗传差异没有贡献：一个已有的身体倾向，可能在新环境中获得不同的表达机会。时间线反对的是单因闭合，不是先替遗传与环境分完份额。

这一篇因此和整个系列接在一个更深的地方。前面十四篇讲的构，都在制度那一层，它们是人有意建立起来的东西，规则，计分表，纪录簿，阈值。这一篇讲的构在认知那一层，它是人在理解世界时，不由自主地要去建立的东西，一个因果的故事。人面对一个说不清的现象，几乎无法忍受没有解释，于是会去构造一个，而最容易构造的解释，是把原因放在一个看得见的东西上，一个身体上。这种构造，和制度那一层的构一样，是为了闭合，为了让一件悬着的事情有一个了结。而它一样闭合不了，因为它闭合所依据的那个因果链，并不存在。它只是看起来存在，因为它的两端，一个真实的身体和一个真实的现象，都是真的。真的两端，连着一条没有被测量的，可能根本不成立的链子，而叙事把这条链子当成了理所当然。这是这个系列里最安静的一种构，因为它不写在任何规则上，它只写在人们说这是因为他们天生如此的时候，那句话的语气里。

edits.before: 这和前面十六篇里的构，都不一样。前面的构，一直在想办法闭合，想办法把一件事判定成一个确定的结果。它建立度量，建立纪录，建立准入线，建立换算表，建立起跑的阈值，每一样都是为了把一件悬着的事情，收成一个唯一的答案。而这里，构明明有能力把这场比赛收成一个唯一的冠军，附加赛就在手边，它却把是否要收这一步，交给了运动员。
edits.after: 这与许多前篇强调的方向不同。那里，构建立度量、纪录、资格线、换算表和起跑阈值，把悬着的事变成现场可执行的决定。这里，继续比赛的办法也已经备好，附加赛就在手边；规则却把是否再走这一步的选择，留给仍然并列第一的运动员共同作出。
edits.reason: 避免与已经校正EP09未作终审等前篇矛盾。

edits.before: 这件事之所以值得单独写一篇，是因为它把这个系列反复出现的一个问题，翻到了另一面。前面十六篇，几乎都在讲构如何努力地，有时是徒劳地，想把一件事闭合成一个确定的答案。而这里，构不缺闭合的能力，它缺的是闭合的意愿，或者更准确地说，它主动地决定，在这一步上不由自己来定夺意愿。一个一直在追求确定的东西，竟然为不确定预留了合法的位置，这是这个案例最反常，也最值得琢磨的地方。
edits.after: 这件事值得单独写，因为它把系列反复出现的问题翻到了另一面。许多前篇讨论，制度怎样把复杂情形收成一个可执行的结果。这里，另一个程序已经备好，制度却允许相关运动员共同决定不再启动它。留下的不是名次不明，而是明确、合法的并列第一。没有唯一赢家，不等于没有最终答案。
edits.reason: 共享第一是确定完整结果，不等于不确定；不必泛称前16篇全部追求唯一。

edits.before: 这一点必须钉死，因为它拆掉了一个很流行的，以为是技术限制的误解。人们常以为，田径的成绩只精确到百分之一秒，是因为再往下机器就测不准了。事实完全相反。机器早就能测得更细，构自己在需要判定晋级平局的时候，就会去读取千分之一秒，而现代的终点扫描，采样间隔已经细到百万分之一秒的量级。所以百分之一秒这个公布精度，不是机器能力的天花板，是构主动选定的一个表示格式。构能看到的，比它愿意公布的细得多。它把一部分它已经掌握的精度，扣在了内部，只在特定的场合才拿出来用。这正是构对自己能力的一种自我限制，而这种自我限制，和东京那个把开关交出去的动作，是同一种性质的东西，都是构在明明有能力做某件事的时候，选择了不做，或者不完全做。
edits.after: 这里要拆开两件事。机器可以提供比正式成绩位数更细的图像记录，规则也会在某些晋级平局里使用千分之一秒；但扫描间隔不等于整套测量的准确度，校准、同步和判读仍然重要。所以百分之一秒不是摄像机简单的能力天花板，也不能反过来说每一个更细的采样点都应成为正式成绩。制度选择怎样公布时间、怎样判名次，会规定哪些信息在什么场合取得裁决力。这与东京有一个相通之处：拥有更多区分手段，并不等于每一次都必须用到尽头。
edits.reason: 采样间隔不等于整体计时准确度/可判读位数；保格式和能力区别。

“Can we have two golds?”

At the Tokyo Olympic men's high-jump final, Mutaz Essa Barshim and Gianmarco Tamberi cleared the same heights with identical failure records and then both missed 2.39 metres. The official explained that a jump-off was available. Barshim asked whether they could have two gold medals. The answer was yes, and the athletes embraced.

The scene is often retold as friendship triumphing over rules. Its deeper interest is that friendship acted through the rules. The athletes did not force an exception on an unprepared system. The tie provisions allowed them to decline the jump-off and remain tied for first.

What the tiebreak had already done

Before first place remained shared, the ordinary countback rules had compared the number of attempts at the last cleared height and total failures. Only after those mechanisms failed to separate the athletes did the question of a jump-off arise.

The construct had therefore exhausted automatic comparison and still possessed one further closure device: continue jumping until one athlete wins. It offered that device rather than imposing it without choice.

Authorization not to close

The crucial power was not a special authority to award two gold medals. Once the tie remained, equal medals followed from the accepted result. The crucial power was the rule's permission not to complete the jump-off.

This is unusual because competitive systems are typically organized to eliminate ambiguity. A final should produce a champion. Yet high jump contains a small authorized pocket in which a first-place tie can survive if the athletes do not continue.

Choice within rather than against the rule

Barshim and Tamberi did not decide that their emotional story outweighed all future competitors. They selected among procedures the event made available. That distinction protects the act from becoming pure discretion. Another pair can encounter the same provision, though they may choose differently.

The same institution has produced both outcomes. Some tied jumpers continue to a jump-off; others share a placing where rules permit it. Consistency lies in the availability of the choice, not in identical human decisions.

A critic can praise the choice and resist the rule

One can regard the Tokyo decision as generous and still argue that championships should always identify one winner. The objection concerns institutional design, not the athletes' character. If a future rule required a jump-off, it would change the available field without proving the earlier athletes wrong.

Conversely, compulsory closure would not be more objective in every sense. After an exhausting final, a jump-off measures another state of fatigue and risk, not simply the performance already completed. Continuing creates new evidence rather than clarifying old evidence.

The deliberately empty cell

Most remainders in record systems arise because the form forgot to make room. Here the empty space was designed. The rules could close the tie but allowed the people most exposed to the cost of closure to refuse.

That refusal did not leave the competition unfinished. It made the shared result the final result. A construct showed maturity not by driving comparison to the last possible distinction, but by recognizing that the capacity to distinguish does not always entail the duty to do so.
