1. The Official Said They Could Continue Before the Athlete Asked Whether They Could Stop

In the men's high-jump final at the Tokyo Olympics in 2021, Barshim and Tamberi had no failures through 2.37 metres, then each failed three times at 2.39. Even the existing countback rules left them exactly equal.

The official came over and spoke first.

What he said was not “I cannot decide” or “You should tie.” It was that they could proceed to a jump-off.

The first information the official supplied was that another procedure remained available. The construct held a means of continuing to separate winner from loser, and the official first laid that means before them.

Then Barshim asked a question.

He asked whether they could have two gold medals.

The official confirmed that this was possible.

That sequence is the whole key to this essay. It was not an official saying they could not be separated and therefore had to tie. It was an official saying that they could continue to be separated, and athletes asking whether they could choose not to be. The construct first explained that it still possessed the means to produce a winner; the athletes then asked whether they could decline to use those means.

This differs from the direction emphasized in many earlier essays. Measurements, records, eligibility lines, scoring tables and starting thresholds turned unsettled matters into actionable decisions. Here a way to continue was also ready: the jump-off. Yet the rules left the choice of taking that next step to the athletes still tied for first, acting jointly.

That is what this essay concerns. The construct has prepared the means of closure, and people may choose not to use them.

The episode turns a recurring question in this series around. Many earlier essays concerned how institutions turn complex situations into an actionable result. Here, another procedure was available, yet the institution allowed the athletes concerned jointly to decline it. What remained was not an uncertain placing but a definite, lawful shared first place. The absence of a sole winner is not the absence of a final answer.

Several popular accounts must first be corrected, because almost every stage of this episode has been misreported.

2. Several Accounts That Must First Be Dismantled

The first account to dismantle is that the Tokyo official proactively suggested awarding two gold medals.

He did not. The official first explained that a jump-off could continue; Barshim then asked whether two gold medals were possible. The athletes proposed not separating the result. The official supplied the option of continuing to separate it.

The second account is that the official could not tell who was stronger, so had no choice but to award two gold medals.

That is not what happened. This was not a problem of adjudicative capacity. The construct was fully capable of continuing to distinguish them. A jump-off was the mechanism: place the bar at a given height, see who clears it and who does not, and the distinction emerges. The construct was not unable to distinguish them; the athletes chose not to enter the procedure that would do so.

The third account is that the rules made an ad hoc exception because of their friendship.

They did not. The two men were good friends with shared experiences of injury. That helps explain why they wanted to share, but it does not explain the result's legality. Its validity rested on a rule that already existed. Even if the athletes had been strangers, or had hated one another, the rule should have produced the same result if they had made the same joint decision. Friendship was the motive, not the legal basis.

The fourth account, and the most important, is that World Athletics permitted shared gold medals only after Tokyo.

It did not. The provision allowing a tie for first place to stand appeared at least as early as the rules cycle effective from 1 November 2009, roughly twelve years before Tokyo.

This point deserves separate attention, because it is the case's institutional premise.

Under the 2008 rules, if athletes remained equal for first place after countback, they had to continue one jump at a time through the prescribed raising and lowering of the bar. Athletes had to jump in each round of the tie-break until the tie was resolved. There was no exit of the kind available today, in which everyone decides not to jump again and the tie for first remains.

The 2009 amendment introduced that exit: if no jump-off took place, including when the athletes concerned decided not to jump further, the tie for first place would stand. The new rule took effect on 1 November 2009.

Tokyo was therefore neither an innovation nor an exception. It was the use in 2021 of a rule written in 2009. That rule had lain quietly in the rulebook for twelve years. Tokyo merely let the whole world see it for the first time.

3. What Was Authorized Was Not Awarding Gold, but Leaving the Result Open

To describe this case accurately, we must see exactly what the rule authorized. It did not authorize an official to award two gold medals. It authorized something more precise and more fundamental.

The rule's legal structure is this: athletes still tied for first after countback should in principle have a jump-off. If no jump-off occurs, with the rule expressly including the athletes' decision not to continue among the possible circumstances, the tie for first place remains.

Look closely at that structure. The rule does not say that an official may award two gold medals. It says that in certain circumstances the tie for first remains. The Olympic medal system then awards a gold medal to each first-place finisher. Two gold medals are therefore a consequence of the placing, not a direct act of awarding an extra medal. The rule first preserves two first places; the medal system consequently gives each a gold. The athletes are not applying to an official for an additional gold medal.

That causal order determines where the power lies. If gold medals were the official's to distribute, this would be an exercise of discretion: the decision would belong to the construct, which could award or withhold them and decide how many. The actual mechanism is different. The rule stipulates that the tie remains in these circumstances. This is an automatic placing consequence, not an exercise of discretion. The official has no discretion here to choose one gold or two. He can only confirm the rule-prescribed placing triggered by the athletes' joint decision. The source of the decision therefore lies not in the official's discretion but in the athletes' shared choice. The official is the intermediate link translating that choice into a placing, which is then translated into a number of medals.

This is not verbal hair-splitting. It determines where the essay's subject lies. If an official awards the gold medals, the decision belongs to the official, to the construct. In fact, the construct preserves the placing of two firsts, and the athletes' joint decision not to jump again triggers that result. The decision therefore rests with the athletes.

That choice must be defined still more precisely, because it is easily described inaccurately.

The inaccurate version is: athletes can refuse a tie-break and keep their gold medal.

The accurate version is: all the athletes concerned who remain tied for the same first place may jointly terminate the tie-breaking procedure.

The difference is substantial. This is not a unilateral veto available to any individual. If one athlete alone decides not to jump and another wishes to continue, the one who declines forfeits the opportunity to take the higher place, and the willing jumper wins. Only when all athletes still tied for first jointly decide not to jump does the tie for first remain. This is a collective right to terminate, not an individual right to veto.

In Tokyo, only Barshim and Tamberi occupied that same first place. Nedasekau, who finished third, also cleared 2.37 metres, but earlier failures had placed him third on countback. It was not a choice among three athletes about sharing gold. The two athletes who were exactly equal, Barshim and Tamberi, jointly decided not to jump again.

4. The Athletes Did Not Rewrite the Rules. They Chose a Path the Rules Supplied.

We must guard here against portraying the athletes as rising above the rules, or the rules as ceasing to apply at this moment.

Neither happened. The athletes rewrote no rule. They chose one of two lawful paths that the rules already provided.

The first path: continue to a jump-off, allowing the construct to close the result into a single first place through further attempts.

The second path: all athletes still concerned in the tie for first jointly stop, and the construct accepts a shared first place.

Both paths had been written into the rules in advance. That declining further jumps could preserve the tie was itself an institutional provision, not a concession won by the athletes on the spot. They stood before two already laid paths and chose the second. Their choice was real, but they chose an option supplied by the construct, not one they had invented.

The essay's subject can therefore be stated precisely: the construct holds firmly onto the capacity for closure, but hands the switch determining whether to keep using that capacity to the people it judges.

Every part of that formulation matters.

The construct retains the capacity for closure. That is true. The jump-off is entirely its mechanism. Raising and lowering the bar, judging clearances and failures: these are all the construct's work. The athletes have no power to invent a tie-breaking method themselves.

But the switch that activates the mechanism is handed to the athletes. The construct says neither that they must be separated nor that they must remain tied. It relinquishes that meta-decision, the decision about whether to continue.

Those whom it judges receive the switch. This is the subtlest point. The athletes are the objects of the construct's judgment. It measures their performances and assigns their places. Yet at this one point, those objects of judgment receive the switch that determines whether the construct will complete its last step. The judge hands a decision to the judged.

5. One Institution, Four Occasions, Two Outcomes

The clearest evidence of this rule's character lies in the opposite results produced by its use in different competitions. The construct stays the same; the people choosing change, and so does the output.

In the men's high jump at the 2015 World Championships in Beijing, the institution was used to the end. Drouin, Bondarenko and Zhang Guowei remained tied for first after the main competition, and all three entered a jump-off. All failed first at 2.36 metres. The bar was lowered to 2.34, which Drouin cleared while the other two failed. Drouin became sole world champion, and the other two shared silver. The athletes chose to continue, and the construct closed the result into a single champion.

Tokyo 2021 was the case described above. The athletes jointly chose not to continue; the construct accepted a shared first place and two gold medals.

In the women's pole vault at the 2023 World Championships in Budapest, Tokyo's structure reappeared in another event. Moon and Kennedy remained equal after countback, chose not to have a jump-off, and shared the world title. World Athletics subsequently stated explicitly that the two agreed to share the title rather than continue with a jump-off.

In the men's high jump at the Paris Olympics in 2024, the same rule produced the opposite of Tokyo's result. Kerr and McEwen both cleared 2.36 metres in the main competition and remained equal on countback. They chose to continue with a jump-off. After further failures, the bar came down, and Kerr cleared 2.34 metres to become the sole gold medallist. McEwen later explicitly defended the choice to contest a single championship.

Place the four together and a pattern emerges. In 2015 they used the mechanism; in 2021 they did not; in 2023 they did not; in 2024 they did. The same institution, the same rule, four competitions, two outcomes. What determined which outcome appeared was not the rule, but the path chosen by the athletes standing at the fork.

That is the proof that Tokyo was not a one-off exception. It was no unrepeatable Olympic accident. It was a general, executable option within the vertical-jump rules. Paris supplies the most valuable counterexample: with the same institutional exit available, Kerr and McEwen chose to continue, turning the outcome from two golds into gold and silver. The construct remained unchanged; the choosers changed; the output changed from two gold medals to one gold and one silver.

Tokyo and Paris should therefore not be framed as warmth against cruelty, or friendship against competition. They embody two lawful normative judgments within the same institution. The Tokyo judgment is that the main competition has already left the athletes equal, and that equality itself is sufficient for them to be first together. The Paris judgment is that the construct should continue closing first place into a single value. The rule recognizes both judgments. Both are lawful.

Something deep deserves a pause here. The disagreement is not about who is right or wrong, but about what a tie itself means. The Tokyo view regards the tie as a genuine competitive result. If two athletes are exactly equal in the main competition and on countback, then they really are equal. That equality is the competition's true conclusion. A jump-off is an extra procedure artificially producing a single placing, rather than a means of revealing that the athletes were actually different. The Paris view treats a tie as a suspension awaiting resolution: the athletes are temporarily level, but the position of champion is inherently singular, so competition must continue until one wins. Both interpretations make sense. Their disagreement corresponds exactly to the question this series has kept asking: is equality a deadlock that must be broken further, or a result valid in its own right? The rule offers no single answer. It leaves the answer to those concerned.

6. A Man Who Endorsed His Choice but Opposed the Rule

The shared gold medal had supporters and critics. The real focus of their dispute is not whether the episode was moving, but who should possess the power of closure.

The supporting side is represented chiefly by official accounts. World Athletics described the result that day as shared success, and its year-end review placed it among the year's outstanding moments. Barshim's own argument was not that they could not be separated, but that the main competition had already demonstrated equal performances on the day and further competition was unnecessary. Tamberi emphasized shared experience, mutual respect and the value of sharing a championship. These interpretations all treat the act as an active choice, not a physical inability to continue or an official's instruction to stop.

The opposing side's central argument is that an Olympic championship should be closed into one person. Some commentators said at the time that a jump-off should have taken place, because Olympic finals should not share gold medals. Some athletics observers likewise expressed disappointment, believing that athletes should fight on until there was a single winner. Note that this opposition does not allege that Tokyo's decision was unlawful. It objects to the rule's values. It accepts the result's legality while arguing that the rule should not have this form.

One of the most substantial criticisms came from Tamberi himself.

A little over a month after Tokyo, Tamberi stated clearly that he did not regret sharing gold with Barshim. At the same time, he said that athletes should not have the opportunity to make that choice.

The statement almost directly strikes the subject of this essay. Tamberi endorsed the specific, personal decision made in Tokyo; he would choose that way. Yet he opposed the rule that handed this institutional decision to athletes. He believed the rule should not ask him to choose.

Those are two entirely different propositions. “I would choose this way” concerns how an individual acts under given rules. “The rules should let me choose” concerns how the rules themselves ought to be designed. Tamberi answered yes to the first and no to the second. Through his own example, he separated the propositions with complete clarity.

Someone who personally benefited from the rule and defends his choice simultaneously opposes the rule's existence. That alone shows that the real issue in this case is not the particular decision but whether the power to make it should be handed over. That is precisely the essay's subject: should the construct entrust its final step to the people it judges?

It is worth placing this question of the power of closure briefly within an earlier history, because two different roles of closure were already at issue when finish photography appeared. At Los Angeles in 1932 there were two cases of opposite character that must be kept separate. In the men's 100 metres, Tolan and Metcalfe both received official times of 10.3 seconds. The finish was extremely close, and officials carefully examined the photographic record. The official result was never changed to a tie: Tolan was first. A later claim often says that Metcalfe would have won under today's rules. That is a historically grounded counterfactual, because the old standard then required the entire torso to pass beyond the finish line, and Tolan fulfilled that standard earlier. But the counterfactual cannot be merged with the actual ruling. The stronger claim that the photography proved Metcalfe had won and the officials deliberately awarded Tolan the title lacks reliable support. What can be established is the controversy, the difference in rules, and the final decision for Tolan. At the same Games, the men's 110-metre hurdles presented the opposite case. Keller was initially placed third; after film review, Finlay was awarded third place and the bronze medal. Here photography did not manufacture controversy. It supplied the evidence that closed it. From the start, then, the construct's interpretive tools operated in two directions. They could be accused of failing to close a dispute that should have been closed, and they could genuinely settle a placing misjudged by the human eye. Those must be distinguished, not lumped together as “controversial cases.”

7. The Construct Can Look More Closely, and Can Also Choose Not To

To understand the weight of Tokyo's step, we must return it to the whole history of the construct's capacity for closure. That history has two directions: the construct continuously acquires stronger powers of closure, and the construct deliberately relinquishes powers it already possesses.

First consider growing capacity.

The Stockholm Olympics in 1912 used finish photography, which the IOC identifies as the technology's Olympic debut. This essay has not obtained enough material to reconstruct all the early system's parameters, so it assigns neither a frame rate nor millisecond accuracy to it. What can be established is that officials gained a recorded tool they could consult after observation by the human eye.

At Los Angeles in 1932, Kirby's two-eye system marked a qualitative change. Its camera ran at approximately 128 frames per second, a nominal frame interval of roughly 0.0078 seconds. Coupled with an electric clock, it could provide readings at the hundredth-of-a-second level. By Paris 2024, the official finish-line scanning system was reportedly capable of 40,000 recordings per second, a nominal sampling interval of approximately 25 microseconds.

The construct sees ever more finely. Its resolving capacity at the finish line now far exceeds the number of decimal places it publishes in official results.

There is also a crucial early phenomenon. The construct's capacity to see more finely does not necessarily mean that official results are published at the same resolution. In the 1932 men's 100 metres, Tolan and Metcalfe both had official times of 10.3 seconds, although automatic timing could yield readings at roughly the 10.38 level. One central function of photography was to establish order, not to turn every finer internal measurement into another official decimal place.

Today this is explicit. World Athletics' own photo-finish guidelines expressly allow rereading to the thousandth of a second for certain ties affecting qualification. Modern Olympic finish-line scanning samples far more finely still. It is therefore no longer tenable to say that athletics does not use thousandths because its machines are insufficiently precise. Not generally publishing official sprint times to thousandths is a choice of rules, not a camera's inability.

Two things need separating. Equipment can supply finer images than official results display, and rules use thousandths in certain qualification ties. But a scanning interval is not the accuracy of the entire measurement system: calibration, synchronization and interpretation still matter. Hundredths are therefore not simply the camera's ceiling, nor should every finer sample automatically become an official decimal place. Rules governing published times and placings decide which information has adjudicative force on which occasions. This has something in common with Tokyo: possessing more means of distinction does not mean always having to use them to the limit.

Now consider deliberate relinquishment, for which swimming provides the clearest example.

In the men's 400-metre individual medley at the 1972 Munich Olympics, Larsson and McKee were both timed at 4:31.98 to the hundredth. The equipment read further: 4:31.981 for Larsson and 4:31.983 for McKee. Larsson won gold by two thousandths of a second.

International swimming subsequently did something: it transformed the third decimal place from data capable of determining a placing into data that must not be used even if the equipment can read it. Its rules expressly require automatic times to be recorded only to hundredths and stipulate that the third decimal place must not be recorded or used to determine time or placing.

Swimming has a strong metrological reason for doing this. Pool geometry admits tolerances. For a 50-metre pool fitted with automatic touchpads, the standard length is 50 metres, with an allowed positive variation of approximately one centimetre. A top swimmer travels only a few millimetres in a thousandth of a second. A timer's ability to read thousandths therefore does not automatically guarantee that the race distances in two lanes are known accurately enough to support a fair comparison at that decimal place.

Caution is needed, however. To say that international swimming formally abolished thousandths because of pool tolerances makes a stronger causal claim than is usually acknowledged. What can be established are the two ends: rules explicitly prohibit using the third decimal place to decide times and placings, and facility specifications allow length tolerances. The policy change after 1972 is also widely associated with that race. But no sentence has been found in the meeting minutes from the time explicitly stating that thousandths were abolished because the pool tolerance was a particular amount. That rationale should therefore remain unresolved, rather than be presented as a fact supported by an original resolution already located. The often-quoted three-centimetre difference between lanes describes historical older specifications, not the present figure. Current tolerances are stricter.

Swimming and athletics thus exhibit two different forms of the construct's self-limitation. In swimming, the equipment has a third decimal place, but the rules deliberately deny it adjudicative force. In athletics, equipment and internal reading can extend to thousandths or finer, while official sprint times remain recorded to hundredths and placings are settled by the finish image. Both demonstrate that the capacity to measure and the legal force an institution chooses to give measurement are not the same thing.

8. A Reserved Box That May Lawfully Remain Unfilled

Let us draw the essay together.

Across the preceding sixteen essays, the construct repeatedly turned complex situations into names, records, placings and victories. Sometimes measurement and explanation remained apart; sometimes eligibility and definition left disputes; sometimes the institution chose not to make a certain judgment. What remained was not always a failure. It showed what a ledger could answer and what it left outside.

Here, for the first time, the construct does the opposite. It has not lost the capacity for closure. It holds the jump-off in its hands and can at any moment turn the Tokyo competition toward a single champion. It has deliberately and in advance legislated permission for an unclosed result to exist. It wrote a path into its own rules that leads to shared first place, a result not reduced to a single value.

That brings us to this essay's remainder, whose form reverses all the earlier ones.

Earlier remainders had different origins. Eligibility rules might exclude a name; surviving evidence might not separate causes; bodily categories might fail to accommodate continuous differences; a start reading might not explain how a movement began. Some involved limits of capacity, others institutional choices. They were not all things the construct wanted but could not obtain. Here the angle changes: the rules reserved a place in advance for the participants' joint choice.

This essay's remainder is what remains when the construct can close but chooses to make closure unnecessary. Shared first place is not the construct's failure, not an inability to distinguish winner from loser. Quite the opposite: it can distinguish them, and chooses not to require it. It is a box reserved in advance in the construct's own ledger that may lawfully remain incompletely filled.

Here a remainder takes another form. It need not be only a limit of measurement or a difficulty of classification; it can be space preserved when an institution deliberately stops pursuing a sole winner. The construct was not confounded by shared first place. It had reserved a lawful place for it. A result not reduced to one person can nevertheless be complete, lawful and final.

That acknowledgment carries weight. An adjudicative institution can easily treat a single answer as the mark of success, making a tie look unfinished. Tokyo shows another possibility: recognize the tie already produced by the competition and let those concerned jointly decline to continue. We need not infer that only powerful institutions dare do this, or that permitting ties signals weakness. The more important question is when further distinction matters, and when stopping together can also be a result an institution takes seriously.

It does so by handing over the switch. It does not decide for itself when a tie is appropriate. It gives that decision to the athletes still equal under the main-competition results and countback rules, allowing them to decide jointly. The construct acknowledges something here: when its own measurements have judged two people exactly equal, when the main-competition results and countback figures are identical, perhaps it should not alone determine whether an additional procedure must force them apart.

This contrasts with Essay 16. There, research recommended lowering the start threshold while the rules retained 0.100 seconds; findings still had to travel into formal revision. Here, a path already written into the rules lets athletes tied for first jointly decide whether to enter a jump-off. One case asks how a standard is reconsidered; the other shows how an institution reserves a choice in advance. Both concern who decides the final step, but not a simple opposition between refusing evidence forever and relinquishing all control.

Retention and delegation are different ways to handle the final step. Some standards need common application while remaining open to evidence and formal revision. Other outcomes already have an exit through which those concerned jointly decide whether to continue. The construct need not pursue a sole winner in every matter. It can also provide that an existing tie is a result, and that the next step is for the people it judges to decide together.

This construct can record every attempt made by two high jumpers, calculate that their results are exactly equal, and raise a bar at any moment for another jump to separate them. It did not do so, not because it could not, but because many years earlier it had written another path for precisely this moment, a path allowing them to say there was no need. It prepared every means of distinguishing winner from loser, then placed the final decision about using those means back in the hands of the two people the main competition and countback had not separated.

The ruler has not yet measured accurately. It is still measuring.

edits.before: 锦标赛那一场，通常没有受雇的兔子。运动员要同时考虑自己的位置，考虑晋级，考虑多轮赛制积累的疲劳，考虑被对手包夹和阻挡，考虑对手的能力，还要为最后的冲刺保留储备。世界田径自己描述锦标赛一万米时就直说，这种比赛不用配速员，运动员往往先保存体力，最后几圈才决胜。最合理的策略，经常不是从第一圈就把平均速度拉到最高，而是保留能量，等待末段提速。
edits.after: 锦标赛那一场，通常没有受雇的兔子。运动员要考虑位置、对手的能力、被包夹的风险，也要为最后冲刺保留储备；在设有预赛和半决赛的距离上，还会有晋级与多轮疲劳，而现代全球锦标赛一万米通常直接进行决赛。世界田径描述锦标赛一万米时也提到，运动员常先保存体力，最后几圈决胜。最合理的策略，经常不是从第一圈便把平均速度拉到最高，而是等待合适的提速时机。
edits.reason: 开场特指10k决赛通常无预半决赛，不能写其必经晋级多轮。

edits.before: 这是两种系统性不同的比赛。它们的目标函数不同，一个是最小化时间，一个是击败对手;它们允许的帮助不同;它们最优的跑法不同。生理学的数据和赛事的数据都证实，它们生成成绩的机制不一样。
edits.after: 这是两种常见而系统性不同的组织方式。一边更重视时间，一边更重视击败对手；实际提供的配速与信息条件也可能不同。它们可以使运动员选择不同的跑法，但并不因此各自适用一套完全相反的帮助规则。差别发生在同一个合法项目之内，也并不是每场比赛都整齐落在两端。
edits.reason: 两种比赛合法帮助一般同一规则，仅赛事实际提供不同；最优也非每种唯一固定。

edits.before: 一万米就是一万米。规则划分的，是一场比赛是否合法，允许哪些帮助，成绩能不能被承认为纪录。规则没有划分的，是这场比赛的组织目的，究竟是去追一个时间，还是去争一个名次。在公开的规则里，找不到一个叫做纪录赛的比赛种类，和一个叫做锦标赛的比赛种类并列。
edits.after: 一万米仍是一万米。规则当然区分世界锦标赛、奥运会与其他层级的赛事，也规定比赛是否合法、哪些帮助允许、成绩怎样取得纪录资格。但它没有因为一场以追时间为主、另一场以争名次为主，就为同一距离设立两套独立的世界纪录项目。这里讨论的不命名，是没有分设纪录类别，不是规则从未给锦标赛一个名字。
edits.reason: 规则明明有锦标赛类别，只是不分两套纪录资格；保论旨。

edits.before: 这就是这一篇要讲的东西。有两个构，它们在实际运行中系统地不同，而它们共用一个名字，共用一张纪录表。构自己在官方的平台上承认它们不同，却在正式的规则里拒绝把它们命名为两回事，然后用一张统一的纪录表，把两者重新合并。
edits.after: 这就是这一篇要讲的东西。有两个构，它们在实际运行中系统地不同，而它们共用一个名字，共用一张纪录表。构自己在官方的平台上承认它们不同，却在正式的规则里没有据此把它们分设为两个世界纪录项目，然后用一张统一的纪录表，把两者重新合并。
edits.reason: 结果是未分设非已证拒绝动机。

edits.before: 要先说清楚这个不命名的意思，因为它不是疏忽。一个构如果没注意到两种比赛的差别，那是它没看见，那不是这一篇要讲的。这一篇要讲的恰恰相反:这个构看得清清楚楚，它在自己的官方文字里，一遍又一遍地描述过这两种比赛怎么不同。它不是没看见，它是看见了，然后决定不在规则里把这个看见的东西，固定成两个名字。看见一个差异和命名一个差异，是两件事，而这个构停在了前一件和后一件之间。
edits.after: 这个不命名，需要说准。官方介绍已经承认两种比赛常有不同节奏和策略，所以不能简单说机构没有注意到差别。但这些描述也不能替代一份明确讨论过分设纪录类别、随后决定拒绝的会议记录。本篇能看到的是结果：差异被描述了，却没有因此成为两套纪录项目。看见差异，与赋予差异独立的法律类别，是两件事。
edits.reason: 不分纪录种类不证明曾明确考虑后拒绝；保可见组织结果。

edits.before: 这个设计很巧妙，而且它正是两个构能共用一张表的机关所在。设想另一种可能:如果规则把配速员定义成赛道外的辅助工具，那么有配速员的比赛，就成了一种被辅助的比赛，它的成绩理应和无辅助的比赛分开记。可规则没有这么定义。它把配速员放进了参赛者的名单，于是有配速员这件事，在法律上就不再是一种外部辅助，而是比赛内部的一种正常构成。一旦兔子是参赛者，雇兔子就和场上任何一个运动员领跑，挡风一样，是比赛内部的事，而不是从外面加进来的东西。这个身份的定义，一笔就把纪录赛和锦标赛之间那道本可以划出来的线，抹掉了。
edits.after: 这个身份安排，是共用纪录体系的一个重要条件。假如配速被列为禁止的外部帮助，相关成绩可能直接失去纪录资格；若另设辅助类别，才可能分开记账，两者都不是自动结果。现行规则把合规配速员放在参赛者中，同时限制套圈、轮换和场外介入。合法配速于是可以成为比赛内部的构成，而不是一出现就把赛事改成另一个纪录项目。
edits.reason: 若定义外部帮助可能直接禁，不必分账；限制身份并非唯一全部纪录条件。

edits.before: 这里还要留一个诚实的空缺。1954年这个成绩被认可，可以确证;它被认可的完整书面理由，拿不到。可以合理地推断，1953年和1954年的关键区别，是1954年两名帮手从枪响起就是同一场合法比赛里的运动员。但没有找到一份会议纪要，逐条写出基于哪些理由所以批准。所以结果是确证的，完整的裁决理由不能冒充为确证的。
edits.after: 这里还要留一个诚实的空缺。1954年成绩被认可，可以确认；本篇尚未取得它获批的完整书面理由。两年的一个可见区别，是1954年没有再采用1953年那种让布拉舍被套圈后接上领跑的安排，而不是只有1954年的帮手才从同一场比赛的枪响开始。这个差别为理解认可结果提供了线索，却不能冒充已经找到的逐条裁决理由。
edits.reason: 1953Brasher被套圈仍同场枪响开始，1954真正区别不套圈轮换；前文已有。

edits.before: 这种纪录型的商业赛，有一套典型的组织模块，可以归纳出来。目标时间预先确定;一组或者多组配速员分段接力承担节奏;主将尽可能长时间地待在挡风，节奏稳定的位置;赛事选择低海拔，快跑道或者平坦的道路;根据天气预报选择更合适的起跑时段;在名次奖金之外，设置时间或者纪录的奖励。这些要素不是每一场都同时出现，但在精英一日赛和快速马拉松里反复出现。
edits.after: 这种纪录型的商业赛，有一套典型的组织模块，可以归纳出来。目标时间预先确定;从枪响起就在同一场比赛中的配速员，先后承担不同阶段的节奏;主将尽可能长时间地待在挡风，节奏稳定的位置;赛事选择低海拔，快跑道或者平坦的道路;根据天气预报选择更合适的起跑时段;在名次奖金之外，设置时间或者纪录的奖励。这些要素不是每一场都同时出现，但在精英一日赛和快速马拉松里反复出现。
edits.reason: 分段接力多组可能误指中途新入，合法同场从枪响限定。

edits.before: 还有一个说法也要拆:节奏灯只能用于非锦标赛，绝不能出现在正式锦标赛。这个作为今天的规则命题，已经不成立了。早期的实务确实主要是在一日赛和纪录尝试里用，但2025年的欧洲室内锦标赛，已经正式部署了节奏灯。所以是否用于锦标赛，是一个赛事实施的选择和规则许可的范围问题，不是一个永久性的纪录赛专用的法律禁区。
edits.after: 还有一个说法要收紧：这种灯光设备永远不能出现在锦标赛。2025年欧洲室内锦标赛确实引入了Wavelight，但欧洲田径明确区分了用途：预赛使用部分赛段的参考灯，决赛在选手接近相关纪录节奏时显示纪录灯，并非照搬钻石联赛为运动员持续设定目标速度的直接配速。这说明设备可以进入锦标赛，却不能据此说两种比赛的灯光帮助完全相同。具体用途与赛事实施，仍然重要。
edits.reason: 官方EA明确不用直接配速，预赛参考灯/决赛靠近才显示；保不是永禁不偷换功能。

edits.before: 这个争论，没有办法用一个实验来了结。没有可靠的实验能说，节奏灯固定贡献了多少秒。顶级的世界纪录，无法做随机的，盲法的技术对照，因为鞋，天气，配速员，运动员的状态，总是同时在变。所以这道光到底帮了多少，和前面几篇里那些无法归因的问题一样，算不清。
edits.after: 这个争论不能只靠一个实验了结：实验可以估计特定条件下节奏灯的影响，却不能独自决定什么帮助应当允许。至于某一次世界纪录，鞋、天气、配速、身体状态同时在场，不能把它重新跑成其他条件完全一样的对照。我们可以用研究和模型提出有条件的估计，不能从最终时间直接拆出灯光贡献了几秒。精确归因的困难，不等于这个问题原则上不能研究。
edits.reason: 单次WR无法重跑不证明研究永不能估计灯光影响，盲法不可非研究不可。

edits.before: 七 三个人的账，和一张合并的表
edits.after: 七 同一个人，不同的比赛
edits.reason: This section uses Chebet's performances only, not three different people as inherited heading claims.

edits.before: 这是同一个人，在同一年，给出的一个近乎理想的自然对照。纪录环境下，十三分五十八;锦标赛夺冠，十四分五十四。中间差了五十六秒。不能把这五十六秒全部归因于状态，因为赛事的目标本身，就改变了最优的策略。
edits.after: 这是同一个人在同一年留下的鲜明对照：纪录环境十三分五十八，锦标赛夺冠十四分五十四，相差约五十六秒。它减少了把差别全归给不同运动员的理由，却没有控制天气、赛程、状态和对手。目标与战术显然值得放进解释，但不能仅凭这两个时间，就证明五十六秒中每一种因素各占多少。
edits.reason: 同年同人不是理想自然实验，不可排除状态。

edits.before: 女子一万米，切贝特又提供了一个更干净的同人对照。破纪录那场，比赛明确被设置为世界纪录尝试，用了目标节奏体系，成绩二十八分五十四;而2025年东京世锦赛，她本人夺冠的成绩是三十分三十七。同一个人，纪录环境二十八分五十四，锦标赛夺冠三十分三十七，差了一百零三秒。不能把这一百零三秒全归于状态，赛事目标改变了最优策略，这是核心的原因。
edits.after: 女子一万米又提供了同人的对照，但不是同一年。切贝特在2024年5月25日的尤金跑出二十八分五十四秒一四，那场比赛既以世界纪录为目标，也兼作肯尼亚奥运选拔。2025年东京世锦赛，她以三十分三十七秒六一夺冠，两次相差约一百零三秒。目标、配速和比赛展开值得比较，但还应同时记住年份、天气和身体状态的差别，不能把全部差额直接记在赛事结构名下。
edits.reason: 28:54.14为2024不是2025；103.47秒非控制实验，双重选拔/纪录目标不能纯二分。

edits.before: 而这一切差异，都被那张统一的纪录表抹平了。切贝特那个二十八分五十四，和一个假想的，在锦标赛环境里跑出的一万米，进的是同一张表，占的是同一个位置。表不记录这个成绩是在哪一种赛事结构里跑出来的，表只记录那个时间。于是赛事结构这个系统性地影响成绩的变量，在纪录表这一层，消失了。
edits.after: 这些差异，并没有因此变成两套纪录类别。切贝特二十八分五十四和一场锦标赛跑出的合法一万米，仍进入同一套项目体系。官方资料可以保留日期、场地和赛事名称，让人继续追查背景；但单看排序中的时间，它不会自动展开配速、战术与目标的差别。赛事结构不是在现实或档案里消失了，而是没有成为这张表独立分账的依据。
edits.reason: 官方表有场地日期，不能说只记时间不记场景；未单独分类而非抹掉全部信息。

edits.before: 用切贝特这个同一个人的对照，是因为它排除了一个最容易的反驳。如果拿两个不同的人比，一个在纪录赛跑得快，一个在锦标赛跑得慢，总可以说是这两个人能力不同。可切贝特是同一个人，同一年，同样处在巅峰状态。二十八分五十四和三十分三十七之间那一百多秒，不可能来自能力的差别，因为是同一具身体。它也不可能全部来自状态，因为跨度太大。剩下的那个最主要的解释，就是赛事结构本身:一场为破纪录组织的比赛，和一场为夺冠进行的比赛，即便是同一个人来跑，也会跑出差着一百多秒的两个时间。而这两个时间，进的是同一张表。
edits.after: 用同一个人的成绩来比较，是为了少跨一道差异，而不是宣称其他差异都消失了。五千米两场在2025年，一万米纪录和东京夺冠则隔着2024与2025两个赛季。同一个人的能力与状态也会变，天气和对手更不会因为名字相同就固定。这样的对照不能给赛事结构单独估价，却提醒我们，时间差不能只用一个脱离比赛目的的“能力”概念解释。读懂数字，还要读它怎样被跑出来。
edits.reason: 关键错误同年/同具身体排除能力状态；保同人对照价值。

edits.before: 把统计的口径定清楚。全球成年室外锦标赛，就是奥运会加上世界田径锦标赛;只数决赛，不数预赛和半决赛;只数正式的世界纪录。在男女一千五百米，五千米，一万米这六个项目里，把世界纪录的进程和锦标赛决赛的日期交叉核对，能确认的全球锦标赛决赛世界纪录，只有七次。
edits.after: 先把统计口径说清楚。这里的全球成年室外锦标赛，指奥运会与世界田径锦标赛；只数男女一千五百米、五千米、一万米六个项目的决赛，不数预赛和半决赛。奥运会男项从1912年数至2024年，女项从各自正式入奥数至2024年；世锦赛从各项正式入项数至2025年东京这一届。把今天回溯确认的世界纪录进程与这些决赛日期交叉核对，可以确认七场决赛创造了进程表中所列的世界纪录。
edits.reason: Editorial reconstruction, explicit event-specific dates and cutoff, and retrospective record-progressions rather than every historical ratification. Full paragraph; retain all examples.

edits.before: 按项目算，以这个项目进入全球锦标赛，并且世界纪录体系可比之后的决赛数为分母，这六个项目一共大约二百二十五场锦标赛决赛，其中产生世界纪录的有七场，大约百分之三点一一。
edits.after: 这是编辑根据官方历届结果重建的计数：奥运会一百一十场，世锦赛一百一十五场，共二百二十五场；七场约占百分之三点一一。奥运会女一千五百米、五千米、一万米分别从1972、1996、1988年起；世锦赛男三项与女一千五百米从1983年、女五千米从1995年、女一万米从1987年起。男一千五百米自1912年数，并非它参加奥运的全部历史。七场按今天回溯的进程统计，不等于当时曾获批准的总数：科勒迈宁1912年奥运万米曾先获批为世界纪录，后来布安那次更快成绩的日期更正至1911年，科勒迈宁的成绩便不再列入进程。
edits.reason: Editorial reconstruction, explicit event-specific dates and cutoff, and retrospective record-progressions rather than every historical ratification. Full paragraph; retain all examples.

edits.before: 而更尖锐的一个结果是:这七个全球锦标赛决赛的世界纪录，全部来自奥运会。1983年才开始的世界田径锦标赛，在这六个项目的决赛里，没有一例世界纪录。进入现代世锦赛时代之后，唯一的那个全球锦标赛决赛的例子，是里约2016年艾亚娜的女子一万米，而那是在奥运会创造的。
edits.after: 在同一截止时间与回溯口径下，这七场全部来自奥运会。1983年至2025年的世界田径锦标赛，在这六个项目各自正式入项后的决赛里，没有一场进入这份世界纪录名单。自1983年现代世锦赛开办以来，名单中唯一的全球锦标赛决赛，是2016年里约艾亚娜的女子一万米；那也是奥运会。

edits.before: 这个百分之三，不能单独证明锦标赛机制压制了世界纪录。因为还有别的混杂变量:气候，赛程的轮次，奖金，当年那个纪录本身的难度，训练水平，跑鞋，以及世界纪录本身已经越来越逼近生理上限。这些都会压低锦标赛决赛破纪录的概率，而它们和赛事结构无关。

edits.before:
One name, two competitions

A championship race and a record attempt may cover the same distance under the same basic running rules. They nevertheless organize action around different products. The championship distributes places among a fixed field on one day. The record attempt engineers the fastest possible time.

Athletes know the difference bodily. A championship rewards positioning, response, and the ability to win from an uncertain pace. A record attempt rewards even distribution, prearranged tempo, and conditions optimized around a target number.

Pacemakers are competitors

Conventional pacemakers enter the race, start with the field, and are entitled to finish. They are not external motors. Their planned withdrawal does not erase their formal status as competitors.

That fact distinguishes legal pacing from assistance supplied by people who join mid-race or are organized outside the permitted field. It also reveals an institutional fiction: someone can be a competitor in the rules while serving mainly as infrastructure for another athlete's result.

Bannister's mile and the race that did not count

Roger Bannister's 1954 four-minute mile used designated pacemakers who started legally with him. Confusion persists because an earlier paced attempt drew objections under rules and practices governing assistance. The famous race survived record scrutiny not because pacing was absent but because the pacers participated in an accepted form.

Modern record attempts industrialize what had once been a small arrangement. Teams calculate lap targets, rotating pacemakers divide labour, weather windows are selected, and wave-light technology displays the desired pace around the track.

Is the light external assistance?

Pacing lights provide information, not propulsion. The distinction sounds clean until one remembers that information changes performance. Knowing the exact relation to a target reduces uncertainty and cognitive load.

Rules must decide which information belongs to the environment. A visible clock, lap caller, coach, pacer, and light are all external in some sense, but not treated identically. Legalization does not prove that an aid has no effect. It declares the effect compatible with the event.

Three ledgers and one merged table

An athlete can have a personal best, a championship record, and a world record. These labels acknowledge different contexts, yet ordinary rankings often merge results into one list. A carefully paced meeting and a tactical global final then appear as comparable entries separated only by seconds.

The merged table is useful for identifying the fastest mark. It is less capable of describing the achievement. Winning a slow championship final may demand decisions that a faster paced race removes.

Finals rarely make ideal record attempts

Championship finalists face heats, uncertain opponents, medal incentives, and the catastrophic cost of leading too aggressively. Rational tactics can produce a slower race. The system asks “Who beat whom?” rather than “How low can the clock go?”

Other sports separate these products more explicitly: time trials from road races, qualifying from match play, records from titles. Athletics often lets them share the same event name and statistical table.

A difference the vocabulary resists

Calling both performances “the 1500 metres” is formally correct. It can conceal two constructs using one geometry. One turns the field into collaborators and obstacles around a time target. The other makes the time subordinate to relative position.

The record book captures whichever number is lower. It cannot, without additional language, say what kind of race produced it. The remainder is not outside the result but inside the name: two institutions inhabit the same word and are mistaken for one.

1. The Same Name, Two Kinds of Race

A 10,000-metre race aimed at breaking a world record and an Olympic 10,000-metre final bear the same name and enter the same world-record table.

Yet the two differ in almost every controllable variable.

In the record attempt, organizers can lawfully hire pacemakers, set target speeds for each lap in advance, use approved pacing lights, and choose a fast track, low altitude and a cool time of day. They can also offer a time or record bonus separate from prize money for placings. The athlete's task is to remain as long as possible in a sheltered position at a steady pace and devote every ounce of effort to approaching the predetermined time.

In the championship race there are usually no hired pacemakers. Athletes consider position, opponents, the risk of being boxed in and reserves for a final sprint. Events with heats and semifinals add qualification and accumulated fatigue; the 10,000 metres at modern global championships is normally a straight final. World Athletics likewise describes championship 10,000-metre racing as often conserving energy before the closing laps. The best strategy is frequently not the highest possible average speed from the first lap, but finding the right moment to accelerate.

These are two common, systematically different ways of organizing a race. One emphasizes time, the other defeating opponents; the pacing and information actually supplied may differ too. They can encourage different strategies without necessarily operating under opposite assistance rules. The distinction lies within one lawful event, and not every race falls neatly at either end.

Yet World Athletics' current rules do not divide them into two events.

A 10,000 metres remains a 10,000 metres. Rules do distinguish World Championships, Olympic Games and other levels of competition, and regulate legality, assistance and record eligibility. But emphasizing a time in one race and a placing in another does not create two separate world-record events at the same distance. “Not naming” here means not establishing separate record categories, not never giving championships a name.

That is this essay's subject. Two constructs differ systematically in actual operation while sharing one name and one record table. The construct itself acknowledges the difference on its official platforms, yet does not thereby establish separate world-record events in its formal rules, then reunites them through one uniform record table.

Essay 17 concerned a construct that had prepared the means of closure and chose not to use them. This essay concerns something adjacent: a construct sees a difference, has the capacity to name it, and chooses not to.

“Not naming” needs precision. Official descriptions recognize different pacing and strategies, so the distinction is not simply unnoticed. Yet those descriptions do not establish a meeting at which separate record categories were considered and rejected. What this essay can observe is the outcome: the difference is described without thereby becoming two record events. Recognizing a difference and giving it a separate legal category are different acts.

2. For the Argument to Hold, One Claim Must First Be Narrowed

Before proceeding, a claim that is too strong must be narrowed, or the entire essay will lack a footing.

The overstrong claim is that record-race and championship performances are fundamentally incomparable, that they are two different sports.

That goes too far. The rules and record system expressly treat them as comparable times in the same event. Championships can also be extremely fast, even producing world records, while record attempts still contain real competition.

The men's 1,500 metres at the Paris Olympics in 2024 supplies an obvious counterexample. There was no commercial pacemaker, but Ingebrigtsen voluntarily led at high speed and raised the pace of the entire race. Hocker won in 3:27.65, only 1.65 seconds outside the world record. A championship final with no hired pacemaker was transformed from within, by its leading athlete, into something approaching a record race. There is no impassable wall between the two.

What, then, is the version of the argument that genuinely holds?

Not that two performances cannot be compared at all, but this: under the name of one event, the rules allow two systematically different mechanisms of performance production. Directly treating a recorded time as an unconditional measurement of the same competitive ability therefore loses a crucial variable: the structure of the competition.

This version is weaker and much firmer. Physiological and competition data support the claim that the production mechanisms differ. World Athletics' regulatory system explicitly contradicts the claim of legal incomparability, because both remain in the same record system as long as they satisfy the rules. The accurate formulation is therefore not two different sports, but two highly stable structures for producing competition, with different objective functions, under a single legally defined event.

Only by holding to this narrower version can the essay avoid slipping into a claim unsupported by the evidence. All the material below supports the narrowed version, not the stronger one.

This narrowing also draws a boundary between the essay and a familiar complaint: that today's records are assembled from pacemakers, lights and fast shoes, and do not count as real ability. That is not the point here. This essay does not judge whether record-race performances count as genuine ability. Athletes really run those times. A pacemaker may shelter them from the wind, but they still have to move their own legs. The point is cooler and more structural: when two systematically different races share a table, a number in that table, considered alone, no longer tells us the structure in which it was produced. This does not belittle any performance. It identifies a variable the table has discarded.

3. A Pacemaker Is a Competitor, Not an Outside Service

To understand these two constructs, we must first see exactly what status a pacemaker has under the rules. That status is not quite what intuition suggests.

The current assistance rules prohibit pacing of several kinds: pacing supplied by people not participating in the same race; pacing supplied by athletes who have been or are about to be lapped; and pacing supplied by unauthorized technical devices.

Notice where the boundary falls. It does not ask whether you are pacing someone else. It asks whether you are a lawful participant in this race and whether you provide help from a normal competitive position.

The road-racing rules put it more explicitly. They directly stipulate that pacemakers employed by organizers are bona fide competitors and require them to start at the gun with the other elite athletes.

A lawful pacemaker is therefore not a staff member standing outside the course to provide a service. Legally, the pacemaker is a competitor; economically, a pacemaker. They enter the start list and, if they complete the distance, may in principle obtain an official result or even win. World Athletics' archives contain examples of athletes hired to pace who ultimately won the race.

This design of status is the institutional basis that allows the two constructs to share a record table. Because a pacemaker is legally a competitor, a paced record attempt remains a normal race under the rules, and its performance can enter the official records. The construct has not treated the pacemaker as an external tool. It has made the pacemaker an internal competitor. Performances achieved with pacing assistance are consequently no different in law from performances achieved without it.

That status is an important condition for a shared record system. If pacing were prohibited outside assistance, the performance might simply lose record eligibility. Separate accounting would require a further choice to create an assisted category; neither outcome is automatic. Existing rules place lawful pacemakers among competitors while restricting lapping, rotation and outside intervention. Legal pacing can thus be part of the race without automatically creating a different record event.

The three unlawful kinds of pacing define the boundaries of this status in reverse. An outsider cannot enter and pace because they are not a competitor. A lapped athlete cannot return as a fresh pacemaker because that creates continuing assistance beyond normal competition. Technical devices outside the exceptions are prohibited. Historically, the sensitive issue has never been simply that everyone agreed on a pace beforehand. It has been whether rotation, the continual introduction of fresh runners, or outside equipment can manufacture sustained assistance beyond the normal competition of the same field.

4. In Bannister's Story, the Rejected Race Was the Year Before

The subtleties of the pacemaker's status are clearest in Bannister's sub-four-minute mile. A widely circulated version of that story is wrong.

First, what actually happened. On 6 May 1954 at Iffley Road in Oxford, Brasher led the early stages, Chataway then took over the pace, and Bannister finally completed the last assault alone, running 3:59.4. The race was arranged within the framework of an official Oxford University versus Amateur Athletic Association meeting. It was not a training test timed solely for Bannister.

The mistaken version says that after the 1954 performance, officials formally investigated whether it had been a genuine race and approved it only after a hearing.

The materials do not support that version. It very likely transplants another incident into 1954.

The performance that British authorities actually rejected as not a bona fide race occurred in 1953, not 1954.

On 27 June 1953 at Motspur Park, Bannister attempted to break four minutes and ran 4:02.0. McMillen paced first, while Brasher followed a special arrangement: he jogged slowly, let Bannister lap him, and then returned in a relatively fresh state to lead Bannister again. The British Amateur Athletic Board subsequently refused to recognize the performance as a British record. Its central reason was that the event did not constitute a bona fide competition within the meaning of the rules.

That 1953 precedent explains why the organization of the 1954 race was especially careful. In 1954, both helpers were athletes in the same lawful race from the gun. The device of returning fresh after being lapped was not repeated.

Allegation and ruling must therefore be separated here. The allegation is that Brasher and Chataway had agreed beforehand to serve Bannister and did not necessarily regard winning themselves as their primary aim. The ruling is that no formal 1954 rejection by the British board on grounds of a non-genuine race has been found. On the contrary, 3:59.4 entered the official world-record progression.

The participants' own testimony exposes the tension. In a first-person recollection, Chataway said that after 1954 the board did not have the nerve to question again whether he and Brasher were genuine competitors. He then admitted with great frankness that, in terms of an actual intention to win, of course they were not.

That statement is crucial. In subjective purpose, Chataway and Brasher were pacemakers. They had no intention of winning. In legal treatment, however, the performance was not rejected as the 1953 one had been. If a nominal competitor has no intention of winning from the outset, the expression “bona fide competitor” acquires a semantic tension. Chataway's candour brings that tension into the open.

An honest gap remains. Recognition of the 1954 performance is established, but this essay has not obtained the complete written reasons. One observable difference is that 1954 did not repeat the 1953 arrangement in which Brasher let himself be lapped before taking up the pace. It is not that only the 1954 helpers started in the same race from the gun. That difference helps interpret the outcome without substituting for a recovered statement of the grounds.

5. From Hiring a Pacemaker to Building a Production System

In Bannister's era, pacing still involved a few friends helping out. Since the 1990s, the most conspicuous change has not been the sudden invention of pacemakers. It has been the institutionalization of record-breaking through the commercial meeting circuit.

Launched in 1998, the Golden League organized one-day meetings in Oslo, Rome, Monaco, Zurich, Brussels and Berlin into a continuous commercial system with large prizes, television coverage and elite fields. World Athletics' own Golden League record archive lists world records achieved at these meetings, including El Guerrouj's 3:26.00 for 1,500 metres in Rome in 1998.

A characteristic set of organizational modules can be identified in this record-oriented commercial racing. The target time is set in advance. Pacemakers who start in the same race from the gun take successive portions of the pace. The principal athlete remains as long as possible in a sheltered position at a stable speed. Organizers select low altitude and a fast track or flat road course, choose a more suitable start time according to the weather forecast, and add time or record rewards to prizes for placings. Not every element appears in every race, but they recur in elite one-day meetings and fast marathons.

One overstrong claim needs guarding against. Some say that record attempts in the 1990s all offered a uniform world-record bonus, such as a fixed US$50,000. That cannot be sustained as a general institutional fact. Rewards have several layers: the series purse, the individual meeting's place prizes, appearance fees, time bonuses, and record bonuses separately offered by organizers or sponsors. The latter items are often determined individually by organizers or contracts, and historical contracts are not necessarily public. The existence of various record and time bonuses can be confirmed. Individual events do not establish a uniform cash price list for world records.

Then came pacing lights. Developed around 2017, the system was first used in competition on 1 June 2018 and received full permission under World Athletics rules in 2020. Approximately 400 lights are installed along the inside of a standard 400-metre track, roughly one per metre. Software advances the lights according to a target time. An abstract lap-time schedule becomes a continuously visible spatial position moving around the track. The athlete no longer needs to calculate mentally how far behind the target they are. They need only follow the light.

What that light does deserves comparison with the door opened in Essay 8. There, the material condition of foam landing mats opened the possibility of the Fosbury flop. Here, pacing-light technology opens something else: it releases athletes from a task that had always belonged to them, judging their own speed. Before pacing lights, an athlete pursuing a record had to assemble bodily sensation, the pacemaker's lead and lap-time feedback to determine whether the pace was fast enough. This was a skill, a skill of self-perception. Pacing lights turn it into the simple act of following a light. What the athlete saves is not physical effort, but part of the work of judgment. Whether an external device should replace that judgment is precisely the core of the next section's debate.

One popular claim about the light must be dismantled: that it is an illegal electronic pacemaker exploiting a loophole. It is not. While prohibiting pacing by technical devices, World Athletics' assistance rules expressly list electronic lights indicating elapsed race time, including the pace of a relevant record, as a permitted exception. The present legal structure is therefore not a blanket ban on technological pacing. It is a general prohibition accompanied by an express exemption for specified visual timing systems.

Another claim needs narrowing: that this lighting equipment can never appear at championships. The 2025 European Indoors did introduce Wavelight, but European Athletics distinguished its role: guide lights during part of the heats and record displays when finalists approached relevant record pace, not the Diamond League's direct aid continuously setting an athlete's target speed. Equipment can enter a championship without the assistance being identical. Its actual use and event implementation still matter.

6. Should the Light Count as Outside Assistance?

Whether pacing lights should be allowed is a dispute with clear arguments on both sides, and World Athletics ultimately chose one. This section lays out both without adjudicating between them.

Those favouring permission say that the light merely supplies elapsed-time information visible to every competitor, equivalent to moving information from screens, clocks and lap calls onto the track and giving it a spatial form. It neither pushes nor pulls athletes, supplies no mechanical energy to any individual, and operates under transparent rules that treat everyone alike. This is the legal position World Athletics ultimately adopted.

Those favouring restriction say that a continuously visible target continually removes errors in athletes' own pacing judgment. It automates pace control, something traditionally accomplished jointly by the athlete, pacemakers and timing feedback. Some analyses particularly note that certain records achieved with pacing lights have extremely small lap-time dispersion, almost no fluctuation, raising a question about historical comparability. Earlier record-holders had to bear part of the task of judging speed themselves. Now that part is outsourced to a light.

No single experiment settles the whole dispute. Experiments can estimate the effect of pacing lights under specified conditions, but cannot alone decide what assistance should be allowed. A particular world record cannot be rerun with shoes, weather, pacing and bodily condition otherwise identical. Studies and models may yield conditional estimates; the finishing time alone cannot tell us how many seconds came from the lights. Difficulty in precise attribution is not impossibility in principle.

What matters here is the dispute's real nature. It is not about whether the light helps; it plainly does. It is about whether that kind of help still belongs among the competitive relationships that the sport ought to accept internally. This and the pacemaker dispute are two versions of the same question.

7. One Athlete, Different Races

Now consider the record table that combines the two constructs. How large are the actual differences?

The women's 5,000 metres offers one of the cleanest examples. Across the five 1,000-metre splits of Chebet's 2025 record, the total range was only about 7.22 seconds, and the fastest split was the final kilometre. It was therefore not a mechanical metronome maintaining exactly the same speed throughout. It combined a highly stable main portion with a deliberate late acceleration. This fits the structure researchers describe for record-oriented distance racing: slightly faster at the two ends, steady in the middle.

Compare it with a championship. The same Chebet won the women's 5,000 metres at the 2025 Tokyo World Championships in 14:54.36, while her world record was 13:58.06. Her last 400 metres in the championship win took approximately 57.6 seconds, against an average of about 71.55 seconds per 400 metres over the whole race. The closing split took almost 20 percent less time than the overall per-lap average.

The same athlete in the same year makes a vivid comparison: 13:58 in a record setting, 14:54 to win a championship, about 56 seconds apart. This reduces the temptation to attribute everything to different runners, but does not control weather, scheduling, form or opponents. Objectives and tactics belong in the explanation. Two times alone do not establish each factor's share of those 56 seconds.

The women's 10,000 metres supplies another within-athlete comparison, but not in the same year. Chebet ran 28:54.14 in Eugene on 25 May 2024, in a race designed as a record attempt that also served as Kenya's Olympic selection race. She won the 2025 Tokyo world title in 30:37.61, about 103 seconds slower. Objectives, pacing and the race's development deserve comparison, alongside differences in year, weather and form. The entire gap cannot simply be booked to competition structure.

But the differences must not be made absolute. We cannot say that record races are always even-paced while championships are jogging followed by a final 400-metre sprint. The Paris 2024 men's 1,500 metres is the counterexample already discussed. In some championships, a favourite unwilling to leave the outcome to a closing sprint deliberately pushes the pace close to personal limits. Conversely, world records often show a slightly faster opening, a stable main section and another acceleration at the end, rather than mathematical constancy. Academically, the more accurate formulation is that the probability distributions of splits differ between the two kinds of race, not that they form two non-overlapping types.

Those differences do not create two record categories. Chebet's 28:54 and a legal championship 10,000 metres still enter the same event system. Official material can preserve dates, venues and meeting names through which context can be traced. The ranked time alone, however, does not unfold differences in pacing, tactics and objectives. Competition structure has not vanished from reality or the archives; it has not become the basis for separate accounting.

Comparing one athlete removes one layer of difference, not every other one. The 5,000-metre races occurred in 2025; the 10,000-metre record and Tokyo victory span the 2024 and 2025 seasons. The same person's ability and form can change, and neither weather nor opponents become fixed by the athlete's name. These comparisons cannot price competition structure independently. They do remind us not to explain times solely through an ability detached from the race's purpose. Understanding the number requires asking how it was run.

8. Championship Finals Almost Never Break Records

If record races and championships really are two systematically different constructs, one consequence should be visible: championship finals rarely produce world records. Historical frequencies support that expectation.

First define the scope. Global senior outdoor championships here means the Olympic Games and the World Athletics Championships. Count finals only in the men’s and women’s 1,500, 5,000 and 10,000 metres, excluding heats and semifinals. For the Olympics, the men’s count runs from 1912 through 2024; each women’s event starts with its official Olympic debut and runs through 2024. World Championship counts start with each event’s official introduction and end at Tokyo 2025. Cross-checking those finals against the retrospectively accepted world-record progressions identifies seven finals that produced records listed in those progressions.

This is an editorial reconstruction from official historical results: 110 Olympic finals and 115 World Championship finals, 225 in all; seven is about 3.11 percent. The Olympic women’s 1,500, 5,000 and 10,000 metres start in 1972, 1996 and 1988 respectively. At Worlds, the men’s three events and women’s 1,500 start in 1983, women’s 5,000 in 1995 and women’s 10,000 in 1987. Counting the men’s Olympic 1,500 from 1912 does not cover its entire Olympic history. The seven follow today’s retrospective progressions, not every historical ratification: Kolehmainen’s 1912 Olympic 10,000 metres was initially ratified as a world record, but Bouin’s faster performance was later redated to 1911, leaving Kolehmainen’s mark out of the progression.

Within the same cutoff and retrospective definition, all seven came at the Olympics. From 1983 through 2025, no World Championship final in these six events, counted from each event’s official introduction, enters this world-record list. Since the modern World Championships began in 1983, the list’s only global championship final is Ayana’s women’s 10,000 metres at Rio 2016, itself an Olympic race.

About three percent cannot by itself prove that a particular competition mechanism suppresses records. Era, weather, the standing record, training and equipment all affect probability. Rounds, incentives and scheduling are themselves parts of competition structure, not factors wholly unrelated to it. The statistic can identify a pattern; estimating causes requires comparable races and attention to these changing conditions.

What it directly tells us is that world records were rare in the championship finals within this stated scope. To say how much higher the per-race rate is in dedicated record attempts, we also need a definition and denominator for those attempts. This one proportion does not supply that comparison. Cases already illustrate differences in objectives and strategy. The historical count adds context without completing every causal or frequency comparison.

9. Other Sports Have Given Different Answers

Athletics declines to name this difference. Other sports have faced the same problem and given different answers. Setting them alongside one another reveals the position of athletics' choice.

Swimming supplies an analogy that holds only halfway.

There is indeed a difference between record-oriented splits and championship-final splits in swimming. World Aquatics records can be set in different official competitions that comply with the rules; they need not occur in Olympic or World Championship finals. A World Championship final can also be deliberately swum at record pace. Swimming therefore also has the distinction between the goal of a record and the goal of a championship.

But swimming cannot be equated directly with athletics' pacemaker issue. Each swimmer occupies a separate lane. One cannot hire someone to swim a metre ahead continuously, sheltering the swimmer from water resistance and calling the pace. Swimming's other ledger arises chiefly from fatigue over heats, semifinals and finals, tactical observation and record objectives, rather than a lawful system of hired pacemakers. Swimming is therefore a good analogy for the difference between record and championship objectives, but not a structurally identical example of the pacemaker institution.

Cycling gives another answer that athletics has not adopted: name the two constructs directly as separate events.

In cycling's rules, the mass-start road race is one event. Position, team cooperation, aerodynamic resistance, breakaways and sprints are its substance. The individual time trial is another. Riders start alone at intervals, and the shortest time determines the result. Similar distances do not force these two events into one record logic asking who rode fastest. They have two names and two ledgers.

Cycling's treatment of outside assistance is particularly instructive. Because proximity to vehicles can produce aerodynamic gains, the governing body increased the minimum distance between an individual time-trial rider and the following vehicle to 25 metres, reducing the effect of the vehicle's airflow on performance. Here the institution recognizes a question with exactly the same roots as pacing lights and pacemakers: when does an external source of information or an object cease merely to facilitate competition and begin to alter the competitive ability being measured?

Cycling can support a proposal for separate ledgers in athletics, not a historical necessity. Cycling defines different racing forms as separate events; athletics has long combined world records, Olympic titles and tactical contests within one event. Preserving that continuity is an intelligible reason for combination, not a complete institutional motive established here. Nor would new categories have to erase old records. Several designs could preserve past performances while adding classifications.

The contrast still matters. Cycling shows that separate events for different racing forms are feasible, while athletics retains a different organizational tradition. Bannister's 3:59.4 belongs to mile-record history, not directly to the 1,500-metre progression; the two must remain distinct. Within each event, continued comparison between old and new legal performances is a real benefit of combination. Whether competition structure deserves further annotation remains debatable. The present system alone does not establish an explicit institutional bargain trading clarity for continuity.

10. A Difference Denied a Name

Let us draw the essay together.

There are two constructs. A record construct: organizers can lawfully hire pacemakers participating in the same race, set target lap speeds, use approved pacing lights, select favourable tracks, weather and times of day, and link financial incentives directly to times or records. A championship construct: usually there are no hired pacemakers; athletes face direct opponents and the goal of a title, with qualifying rounds added in events that have them; the most rational strategy is often to conserve energy, change position and wait for a late acceleration.

The two constructs generate performances through systematically different mechanisms. World Athletics itself repeatedly describes that difference on its official platforms. It says that championships have no pacemakers and that record attempts are usually paced races. It knows perfectly well that these are two different operational logics.

It has not thereby established two world-record events. Legal times produced under different organizing conditions still enter one event's record system. Describing a difference and giving it independent record status are different institutional acts.

That is this essay's remainder, whose form again differs from all its predecessors.

Earlier remainders included what the construct could not contain, could not calculate, could not reach, or deliberately reserved. Here the remainder is the difference itself, real but not classified separately for records. Competition structure systematically affects performance. The construct sees it, describes it on official platforms, and even has the capacity to name it, as cycling has done. It has not become a separate record category, and a listed time alone does not unfold it.

The difference therefore remains beyond the number. It helps shape races such as the 28:54 and the 30:37 without becoming an independent category in record ranking. The table can compare legal times. If we read a time as ability unaffected by context, however, we lose the conditions that produced it. The table need not explicitly claim that; a clear number can tempt us to treat it as too complete an answer.

This is another way of handling difference. A construct may recognize and describe it without turning every difference into a separate event or record category. That need be neither denial nor the only reasonable design. We can still ask what one name and one table preserve, and what readers must recognize beyond the table.

The three layers are worth distinguishing. First, record eligibility does not split the event into time-seeking and placing-seeking categories. Second, organizers produce different combinations of pacing, information, scheduling and strategy; not every race is the same. Third, legal times remain ranked within one event. All three can hold without replacing one another. Record classification is not a complete description of organization, nor is ranking a complete account of how a result arose.

Rules classify events, organizers produce particular conditions, and tables compare lawful times. There is tension between these layers, not necessarily a logical contradiction. The point worth retaining is that one measure can lawfully compare two performances without making all their conditions identical or ending judgment about ability and tactics.

This construct can hire someone to shelter you from the wind, install 400 lights to mark your pace, choose a cool evening and the fastest track, and write all this assistance into lawful rules so that your time enters the official records. In another race, it can remove all those aids and leave you to face opponents, fatigue and position alone. Official descriptions already recognize that these races often differ in organization and strategy. Yet when it keeps the accounts, it writes the times produced by both on the same line. It has created no separate record category for that difference. The difference therefore remains quietly in every second that the table cannot explain.

The ruler has not yet measured accurately. It is still measuring.

edits.before: 最短可能路线这个规矩，背后有一个和整个丈量方法一致的谨慎。它假设的，是一个会把每一个合法便宜都占尽的运动员，而不是一个老老实实沿路中间跑的运动员。为什么要按最坏的情况来量。因为纪录要防的，恰恰是那个占尽便宜的人:如果赛道是按路中心线量的四十二点一九五公里，而一个运动员切了每一个弯，他实际跑的就短于四十二点一九五公里，他的纪录就建立在一段不足的距离上。所以构不按平均的跑者来量，按那个能把路线跑到最短的跑者来量。它量的不是大多数人会跑多远，是最少可能跑多远。这和短程预防系数是同一个方向的谨慎，都是把每一个可能让赛道偏短的因素，提前堵死。

edits.before: 这不是说每一条认证的马拉松，都被断言物理上恰好是四十二点二三七一九五公里长。它是一个计量上的安全系数。它做的事情，是故意把误差推到无害的那一侧。因为测量总有千分之一的不确定，那么与其冒一条赛道实际偏短的风险，不如故意把它量得稍微长一点。宁可长一点，也不可短一点。长一点，运动员只是多跑了几十米，无伤大雅；短一点，成绩就建立在一条不合格的赛道上，纪录就不成立。
edits.after: 这不是说每一条认证的马拉松，都被断言物理上恰好是四十二点二三七一九五公里长。它是一个计量上的安全系数，故意留一点偏长的余量，以降低复测时发现距离不足的风险。千分之一是这里采用的防短系数，不是每一次测量都必然具有的固定误差。这个取舍很清楚：稍长会让运动员多跑，不能说毫无影响；但对于纪录资格，距离不足会使成绩失去赖以成立的合格赛程。宁可预留一点长度，也不冒距离不足的赛道上产生纪录的风险。这不是消灭误差，而是在误差仍可能存在时，选择怎样防范。

edits.before: 所以这两条线，和这个系列前面那些线，是同一种东西。第七篇里，十项全能计分表的系数，没有公开推导。第十二篇里，跑鞋的四十毫米，没有推导。第十四篇里，睾酮的阈值，不是从效应量算出来的。第十六篇里，起跑的零点一零零秒，不是一个稳定的生理常数。现在是这一篇，百分之五十和每公里一米，同样不是从生理里读出来的。它们是可辩护的标准化阈值，为了可复现的可比性而选定，而不是人类生理的常数。
edits.after: 所以这两条线，和前面几篇讨论的边界有相近之处。第七篇里，查到的计分材料没有交出每一个系数的完整推导；第十二篇里，四十毫米有公开的政策理由，但没有找到一个把它唯一算出来的定量过程。第十四篇讨论比赛资格条件，第十六篇讨论零点一零零秒警戒线，都不能把一条制度边界直接当成对每个身体通用的生理常数。现在的百分之五十和每公里一米，也是一组为了可比性而制定、可以解释和辩护的规则，不是从人体里直接读出的常数。

edits.before: 这几条线合起来，说明了一件关于构的普遍的事。构要制造可比性，就必须划线。而它要划的那条线，几乎总是划在一个连续的，没有自然断点的量上。坡度是连续的，间距是连续的，于是任何一条具体的线，都必然是切出来的，可以被解释，可以被辩护，但无法被证明它切在了那个唯一正确的位置上，因为那个位置不存在。构不是先找到了自然的边界再划线，是它必须划线，然后在一个没有边界的地方，切了一条。
edits.after: 把这几条线放在一起，可以看清这一类可比性规则怎样工作。坡度和起终点间距都是连续的量，数据能帮助我们判断差异有多大，却不会单靠自己宣布应该把哪些成绩放在同一栏。具体的阈值仍要联系比较的目的、可接受的差异与执行条件来选择。它可以被解释，也可以被辩护；这里没有找到一个仅凭生理数据就能唯一推出百分之五十或每公里一米的过程。构不是没有理由地划线，而是要把关于差异的证据，接到关于怎样比较的判断上。
edits.reason: Local slope/separation variables are continuous. This does not establish almost every construct has a continuous variable or that no uniquely defensible optimum could exist for a specified decision objective. As already acceptedEP12, no uniquely compelled answer from physiology alone is not no reasons or arbitrary. Scope the thesis to these thresholds, preserving the author’s philosophical argument.

edits.before: 这里可以看到路跑和短跑在同一个问题上的不同做法，而这个不同本身很说明问题。短跑防顺风，用的是一个直接测量的风速，超过加二点零米每秒就不算。这条线也是切出来的，二点零和二点一之间没有生理的悬崖。可是短跑至少能直接测那个风。路跑没法在四十二公里的整条赛道上，测一个有意义的风速，因为不同路段的风向风力都不一样。所以路跑退而求其次，不去测那个测不了的风，而去限制赛道的几何，让顺风没有机会在一段长直线上系统性地帮忙。同一个防顺风的目的，短跑用测量，路跑用几何，因为路跑那个要测的东西，测不了。构选择规范什么，一部分取决于什么是它能测，能控制的。
edits.after: 这里可以看到路跑和短跑在同一个问题上的不同做法。短跑的纪录资格使用直接测得的风速，加二点零米每秒是一条明确的线；二点零和二点一之间并没有生理的悬崖。路跑沿途当然也能测风，可是四十二公里上不同路段、不同时间的风向风力，不能用一次短时读数代表。于是路跑纪录不照搬短跑那一套，而用赛道几何作一层代理限制，减少一条长直线持续借助顺风的机会。这没有把天气影响消掉。同一个可比性问题，短跑主要用规定时段的风速读数，路跑则部分借助几何条件。构选择规范什么，也受测量与执行条件的影响。

edits.after: 国际田联后来分两步调整。2011年11月，摩纳哥理事会保留了既有女子路跑世界纪录，包括在混合比赛中创造的纪录，但当时仍规定，新的纪录只能在纯女子比赛中产生。拉德克利夫的两小时十五分二十五秒因此没有被永久降格。直到2013年11月1日起，规则才正式并列承认混合与纯女子比赛的两类世界纪录，形成今天沿用的平行结构。

edits.before: 而这里的争论，和跑鞋那一篇是同一种结构。跟在别人后面能减少空气阻力，改善跑步经济性，这个物理事实不是争议的部分。有争议的那一步，是把跟跑和配速这个连续的情形，变成一个基于比赛性别构成的，非此即彼的分类。建模没有测量拉德克利夫2003年到底得到了多少帮助，也不能确立她在一场纯女子比赛里的反事实成绩会是多少。所以主张两个类别的一方，和最初主张一个类别的国际田联，都承认条件不同，他们分歧的是，要不要把这个不同，固化成一条分类的线。
edits.after: 而这里的争论，和跑鞋那一篇有相近的结构。跟跑能减少空气阻力、改善跑步经济性，这不是争论的全部。有争议的是，这种比赛条件差异应当怎样进入纪录簿。现有模型不能单独给出拉德克利夫2003年在纯女子比赛中会跑出多少的确定答案。国际田联当初的“纯女子世界纪录加混合比赛世界最好”，和反对者主张的“两类世界纪录”，其实都区分了条件；双方争的是混合比赛成绩应得到什么地位，以及未来能否继续在那一栏创造世界纪录。

edits.before:
Accurate distance, ineligible geometry

A road course can be certified as 42.195 kilometres and still be ineligible for a world marathon record. World Athletics asks not only whether the course is the correct length, but whether start and finish are separated by no more than half the race distance and whether net elevation loss is no more than one metre per kilometre.

Boston is measured with professional care. Its point-to-point geography exceeds both record limits: the start and finish are too far apart, and the net downhill is too great. The course can produce valid race results, famous victories, and historically fast performances without producing a ratifiable world record.

The calibrated bicycle does not trust itself

Road measurement uses a calibrated bicycle equipped with a counter. The measurer rides the shortest possible route an athlete could take, calibrates before and after, and applies a short-course prevention factor. The purpose is revealing: the certification process would rather make a course slightly long than risk making it short.

This is not ordinary uncertainty. It is uncertainty assigned a direction. A result from an overly long course remains an honest burden on the athlete; a short course invalidates the event's claim to the distance. The construct protects its definition by placing the safety margin on competitors.

A geometric line, not a physiological theorem

The 50-percent separation and one-metre-per-kilometre drop limits reduce the likelihood that a course will receive a persistent tailwind or excessive gravitational assistance. They do not calculate the actual advantage in every race. A loop course can have unusual wind; a point-to-point course can have none.

The rule standardizes geometry because geometry is auditable before and after the event. It substitutes a stable proxy for a causal assessment that would be contested and weather-dependent.

Boston remains Boston

In 2011 Geoffrey Mutai ran 2:03:02 at Boston, faster than the ratified world record of the time. The performance did not become a world record, but it did not shrink into a meaningless exhibition. It remained a Boston course record and one of the great marathon performances.

This is what two ledgers permit. One asks who ran fastest on a historically specific course. The other asks which performances meet a standardized global record definition. Neither needs to erase the other.

What the rules leave unregulated

Road records control course length, separation, drop, timing, competition, and other conditions. They cannot equalize turns, road surface, temperature, humidity, air pollution, crowding, or tactical assistance. The standardized object remains partly open to place.

That openness is not accidental negligence. Complete environmental equality would eliminate road racing as road racing. The institution chooses which differences threaten the category and which differences give events their character.

Gun time and personal time

Mass races add another pair of ledgers: gun time, beginning when the race starts, and chip time, beginning when an individual crosses the start line. Elite placing normally belongs to gun time because competitors race one another from a common signal. Personal participation may be better described by chip time.

Again one distance produces two valid answers because the questions differ. A record line achieves comparability by excluding some accurate performances and selecting one clock. The line is necessary. What it leaves outside—Boston's history, a runner's personal passage, the texture of a course—does not thereby become unreal.
